title: Cardinals open training camp Wednesday as arguably NFL's most depressing team
content: The Arizona Cardinals will report to training camp on Wednesday, and this annual rite of summer signals the first step toward a looming NFL season. For the 2026 Cardinals, it signals pain. There will be a lot of it for this club and its fans in the coming season. We know this. NFL SUSPENDS ARIZONA CARDINALS EXECUTIVE FOR VIOLATING GAMBLING POLICY, LEAKING DRAFT INFO Most club observers believe this. Soon, when the team is actually asked to perform, the entire NFL will understand this. The Cardinals are poised to embark on perhaps one of their worst seasons — and that's saying a lot because, only last season, they suffered through a 3-14 campaign. So, the season ahead has the potential to make 2025 feel like the good old days. But why all the doom and gloom? The Cardinals, after all, have a new head coach in 39-year-old Mike LaFleur and he comes from a football family that includes older brother and Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur. He also worked under coach Sean McVay as the Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator the past three seasons and last year that team led the league in yards and points. The problem for LaFleur and the Cardinals is McVay's team plays in the same division. And the Rams, in the NFC Championship game last season, had a great offseason and could have the NFL's best roster. The Rams lost to the Seattle Seahawks in that conference title game last January. Then the Seahawks blew out the New England Patriots to win the Super Bowl. And, yes, the Seahawks will also play (beat?) the Cardinals twice this season because they play in the same NFC West. The remaining division opponent for the Cardinals is the San Francisco 49ers . Like the Seahawks and the Rams, the 49ers also made the playoffs last season after winning almost as many games (12) as the Cardinals lost (13). This division is brutal. The Rams have defending NFL MVP Matthew Stafford at quarterback. The Seahawks have Sam Darnold fresh off leading his team to the Super Bowl title. And the 49ers also have a Super Bowl quarterback in Brock Purdy. The Cardinals match up with ... Jacoby Brissett . Brissett has made himself a tidy NFL career the past 10 seasons. But he's a well-suited backup option in a league reliant on talented starters. Brissett started 12 games for the Cardinals last year because injuries sidelined starter Kyler Murray. The Cardinals had a 1-11 record in the games Brissett started. The Cardinals did precious little to upgrade their quarterback room this year. They signed plucky Gardner Minshew to play for his fifth team in five years. And they selected Carson Beck out of the University of Miami in the third round of the draft. So the Cards are likely to shuffle the starts among their quarterbacks because they'll want to see what Beck can do. Minshew has been around the entire offseason, and Brissett has the most experience of the bunch. Did we mention Brissett is kind of peeved at the team? He has missed the entire voluntary part of the offseason program — the one in which LaFleur introduced the new offense to the players who were present – because he's dissatisfied with his contract. Brissett, 33, wants a raise from the $4.88 million he's due to earn this season because when he signed his contract last season it was with the understanding he'd be the backup rather than the starter. Brissett's interactions with the team this offseason have mostly limited to acting as his own agent and trying to get a raise rather than, you know, learning the new offense, working on winning the starting job and playing well. The Cardinals acknowledge Brissett would be underpaid as a starter, but haven't so far offered the quarterback enough to compel him to sign an adjusted deal. That means the biggest drama surrounding Brissett on Wednesday is whether he'll report to camp on time or hold out. Perhaps he'll report and decline to work in what has become popular among some players as a so-called hold-in. The Cardinals also aren't certain about starting guard Isaiah Adams, who was arrested over the weekend in his native Canada on gun charges. He's charged with possessing a firearm obtained by crime, possessing a firearm without a permit and possessing a prohibited device. The gun, by the way, was an Uzi-style weapon. Most teams depend on winning games for their drama and entertainment. Arizona's greatest hope for 2026 could be tied to being bad enough to get the first pick in the 2027 draft. Such is your life, Cardinals fans. Follow Armando Salguero on X: @ArmandoSalguero

title: One Morning of Controlled Chaos in Maine
content: Photographs by Cassandra Klos Kathie Purdy doesn’t mind the phone calls. And there have been a lot of them—producing a sustained buzzing from her iPhone throughout the nearly two weeks since Graham Platner announced that he would drop out of the Maine Senate race. At one point, Purdy’s device grew so hot that she had to take it out of its case to let it breathe. But that was okay, she told me. As chair of the York County Democratic Committee, it was her job to help guide Mainers through this confusing moment. What Purdy did not appreciate was the insinuation—from other Democrats, from members of the media, from online trolls—that the process to replace Platner was somehow undemocratic. “This is what I’m talking about,” Purdy told me on Sunday, showing me a text from a voter asking whom “leadership had picked” for the nomination. It was early afternoon in the Sanford Performing Arts Center, and we were sitting side by side on the stage, looking out over the democratic process in action. Purdy rolled her eyes, exasperated. “Actually, right now we are conducting the caucus-type meeting in Sanford where the participants vote for a group of delegates,” she replied, using voice-to-text. “That’s the folks who’ll be voting for your Senate candidate.” Choosing those delegates was not a tidy affair. All morning, the room had been crowded, even though the state party had urged people to please consider voting from home. Mainers who wanted to be delegates and Mainers who came to meet delegate candidates and campaign volunteers proffering lists of allied delegates wove in between the aisles of red-upholstered chairs, shaking hands and arguing and complaining about various parts of the process in which they were taking part. Some struggled with the Wi-Fi. Occasionally, Purdy took the stage to make an announcement: We found a pair of car keys. Please come to the stage if they’re yours! Looking around, I imagined that, somewhere a few hours north, Susan Collins was rubbing her hands together with delight. Maine Democrats have failed to unseat her for nearly three decades, and there’s plenty of reason to believe that in three months they’ll come up short again. Zoomed out, the situation is, objectively, ridiculous. Maine Democrats nominated Platner despite a bouquet of red flags, including a Nazi tattoo and allegations of volatile behavior from past girlfriends. Now that an accusation of rape has toppled Platner’s candidacy, the Democrats who selected him are desperately trying to pick up the pieces of a race that might be their party’s best shot to take back the Senate. [ Read: Platner just made things harder for Democrats ] Cassandra Klos for The Atlantic Kathie Purdy, chair of the York County Democratic committee, organizes the vote for delegates. Cassandra Klos for The Atlantic A list of progressive delegates Yet the predictable conclusion—that the Democrats are once again in disarray —could not be drawn, at least not fully. Because ultimately, after all the hemming and hawing and arguing and complaining, the Democrats of York County sat down and voted. Totals were reached surprisingly quickly. Only a few hours after most attendees had arrived, Purdy was reading out the names of the 84 delegates and 17 alternates who would go to the party’s nominating convention in Bangor. Plenty of people were frustrated with the results, which, across Maine, were very good for Troy Jackson, a progressive former state legislator. Others had issues with the process itself. But “that’s democracy,” Purdy told me. So far, in Maine, it’s going pretty well. In the days after Platner announced that he was dropping out of the race, there was much consternation about how the Democrats would replace him. The party wouldn’t have time to conduct another primary. But if state Democratic leaders simply chose a new nominee on their own, voters might be indignant. Much of Platner’s support, after all, had come from people exhausted with the so-called establishment. The Maine Democrats had settled on a compromise: They would hold a convention on July 25, where 601 delegates would choose Platner’s replacement. Before that, each county would have an election to choose its portion of delegates. People were not exactly pleased about this. Whereas independent Mainers had been able to participate in the June primary, only registered Democrats were allowed to select the replacement nominee. “As an independent you’re saying my vote doesn’t count now,” one commenter on the York County Democratic Committee Facebook page wrote. (Much of the debate has played out on Facebook.) Another self-proclaimed former Democrat weighed in: “If you believe primary voters should choose nominees, not party insiders, consider whether your party registration still reflects your values.” Meanwhile, the county committee chairs—who, as volunteers, are paid precisely zero dollars for their work—were under a lot of stress. No one from the Maine Democrats returned any of my calls or emails. Purdy was begging people to be kind. “I would really appreciate some respect,” she wrote on Facebook. “Please stop the snark.” Joseph Zamboni, the chair of the Cumberland County Democratic Committee, seemed on the verge of tears when I spoke with him on the phone about where and when the nominating meeting would take place. In one of his many lengthy social-media updates, Zamboni tried to shed some light on the stressful decision-making process. “Nobel Prize–winning scholar Herbert Simon, whose work transformed the fields of economics, psychology, and administration, argued that people rarely make perfectly informed or ‘optimal’ decisions because none of us has unlimited time, information, or mental capacity,” he wrote. Cassandra Klos for The Atlantic Voters confer over delegate slates. Cassandra Klos for The Atlantic Voters wore stickers and T-shirts representing their Senate candidate of choice. Cassandra Klos for The Atlantic An attendee waits in Sanford, Maine. So I did not know what I would find on Sunday. But when I arrived at the auditorium in Sanford at 9 a.m. sharp, I was greeted with a dozen volunteers and a box of donut holes. In the parking lot outside, supporters held a rally for Jackson while, inside, dozens of people were already circulating. “Usually, when we hold a convention, we have to go begging” for delegates, one county committee chair told me, “Right now we’re fighting ’em off.” (In York County, more than 400 people had applied to fill 101 positions.) For two hours before voting began, people made the case for their candidates. Most were either supporting Jackson, a logger and former state-Senate president, or Nirav Shah, the former leader of the Maine CDC, who has since dropped out of the race. Jackson’s supporters said they liked him because his positions are most closely aligned with those of Platner, and he could, they believe, more easily inherit Platner’s movement. “We’ve lost a lot of momentum, and he has the best chance of keeping them engaged,” Reed Gordon, a 29-year-old delegate candidate, told me. The case for Shah was that he is slightly more moderate and might, therefore, be an easier sell for independent and moderate Mainers. Platner was too aggressive, Paula Busby, a 62-year-old from the town of Lebanon, told me. “We need to stand up against” President Trump, she said, “but we have to be measured.” Because the Democrats at these county meetings were choosing delegates rather than voting directly for candidates themselves, campaigns had made lists of allied delegates ahead of time and passed them out. Delegate selection was, basically, a proxy election: If you wanted Jackson to win, you’d vote for Jackson’s slate. This was upsetting to the Mainers who’d hoped that the people sent to the convention would be impartial. “This isn’t the way I’d have done it,” Julian Rogers, the former vice chair of the Maine Democrats and a delegate candidate himself, told me. “Rather than sort of coronating one person, I think we need to hear from these other people and have a little more balance.” Leah Macomber, a game developer from Saco, was also on the ballot to be a delegate, but she didn’t know anything about the slates until Sunday morning. “I was so pissed off,” she told me. “I’m a Mainer, and I don’t like being told what to do, or especially who to vote for.” So she made a T-shirt reading Vote Independent Thinker and wore it to the event. She also handed out lollipops labeled Susan sucks to try to stand out to voters. Neither she nor Rogers were selected as delegates. [ Read: Can Democrats salvage their chances in Maine? ] Cassandra Klos for The Atlantic The scene at the Sanford Performing Arts Center Still, even they were impressed at how quickly the process had been put into place, and how clear the communication had been from the state and county parties. It was preferable, some Mainers told me, to the 2024 process to replace Joe Biden, which was ultimately an anointing of Kamala Harris. And it was obviously better than powering through with a toxic nominee. The Democrats got a redo, a freebie, to try again and get someone better. “I was so disappointed when Platner dropped out,” Diana Garry, a retired nurse from Shapleigh, told me. “I was so discouraged. But now I’m thinking it’s a blessing.” By 11:15 a.m., people were in their seats, with their phones and iPads open, ready to vote. “It’ll all be electronic, so it’ll be fast,” Purdy said from the stage. I wondered whether she was tempting fate. The Democrats, after all, do not have the best track record when it comes to using technology to facilitate important elections . And when Purdy began reading out instructions for voting through the link sent via email—“To edit your submission, hit ‘Continue,’ then ‘Edit,’ then ‘Continue’ again”—a feeling of dread came over me. It was not assuaged by the line for technical support that quickly formed down the center aisle of the auditorium. But my concerns proved unfounded. The vote was going smoothly. An hour in, all of the people in line had been helped. Some Mainers had left; they’d see the results posted online. Soon, Purdy was onstage giving a 10-minute warning. “Can I get a ‘yay’?” she asked the now-dwindling crowd. “Yay!” people replied, more enthusiastically than I’d expected. She sat back down next to me. “I’m proud of what we’ve done,” she said, looking relieved. “We had a very short time to do something herculean.” Thanks to Sunday’s elections, next weekend’s convention will be pretty straightforward. The question now is whether Purdy and all the rest of Maine’s Democrats can pull off something similarly herculean in November.

title: Iran regime change talk resurfaces as Trump says Tehran 'wants to meet' amid US strikes
content: Elements of the Trump administration are again debating whether the United States should support the downfall of Iran’s government as the war intensifies again, according to a recent analysis. The analysis, published Monday by Financial Times columnist Gideon Rachman , says the discussion reportedly includes efforts to encourage an internal uprising and the possible revival of proposals to support armed Iranian opposition groups, including Kurdish factions that have fought Iran for decades. The question has gained urgency as the United States resumes strikes against Iranian military targets and officials debate whether continued pressure should remain narrowly focused on maritime security or evolve into a broader effort to weaken the Islamic Republic from within. Such a shift would present President Donald Trump with a consequential choice: continue using military and economic pressure to force Iranian concessions, or adopt the far more ambitious objective of helping Iranians remove the Islamic Republic from power. IRAN REQUESTS TALKS WITH US AS WHITE HOUSE WARNS 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE' Trump, however, signaled Tuesday that he has not closed the door on diplomacy, saying Iran is seeking talks behind the scenes. "They want to meet desperately to try and end it because they’re getting decimated," Trump told reporters during a Tuesday press conference. Asked what talks were possible, Trump said: "They want to desperately meet. And until they’re ready to meet in a meaningful way, we have no interest…" "Honestly, they haven't seen anything yet. We've been nice," the president added. US OFFICIAL SAYS JD VANCE MADE 'GREAT PROGRESS' IN IRAN TALKS, CALLS SNUB REPORTS 'FOREIGN PROPAGANDA' Trump’s comments suggest that military pressure and diplomacy remain intertwined, even as questions grow over whether some administration officials favor a broader strategy aimed at weakening or ultimately replacing Iran’s leadership. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), the military command responsible for American operations across the Middle East, said Monday that it struck Iranian military command centers , maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites and air-defense systems as part of an effort to reduce Iran’s ability to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz . The current military mission remains focused on protecting global shipping, Secretary of State Marco Rubio similarly said Sunday. "The only reason why the U.S. is conducting strikes is against assets of Iran that are being used to attack global commercial shipping," Rubio told reporters Sunday at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. "That’s what the objective of this mission is. That’s what it continues to be." Experts say the distinction between weakening the regime and making its collapse a formal military objective is critical. "Collapsing the regime remains a long-term goal using all forms of national power, but it doesn’t appear to be a military objective right now," Richard Goldberg, a senior advisor at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, told Fox News Digital. "This is Project Freedom — it’s focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, and any escalation is likely tied to that mission." Goldberg said some high-value targets, including nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, could be treated as exceptions because of their strategic importance. Pickaxe Mountain is a deeply buried and largely uninspected complex near Iran’s Natanz nuclear facility that U.S. and Israeli officials suspect could be connected to Iran’s nuclear program. But, he argued that most current U.S. operations are designed to advance maritime security rather than trigger a broader campaign to topple the government. STEVE FORBES URGES TRUMP TO KEEP THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ OPEN AT ALL COSTS "Where this gets confusing is when Central Command targets assets that are necessary for the Hormuz mission but could still provoke wider escalation, like dual-use infrastructure or certain leadership figures," Goldberg said. "That doesn’t mean the U.S. wouldn’t welcome the regime’s collapse, but that outcome is more likely to come through economic pressure, covert action and targeted decapitations over time." Any move toward regime change would immediately raise questions about who could replace Iran’s rulers and whether Washington could support a political transition without becoming responsible for another prolonged Middle Eastern conflict . One proposal reportedly discussed earlier in the war involved assisting Iranian Kurdish groups operating near the Iraqi border. Trump was open to supporting armed factions willing to fight Iran’s government, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal in March. The administration had contacted Kurdish leaders about possible assistance, The Washington Post separately reported. Such groups could provide Washington with partners on the ground without the deployment of U.S. forces. But they remain divided, militarily constrained and vulnerable to retaliation against their bases and supporters in neighboring Iraq. The central question is whether those groups are now positioned to exploit perceived weakness inside Iran or whether increased fighting amounts to another round of limited clashes. Majeed Gly, president of the American Kurdish Committee, said recent clashes involving Kurdish groups indicate a change in how some opposition forces perceive the regime’s strength. He cautioned that the violence should not be mistaken for a full-scale uprising, but said it should not be dismissed as routine border fighting. "What I’m hearing is, this is not business as usual," Gly told Fox News Digital earlier in July. "This is not like periodic clashes on the border. This is operations, and it seems to be deep inside." "What has changed is the perception of weakness of Iran," Gly added. "They are less afraid of the regime." The broader Iranian opposition remains fragmented among monarchists, ethnic movements, secular activists, left-wing organizations and other groups that disagree over leadership and the structure of a future government. That leaves the administration confronting the same problem that has complicated previous attempts to encourage political change in Iran: widespread opposition to the Islamic Republic does not necessarily translate into a unified movement capable of replacing it.

title: State Department rips revolutionary socialist Nicaraguan regime as far-left leader ends country's elections
content: Nicaragua's co-president is taking intense heat from the State Department after the socialist revolutionary declared that the Central American country he rules alongside his wife will no longer hold elections. The State Department on Tuesday condemned Daniel Ortega, who has retained power as the country's leader for nearly 20 years, writing his "declaration that under his family’s dictatorship Nicaragua will never again hold elections lays bare their true authoritarian nature and that, "Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo have abandoned even the pretense of popular consent." "Rosario Murillo and Daniel Ortega, along with their enablers, continue to threaten our national security interests in our region. Their facilitation of illegal immigration, deepening of adversarial relationships, and abuse of human rights and repression of Nicaraguans destabilizes our hemisphere, in defiance of the Trump Administration’s efforts to generate safety and prosperity," a State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "The Nicaraguan regime is an enemy of humanity." Ortega, now 80, said on Monday that he would cancel future elections to stop opposition parties from taking power in Nicaragua, which he classified as attempts to "seize the government." From the 1960s to the 1990s, Ortega was a leader of the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN), a radical far–left guerrilla movement inspired by Marxism, Cuban revolutionary politics and anti-imperialism. When the Sandinistas overthrew the U.S.-backed Samoza family dictatorship in 1979, Ortega emerged as a leader. The country aligned itself with Cuba and Russia during the Cold War, and nationalized banks and industry. NICARAGUA'S ORTEGA SAYS COUNTRY WILL 'NEVER AGAIN' HOLD ELECTIONS, SHUTTING OUT OPPOSITION Ortega assumed power after the revolution, and led the country until 1990. He was voted out of office, and accepted the results of that election. For the next 16 years, he led an opposition movement before finally being reelected in 2016. Since then, he and his family have rapidly consolidated power, including changing the country's constitution in 2025 to create the role of co-president , which Ortega then gave to his wife Rosario Murillo, who now addresses the nation daily. In 2018, anti-Ortega unrest gripped the nation, but was swiftly put down by the left-wing government. Some observers note that since retaking power in 2007, Ortega has softened his revolutionary tendencies and embraced a left-wing populism, and that he holds conservative social beliefs. "There won’t be any more elections here for them to try to seize ⁠the government and seize power," Ortega, now 80, said on Monday. "The days when parties backed by the Yankees and the Somocistas would return ‌to power are over — ‌never again." TRUMP EXPANDS CUBA SANCTIONS BEYOND US COMPANIES IN MAJOR CRACKDOWN ON FOREIGN ENABLERS The term "Somocistas" refers to supporters of the Somoza family dictatorship. "The Nicaraguan people have the right to choose their own leaders through democratic elections," the State Department's message continued. "The United States calls on the international community to join forces to demonstrate to the Murillo-Ortega dictatorship that it cannot expect to maintain business as usual with other nations when it is thwarting the basic tenets of our democratic hemisphere." Several of Ortega and Murillo's children occupy powerful government positions, including Daniel Edmundo Ortega Murillo, who is the government's chief of communications and oversees state-run media. Another son operates a radio and television station that props up Ortega's messaging. The couple's daughter, Camila Ortega Murillo, runs the country's state-backed cultural and fashion initiatives. Laureano Ortega Murillo, perhaps the most forward-facing of the children, controls the country's diplomatic relations with China and Russia, and works with those countries on investments and trade.

title: Nigerian pastor highlighted by Trump says he’s next after militia kills his relatives
content: JOHANNESBURG: A Nigerian Pastor highlighted by President Trump on social media, says that nine members of his family have been killed. The minister is an outspoken critic of the killing of Christians by radicalized Muslim members of the Fulani militia. Rev. Ezekiel Dachomo now says that the same militia has issued a death threat against him. Dachomo, is the regional leader of the Church of Christ in Nations, in Nigeria’s Middle Belt. The State Department and a leading U.S. non-profit Christian organization have demanded the Nigerian government take more action to stop what the State Department described to Fox News Digital as "a shocking level of violence against Christians ". AMERICANS TRAVEL TO PAKISTAN TO FREE CHRISTIANS TRAPPED IN MODERN-DAY SLAVERY: 'GOD'S HAND WAS IN IT' Multiple sources reported nine of his extended family were killed in an attack on their family compound in the Riyom district of Plateau State on July 12. A two-month-old baby is said to be among those killed. The attackers were allegedly looking for Dachomo, reportedly asking as they arrived "where is the father of this house?" adding, "Today, you will learn a hard lesson", before opening fire indiscriminately. This past week, he posted on X "A few days ago, Fulani herdsmen sent a threatening letter to me and to members of my church. It’s message was terrifying. They vowed to attack me and kill me soon, just as they killed nine of my relatives." The pastor continued, "I know what it means to stand before grieving families whose only crime was refusing to deny Jesus Christ." PASTOR FREED FROM CHINESE PRISON AFTER TRUMP RAISED HIS CASE WITH XI JINPING "Now they say I will be next. But I ask the world, what is my crime?" he posted. "Is my crime that I tell the stories of persecuted Christians in Nigeria, so the world will not forget them?" "The Islamist Fulani ethnic militia hate Pastor Ezekiel and targeted him because he is waking up Christians to the reality of what they are facing," Judd Saul, founder of Equipping the Persecuted, a nonprofit, told Fox News Digital. Saul’s organization works to end religious persecution in Nigeria, specifically aiming to end radical Islamist violence against Christians. By the end of 2025, Dachomo said he had to conduct over 70 mass burials of Christians. The burials have continued this year, with the post highlighted by President Trump showing the Pastor presiding over the funeral of some 20 believers. CHRISTIAN FARMING COMMUNITIES UNDER SIEGE AS US REPORT NAMES FULANI MILITANTS NIGERIA'S DEADLIEST THREAT Saul believes the killing will continue, saying "Equipping the Persecuted have documented overwhelming evidence that the Islamist Fulani ethnic militia are responsible for the vast majority of killings of Christians in Nigeria. Within the last week alone, over 40 Christians have been killed, and we have been warning that there are major attacks about to occur within the next few days." Islamic Fulani militias are by far the deadliest persecutors of Christians in Nigeria, according to a six-year study conducted by the Observatory for Religious Freedom in Africa (ORFA) just published. The study found that the network of Fulani militias is responsible for four times more civilian deaths than the two prominent Islamic terror organizations, Boko Haram, and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) combined. Boko Haram was previously allied to Al Qaeda , and ISWAP is currently linked to ISIS. The ORFA report shows that terror-related violence killed 79,323 people from 2019 to September 2025 in Nigeria. This equates to 36 people a day. Islamic Fulani accounted for 44% of the deaths — far more than the 12% that Boko Haram and ISWAP killed combined. Referring to the killings of Dachomo’s family, a State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "We have seen reports of the killing of nine Christians in Plateau State in Nigeria. There remains a shocking level of violence against Christians in the Middle Belt committed by Fulani Ethnic Militia." "The United States offers its sincerest condolences to the family and loved ones of those who lost their lives," the spokesperson continued, "We unequivocally condemn this heinous act. We urge the Nigerian authorities to hold the perpetrators accountable and take specific steps that will improve security for Christians." The spokesperson added, "During meetings with Nigerian officials in Abuja July 13–15, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, Frank Garcia, and the accompanying U.S. delegation stressed the United States’ grave concern regarding the violence Christians face in Nigeria and the need for concrete action. As President Trump has made clear, the United States will continue to work with the Government of Nigeria to protect Christians and advance religious freedom in Nigeria." The Trump administration has carried out a series of air strikes in Nigeria, aimed at stopping the killing of Christians. However, these have all been in the north of the country, and specifically against Boko Haram, and ISWAP Islamists . There has been no reported targeting of Fulani groups operating in the coutry’s Middle Belt. On this, Equipping the Persecuted’s Saul added, "We want the Trump Administration to put laser focus on the Middle Belt of Nigeria, and the Fulani ethnic militia." Dachomo told Fox News Digital, "We ask President Trump to stop the Fulani terrorists from killing our people in Nigeria’s Middle Belt and surrounding regions. These attacks against Christian communities have been going on for years and must be stopped. We need the United States to stand with us." In an X post, the Pastor pleaded to the President of Nigeria: "Tinubu, I am begging you in the name of Jesus, stop Islamic agenda. Muslim(s), they want to finish us. Christian(s) wake up, open your eyes." Quoting from the Bible Psalm 118:6, he added, "The Lord is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do unto me?" He concluded, "They may threaten my life, but they cannot silence the truth. They may kill the messenger, but they cannot kill the message." Contacted by Fox News Digital, Rabiu Ibrahim, spokesperson at the Nigerian Ministry of Information and National Orientation, offered condolences to the Rev. Dachomo but responded to the pastor’s accusations by saying, "The Government rejects attempts to portray the nation’s security crisis as a conflict between faiths. Such narratives oversimplify a complicated situation and risk serving the interests of criminal groups who seek to exploit existing fault lines, create fear and undermine national cohesion." Ibrahim continued, "The unfortunate incident involving Rev. Dachomo’s family is being treated with the seriousness that every loss of Nigerian life deserves. However, allegations regarding the identity, motivation and affiliation of perpetrators must be subjected to proper investigation and established through credible security findings. Nigeria’s security agencies remain committed to thoroughly investigating all attacks and bringing perpetrators to justice, regardless of their identity or background."

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton wrestled with major decision over Prince George's future: expert
content: Prince William and Kate Middleton wrestled with a major decision about Prince George's future. Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair's royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," first reported that Prince George received "no special treatment" and had to pass Eton College's entrance exams just like every other applicant. Kensington Palace recently announced that George, who turns 13 on July 22, will attend the prestigious boarding school where his father and uncle, Prince Harry, were educated. PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON 'CAUTIOUS' ABOUT WHICH ROYAL APPEARANCES THEIR CHILDREN MAKE: SOURCE "I had been reporting for a while that Eton was the top choice," Nicholl told Fox News Digital. "Although behind the scenes, I think there was a bit of yo-yoing about whether it was the right choice. You've got to remember that George will one day be king. And, of course, William and Catherine are thinking about the future. They're thinking about creating a very modern monarchy that feels relevant." "One of the things they were discussing was whether Eton was the right choice because it’s very much traditional, steeped in years of history and heritage and very much seen as an ‘old boys’ club.’ They weren’t sure if that was the right look for Prince George, or at least Catherine had her reservations." Nicholl reported that Kate was initially "on the fence" about Eton. On her "short list" was her alma mater, the coed Marlborough College. However, "it is understood that, from the outset, William was very keen for his eldest son to be educated at Eton." WATCH: PRINCE GEORGE EARNED ETON COLLEGE SPOT WITH ‘NO SPECIAL TREATMENT’: EXPERT Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment. "I think that on this one, William was pushing hard for Eton, and they did flip-flop over the issue of where to send George," royal expert Charlotte Griffiths told Nicholl. "Ultimately, it would have been a joint decision, but William always wanted Eton and thinks it's the right place for George. It breeds leaders." British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that Eton College holds particular sentimental value for William. People magazine previously reported that after William's mother, Princess Diana , died in 1997 at age 36, Eton provided stability for the grieving prince. He also developed a close bond with housemaster Andrew Gailey, and several friends from Eton remain close members of his inner circle. "Eton, being in proximity to Windsor Castle, enabled him to walk over on Sundays for tea or lunch with his beloved grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II ," Fordwich explained. "This provided him with a natural and casual way to receive guidance directly from her. No doubt Princess Catherine and Prince William are also anticipating staying close to Prince George in a similar manner." "Additionally, Eton is well-versed in protecting its students from media scrutiny with global elites in attendance," Fordwich noted. According to Nicholl, it was an easy choice for George, who was eager to follow in his father's footsteps. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER "I revealed in Vanity Fair that he had to sit [through] the assessments and the exams, pass all of those, just like everyone else who applied," said Nicholl. "There was no special treatment. And I think there is just a sense of great relief that the decision has been made, the place has been accepted, and Prince George will be starting Eton in September. I know that William's absolutely delighted, and George, I'm told, is very proud to be going too." "William and George are very close, and William will be making sure George is well-prepared," Griffiths also said in Nicholl's reporting. "They will hunker down and spend the summer together in Norfolk before the big move to Eton. It's an exciting time for them all." Eton College, founded in 1440 by King Henry VI, costs about $80,000 a year, according to People magazine . It has educated generations of leaders, including 20 British prime ministers. It's also where George will likely meet many of his future peers before he becomes king. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that Eton is known to teach its pupils "to be leaders, not followers." "George will make many friends for life," said Turner. "He will also see the value of the school playing a part in a collective of power-based individuals." LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Other royal experts told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales likely learned lessons from King Charles III's experiences when considering George's future. "The lessons the royals learned after sending the then-Prince Charles to Cheam and Gordonstoun, both of which he hated, are that balance is required, which William and Catherine are aware of," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "It's imperative that the decisions surrounding the futures of their children fit each child's character. George, from what we know, will relish Eton, and it is also near their home at Forest Lodge. Charles was sensitive and sent to a faraway school, which was a bad mistake." "Like both of his parents, Prince George is down to earth," Fordwich said. "From what I hear, he's a charming, well-mannered, kind-hearted, yet reserved young man." Royal author Robert Jobson told the U.K.'s Daily Mail that George is eager to take on the challenge. Jobson reported that George asked his parents if he could try boarding at Lambrook School, where he attends with his younger siblings, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8. "Prince William and Catherine have consistently tried to remove the unnecessary trappings of royalty while preserving the institution itself," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "They aren't pretending Prince George is an ordinary child," she said. "That would be absurd. But they're also avoiding the sort of visible favoritism that feeds the outdated narrative that royals believe different rules apply to them. It's modernization through restraint rather than reinvention." Schofield said William and Kate are raising George to embrace responsibility, not royal privilege. "William and Catherine appear determined to teach George that being king is about responsibility, not entitlement," Schofield said. "By denying him unnecessary special treatment now, they're strengthening his credibility decades before he ever wears the crown." "They understand that the monarchy survives because the public believes the family lives by many of the same rules everyone else does," she continued. "While George will never have a normal life, they seem determined not to manufacture unnecessary exceptions just because they can. That message is politically valuable and, honestly, good parenting ." While Kate may have initially questioned whether Eton was the right fit for her son, the Princess of Wales is now fully behind the decision as she and William continue to prioritize humility over privilege. "There is no avoiding George’s royal lineage," said Fordwich. "Nevertheless, he has been brought up with solid family values . There are zero accounts of him ever behaving in an entitled manner because he hasn’t been pampered at all."

title: Cyclospora outbreak: Is it still safe to eat at restaurants? Here's what to know
content: While federal investigators continue to search for the source of the ongoing cyclospora outbreak, many people may be wondering what they should order when dining out. Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite known to cause cyclosporiasis, Fox News Digital previously reported . The hallmark symptom of the infection is watery, "explosive" diarrhea that can last for weeks or even months if left untreated, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Cyclosporiasis is often caused by consuming contaminated produce. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) initially linked the outbreak to iceberg lettuce but later said the lab the agency used had produced a false positive . SCIENTISTS SAY YOU'VE BEEN THROWING AWAY PERFECTLY GOOD MEAT BECAUSE OF ONE COMMON MISTAKE When it comes to eating at restaurants , it's important for consumers to remember that "science follows evidence, not headlines," said Darin Detwiler, professor of food policy and corporate social responsibility at Northeastern University in Boston. "When people hear about an outbreak, it's natural to wonder whether they should stop eating out," Detwiler told Fox News Digital. "My answer is no. Consumers should approach dining out with informed awareness rather than fear." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The restaurant where someone becomes ill is not necessarily where the contamination occurred, Detwiler said. "Fresh produce often travels through a long and complex supply chain before it reaches a kitchen," he said. "A restaurant may receive ingredients exactly as they were shipped from an approved supplier, while the root cause lies much farther upstream – in agricultural practices, water quality, processing or distribution. That's why food safety is a systems issue, not simply a restaurant issue." The advice for going out to eat is straightforward, Detwiler said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Stay informed about public health advisories and recalls, and if you're older, pregnant, immunocompromised or otherwise at higher risk, you may wish to choose cooked vegetables over raw leafy greens while investigators continue their work," he said. "If you experience persistent diarrhea after eating fresh produce, seek medical care, as cyclospora requires specific treatment," he advised. The science is working, Detwiler said, but "social media demands certainty long before the facts are fully known." "Food safety is the top priority for the restaurant industry," the National Restaurant Association said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "In light of new information from the [FDA] that lettuce or leafy greens are likely the source [of] the outbreak, restaurant operators are coordinating with their suppliers to check their food sources and will make menu changes as needed." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Restaurants are governed by the FDA Food Code, along with state and local regulations, to help staff "handle food properly and make appropriate food safety decisions," the Washington, D.C.-based organization added. The bigger story isn't about a parasite, "it's about trust," Detwiler said. Consumers should be asking how the outbreak happened and what is being done to prevent similar outbreaks in the future, Detwiler said. No food system can promise zero risk, he pointed out. "What we expect – and deserve – is accountability," Detwiler said. "Public confidence is built through transparency, not perfection." "Ultimately, every foodborne illness outbreak asks the same question: Can consumers trust the system that produced and delivered their food?" he added. "How industry and public health leaders answer that question will shape public confidence long after this investigation is over." Khloe Quill of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

title: GOP gov claims swing-state opponent's agenda carries $18B price tag in explosive report as key midterm nears
content: FIRST ON FOX : Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo’s campaign estimates that Democratic rival Aaron Ford’s policy agenda would generate $18.1 billion in government and private-sector costs — burdening residents over four years — including nearly $8 billion in projected Nevada state spending — calculations Ford’s campaign sharply disputes. The Lombardo campaign report assigns estimated costs to 76 Ford proposals, combining projected Nevada spending with costs it says would be borne by businesses and the federal government that ultimately fall to the taxpayers and the public. Ford’s campaign argues the analysis invents implementation plans Ford never proposed and misclassifies some federal and private costs as consequences of his platform. The analysis projects $7.93 billion in direct state spending over a four-year term. Lombardo’s campaign argues Nevada could not absorb spending on that scale without higher taxes, new fees or cuts elsewhere, while Ford’s campaign says many of the projected expenses would not require new state appropriations. In a statement to Fox News Digital, University of Nevada, Reno professor Mark Pingle backed the report's findings, saying, "Based on a review of Aaron Ford's policy proposals, an estimated cost of $18 billion is a reasonable assessment." DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM? "The bottom line is simple: these proposals would require a record-breaking increase in spending. Before moving forward with a plan this expensive, Nevadans deserve clear answers about how it would be paid for, who would bear the cost, and what it would mean for the state's long-term financial stability. Regardless of political party, $18 billion in new spending deserves careful review and an explanation of how it would be paid for." Because Nevada has no personal income tax, significant new recurring state spending would likely require additional revenue from other taxes or fees, reductions in other spending, or some combination of the two. Ford's healthcare agenda, according to the report, carries the largest price tag at an estimated $4.25 billion for proposals addressing medical debt and predatory healthcare practices, including $3.5 billion for a proposal to cancel medical debt . The report estimates an extra $1.76 billion would be needed to expand healthcare affordability and access through Medicaid protections, workforce expansion and preventive care. ILLINOIS DEMOCRATIC GOVERNOR BUCKS TEACHERS' UNIONS IN SUPPORT FOR STATEWIDE CLASSROOM PHONE BAN Ford's K-12 education plan is estimated to cost $3.68 billion alone, including raising Nevada's per-pupil funding to the national average, expanding pre-K, providing universal school meals, and increasing pay for teachers and support staff, the report projects. The report estimates households would receive $17.88 billion in savings and other benefits while businesses, the state and the federal government would bear nearly the same amount in costs. Overall, according to the report, Ford's platform would cost roughly $4.9 billion for education, $4.8 billion for housing, more than $6 billion for healthcare, about $1.5 billion for energy and nearly $900 million for economic development. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Ford campaign spokesperson Prerna Jagadeesh said, "General Ford won’t be lectured by a governor who proposed a budget with a $335 million unconstitutional deficit and twice broke his pledge to never raise taxes." Jagadeesh continued, "The Lombardo campaign is embarrassing themselves and insulting the intelligence of voters by pushing this fraudulent report. The report lies about Attorney General Ford’s policies and assigns fake costs to programs that won’t cost the state a penny and will actually save taxpayers money, and incorrectly attributes costs to the state. Lombardo’s campaign rushed out this incredibly sloppy report in a desperate attempt to divert attention from a viral video of Lombardo abusing his position of power to evade consequences for breaking the law. Nevadans already know Lombardo has spent the last four years raising costs on working families and is offering no solutions to the problems they’re facing." The Ford campaign specifically disputes several of the report's largest assumptions, arguing Lombardo's team assigned costs to implementation measures Ford never proposed. Among other examples, the campaign says the report wrongly assumes Ford would spend hundreds of millions expanding the state’s Battle Born health plans and partially replacing federal Medicaid reductions. Ford’s campaign says his platform instead calls for outreach surrounding the existing Battle Born program and federal advocacy to prevent or reverse Medicaid cuts, not new state appropriations to backfill them. The Ford campaign also showed Fox News Digital its own fiscal analysis, arguing the platform could be implemented without raising taxes and with substantially lower direct state costs than those projected by Lombardo's campaign. Asked about Ford's contention that the report assigns costs to implementation measures not contained in his platform, the Lombardo campaign said it estimated what it would actually take to fulfill Ford's campaign promises, arguing that regulatory changes, enforcement initiatives and expanded benefits all require staffing, oversight or funding even when those costs are not explicitly identified by the campaign. Former Nevada state Sen. Ben Kieckhefer, who previously served as chief of staff to Lombardo , told Fox News Digital that Ford's proposals would require significant tax increases, saying the level of spending "is simply not sustainable for Nevada." WATCH: DR. OZ SAYS NEWSOM, OTHER BLUE STATES HAVE TURNED MEDICAID FRAUD INTO A 'FEATURE' "There is no realistic way to absorb costs of that scale without significant tax increases," he said. "Regardless of political party, proposals of this magnitude deserve serious scrutiny because Nevadans expect responsible budgeting, fiscal discipline, and a clear explanation of how these promises would actually be paid for." Nevada Democratic lawmaker Daniele Monroe-Moreno, chair of the Assembly Ways and Means Committee, told Fox News Digital the Lombardo report "uses fake math to lie about Attorney General Ford’s policy positions" and said Ford's platform consists of "common-sense policies that will save Nevadans money at very little to no cost to the state." The attorney general has also faced mounting questions over his spending during his tenure. In March, state records reviewed by Fox News Digital found Ford racked up more than $410,000 in travel costs since taking office in 2019, while local outlets reported he spent more than 100 days outside Nevada. A spokesperson for the attorney general's office said the trips were tied to Ford's official duties and campaign activities and were permitted under Nevada law. Ford is currently under investigation by the Nevada Commission on Ethics over allegations he accepted improper gifts or benefits and used his office to improperly benefit himself, according to documents obtained by local outlets. Lombardo is seeking a second term and will face Ford in November in one of the most closely watched gubernatorial races of the midterm elections.

title: Scoop: "Regime Change" sells 500,000 — on track for nonfiction bestseller of '26
content: " Regime Change ," the juicy exposé on President Trump's second term by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, has passed the publishing milestone of 500,000 units sold (hardcover, audio, e-book) in just one month. Publishing sources tell me the blockbuster is on track to be the bestselling nonfiction book of 2026. Simon & Schuster has ordered a seventh printing, bringing the total hardcovers in print to 460,000. "Reports of the death of the nonfiction book have been greatly exaggerated," said Matt Latimer of the Javelin agency, which represents Haberman. But this is a rare feat. "This doesn't necessarily mean that Trump books are back," said Keith Urbahn , Latimer's co-founder at Javelin. "It's still uphill sledding for political books." "This book is different," he added. "Maggie and Swan pierced the veil of a White House that has been pretty locked down on scoops and scenes. 'Regime Change' is a unicorn of publishing. It goes well beyond political circles to people who are hungry for a narrative and frame to make sense of Trump 2.0. Even Trump and his team aren't disputing the facts." Zoom in: The book has been No. 1 on the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list for three weeks running. "Regime Change" has also been No. 1 in Canada, Australia and the Netherlands, and No. 2 in the UK. The big picture: Just two months ago, a Wall Street Journal article declared that "Dad Books" — including books about politics and current affairs, as well as biographies and histories — "are a dying breed." The proximate causes: audiobooks, Substack newsletters, Netflix documentaries, YouTube videos and podcasts. Upcoming author appearances .

title: Campus conflict exposed at the core of SJSU's messy fight vs Trump admin over volleyball scandal
content: EXCLUSIVE : Since the start of 2026, San Jose State University (SJSU) has had a donor ask to be removed from a key list in protest, a parade of pro-trans activists shout demands at administrators in an organized meeting, and assault allegations surface against its head volleyball coach. Fox News Digital has obtained exclusive video and documents from independent verified sources, and emails via a public records request that reveal a university paralyzed and divided over its 2024 volleyball scandal involving Blaire Fleming and Brooke Slusser. INSIDE THE FALLOUT OF THE SJSU VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL: ‘THIS IS AN OBVIOUS PROBLEM’ SJSU and the California State University system (CSU) are currently waging a lawsuit against President Donald Trump's administration to assert the school followed the law in its handling of the scandal, and to reject the findings of a federal investigation. The lawsuit may set a national precedent for Title IX enforcement for public universities going forward, as SJSU faces internal and external friction. On Feb. 26, a town hall was held in the SJSU engineering building. A copy of an invitation obtained by Fox News Digital included the title "Trans Gender Rights Town Hall with SJSU Administration" in big, bold all-caps letters. The subject to be discussed was SJSU's response to the Trump administration's resolution proposal. "Please come to a Town Hall with SJSU’s President and top administration, and tell them they must stand up for our transgender students," it wrote. A sign-up form said that SJSU President Cynthia Teniente-Matson would be in attendance. But she was not there, as seen in footage of the meeting provided to Fox News Digital from an independent verified source. Just two administrators were seen in attendance. One by one, pro-trans activists came up to a lectern and unleashed emotionally charged rants, often directed at the two administrators. At one point, one of the speakers expressed being "glad" that the meeting was being recorded, so it could be sent to Teniente-Matson later. A separate video camera was seen recording the event, in the obtained footage. Harsh orders were delivered to the two administrators there to tell their superiors not to accept the resolution agreement. "It is about protecting all of the oppressed communities here on campus, doing more than lip service, and doing your job of going to the CSU and saying, 'We will not capitulate to violent transphobic demands or any other oppressive demands that come from this heinous, heinous current administration at all!'" one person exclaimed. At one point in the meeting, a speaker declared, "It is your job to get in the room with Cynthia to make sure that she conveys all of this information to the relevant people. This isn’t a compromise. We’re talking about people’s human rights. We’re talking about enforcing segregation on our campus. That’s not something we can capitulate to. That’s not something negotiable." Teniente-Matson's absence at the meeting was a frequent point of outrage for multiple speakers. One of them shouted, "We heard from administration, ‘We’re doing our best. We’re doing what we can with the cards we’ve been given.’ Bull f—ing s—. Bulls—. No. Uh-uh ... Your best isn’t f—ing adequate. Like, just point blank. You can do the best. You can say it’s your best. It’s not adequate. People are harmed. People are scared." Another cried, "45 minutes. They handed over 45 minutes for this issue, 45 minutes. And they didn’t even give us 45. They gave us zero because two of these seats are f—ing empty right now. They didn’t even show up. Gave a bulls— email about two hours before the event started." Just eight days later, on March 6, SJSU and the entire CSU system announced they were suing the federal government to challenge the ED investigation and its findings. In her announcement of the lawsuit, Teniente-Matson wrote, "Our support for the LGBTQ members of our community, who have experienced threats and harms over the last several years remains unwavering... We’ve heard the fear and anxiety that it has created and recognize that waiting for the university’s response has been difficult at a time already filled with uncertainty." Administrator inboxes received responses from faculty, students and alumni, with reactions to the news, as seen in public records obtained by Fox News Digital. "I attended the town hall and heard the students anxiety and pain," one professor wrote to Teniente-Matson. "Thank you for showing the nation how to fight with dignity." Another SJSU employee sent an email to Vice President of University Advancement Judy Nagai, voicing concerns. That email was then flagged to other administrators. "It’s worth noting that the university’s communications don’t directly address concerns about fairness and privacy for women," the email wrote. "It’s easy to see how the messaging might come across as ambiguous or even dismissive of women’s rights for some, especially given the strong emphasis on inclusivity for LGBTQ students." Nagai forwarded that email to Teniente-Matson and other admins and wrote, "[redacted] replied with a lengthy response below. He will likely attend the alumni board meeting." Nagai later sent out a mass email, advising admins on how to handle individuals with concerns about the lawsuit. "If you receive any questions, comments, or concerns about this topic from alumni, volunteers, and donors, please connect with [Associate Vice President of Strategy & Campaigns Manaf Mansure] so he can track and assess an appropriate response with guidance from UMC and university leadership," Nagai wrote. "This includes all forms of communication -- phone calls, emails, texts and mobile messages and in-person conversations." A month before the town hall, and five days before the U.S. Department of Education (ED) announced it had determined SJSU violated Title IX, a donor sent an email to the school that was forwarded to Nagai. It was in response to an announcement about the school's dedicated philanthropy partner, The Tower Foundation. The subject line read "no more giving to SJSU." "Judy, please remove me from your list. I am totally against trans athletes playing in women’s sports. I am fine with trans people but the women who work so hard to advance their careers in athletics are getting robbed of their chances to rank and be recognized," the donor wrote. "I was on the Tower Foundation for years and was a supporter. I wrote to the Chair and asked him to let the President know my feelings about this. A separate trans program is fine for me and makes sense. Title IX, in my view was to advance and protect women." SJSU has addressed the donor's email in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The University takes very seriously its legal obligations under Title IX. The University has followed and continues to follow the law," the statement wrote. The email was provided to Fox News Digital in response to a public records request. The identity of the person who sent the email was redacted by SJSU. Less than a week later on Jan. 28, ED announced that SJSU was found in violation of Title IX after conducting a nearly-year-long investigation into the volleyball scandal. ED gave SJSU an ultimatum to agree to resolve the violation that would have included an apology to players and changes to official program records, but no monetary fines. But later that same day, SJSU’s Risk Manager Karen Vogler sent an email to a finance colleague, about a potentially different risk. "It doesn't appear that SJSU will face any fines or monetary penalties as a result of the U.S. Department of Education's investigation. However, claims/litigation may increase given their findings that the Title IX violation goes back to 2022," Vogler wrote. Over the last two weeks, Fox News Digital has reported on decades-old allegations against the coach who oversaw the controversial 2024 team. One of Kress's former players at Fairfield University sent a letter to SJSU in October 2024, near the height of the scandal's national exposure, with a letter that included allegations Kress attacked her in a hotel room in 1998. The former player made her first public statements on Tuesday, since the allegations first surfaced on July 7 in a Fox News Digital report. "SJSU has known I feared for the safety of the women in the program since October of 2024 and yet they have allowed Todd to continue to coach and travel with the team," she told Fox News Digital on the condition of anonymity. "I informed both Fairfield and SJSU of my 1998 encounter with Todd after reading accounts of young women on the 2024 SJSU team describing his intimidation, coercive, and manipulative behaviors." SJSU is in this predicament three years after Slusser was allegedly convinced by Kress to move into an apartment with Fleming. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM The alleged treatment of Slusser, and every other player on those teams from 2022-24, would be codified in ED's 45-page findings were SJSU to agree to the resolution agreement. But SJSU and CSU are seeking to have the entire investigation vacated, as stated in a copy of their lawsuit obtained by Fox News Digital. CSU and the federal government filed a joint proposed order on March 27, 2026, that would prevent ED from using its findings to immediately disrupt federal funding. Meanwhile, Slusser and former SJSU associate head coach Melissa Batie-Smoose continue to wage their own individual lawsuits against the institutions. Slusser's lawsuit is set to soon receive a decision on motions to dismiss, after a federal judge delayed final ruling on the Title IX charges in the lawsuit until after the recent Supreme Court cases on trans athletes in women's sports. All nine justices in the cases, all nine justices unanimously agreed that federal Title IX law does not prohibit states from maintaining separate sports teams for biological females or from excluding transgender girls and women from women’s and girls' sports teams. The unanimous interpretation of Title IX could prove to strengthen Slusser's chances of advancing past motions to dismiss, but does not guarantee it. Meanwhile, Batie-Smoose is engaged in a wrongful termination lawsuit with SJSU. Oral arguments for that case are scheduled for Aug. 21.

title: Hundreds of illegitimate donation bins scattered across San Jose
content: Hundreds of donation bins in San Jose are misleading donors, operating without permission, and taking donations away from charities that serve the community, city leaders and local nonprofits said Tuesday. Goodwill Silicon Valley estimates there are at least 300 illegitimate bins scattered throughout San Jose. Goodwill said most are placed illegally in parking lots, near schools and on private property – collecting donations people believe are staying local. “We’ve got some bad actors out there that are trying to take advantage of our community,” San Jose Councilmember Michael Mulcahy said. City leaders said many of the bins aren’t connected to legitimate charities at all. “We started doing some research and realized that these are not authorized,” Mulcahy said. “I called property owners all over the city, the district that I represent, and nobody had given any permission to put these out.” Goodwill said many of the bins are operated by for-profit companies that sell donated items in bulk or overseas. The bins also often become magnets for illegal dumping, graffiti and overflowing trash. San Jose passed an ordinance years ago limiting donation bins and requiring permits, but officials said enforcement has lagged, allowing unapproved bins to multiply. They said it’s now unclear whether any permitted donation bins are even operating in the city, making it difficult for donors to know which bins they can trust. Goodwill is working with the city on possible solutions. In the meantime, Goodwill said if people are planning to donate, the safest bet is to take their items directly to a nonprofit’s staffed donation center or retail location.

title: Exclusive: Nvidia's Jensen Huang defends Chinese AI amid Kimi panic
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang believes America has nothing to fear from China's open-source AI models — and everything to fear from the growing campaign to ban them. "These Chinese models are excellent," Huang told Axios' Mike Allen on Tuesday in an exclusive interview for our "Behind the Curtain" video series. "Open-source models that are excellent should be used." Why it matters: The world's top AI chipmaker says American companies should "absolutely" be allowed to use Chinese models — a direct challenge to Trump officials and the U.S. labs lobbying Washington to shut them out. Among them are Nvidia's own customers, OpenAI and Anthropic , which have accused Chinese rivals of siphoning capabilities from their models and warned that Beijing's open-source surge threatens America's AI lead. Huang rejected the idea that OpenAI and Anthropic should be afraid of open models, arguing they expand the market by giving more people a first taste of AI, while many users will still pay for the convenience, reliability and stronger performance of closed services. "There's no scenario where China runs U.S. companies off the road," Huang told us. "Zero possibility." Huang sat down with Axios in Fort Worth, Texas, at the opening of a new phase of an advanced manufacturing plant where Taiwan-based Wistron makes AI infrastructure for Nvidia, showing the U.S. is capable of some of the world's most sophisticated manufacturing. The big picture: The release of Kimi K3 by Beijing-based Moonshot AI has triggered the most intense bout of AI panic since DeepSeek rattled financial markets in January 2025. Kimi combines three qualities rarely seen together: near-frontier performance, dramatically lower prices and open weights that developers will soon be able to download and customize. That combination helped fuel a sell-off of Nvidia and other chip stocks, reviving fears that cheaper, more efficient models could undercut the case for the industry's massive AI infrastructure buildout. Zoom in: Huang says Wall Street and Washington have the Kimi shock exactly backward. "The market misunderstood the impact of DeepSeek the first time," he told Axios, adding that Wall Street has "misunderstood the impact of Kimi again this time." His argument is simple: Cheaper, open models will bring AI to more people and businesses, increasing demand for the chips, data centers and computing power Nvidia sells. "Free AI should be great for hardware," Huang said. "Free AI should be great for chips. Free AI should be great for data centers." Zoom out: When it comes to policy, Huang believes restricting open models in the name of national security could leave America more vulnerable. He rejected the "misconception" that downloaded Chinese models create a "backdoor" to Beijing, arguing that companies can customize them and control their access inside secure "sandboxes." Huang suggested openness makes AI more secure, not less, because outside researchers can inspect the models, expose weaknesses and build defenses. "If everything just becomes one single model, one single point of attack, one single source of failure, I think the world is much, much more vulnerable," he said. Huang applied the same logic to American models, and called for Anthropic to make its restricted cyber model, Claude Mythos , available to "everyone" rather than limiting access. Huang argued that companies should harden powerful models through testing and rapid fixes rather than restricting access from the outset. "Mythos should be available as a service," he said. "Remember: Just because Mythos is not available, open models are available anyhow. So I think: Let Anthropic run." "Holding Anthropic back is not in the benefit of the United States," he said. Between the lines: Huang sees the AI race itself very differently from Washington, where some Trump advisers have cast China's gains as a five-alarm threat to U.S. dominance. He dismissed the notion that it's "a race with an endpoint": "We're going to continue to use AI forever. The United States is going to be here for a long time. China's going to be here for a long time." The intrigue: Huang's comments came hours after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox Business that the administration is examining Chinese AI models for stolen U.S. intellectual property — and considering sanctions in response. "If we see ... that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them because of this theft," Bessent said, citing "watermarks" of U.S. models inside Chinese ones. Huang drew a different conclusion. "Distillation, learning from AI, learning from other sources of knowledge, is fundamental to intelligence," he told Axios. He said companies should still face consequences for violating privacy or contracts, but his broader message was clear: Target the misconduct, not the models.

title: Hegseth turns tables on Dems as sparks fly during hearing clash: 'I put this on you'
content: Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth blasted Democratic senators at a hearing on Tuesday, clashing forcefully with accusations that the United States had demonstrated a failure of leadership in its war with Iran, among other areas. Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., raised skepticism with Hegseth, pressing him on whether the administration had a plan to bring the protracted war with Iran to a close. Peters accused Hegseth of leaving the country in a worse position than when the war began. PETE HEGSETH HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL TO DEFEND TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS 60-DAY CONGRESSIONAL DEADLINE LOOMS "You — you don’t have a strategy, you don’t have a long-term plan to actually win this war. Win the war! The men and women are going to be able to do it, but they need leadership. When will you show leadership?" Despite promises to end the conflict with Iran in under 60 days and multiple attempts to broker a peace deal, the U.S. remains in a struggle with Tehran over control of the strait of Hormuz , a key waterway in the Middle East that acts as a bottleneck for much of the world’s oil trade. The U.S. first began the war in joint strikes with Israel on Feb. 28 that killed Ayatollah Ali Kahmenei . Hegseth fired back at Peters, pointing out that Democrats had allowed hesitations about the administration’s border enforcement policies to also extend to funding the government, including servicemembers. IRAN WAR'S PRICE TAG HITS $80B — MORE THAN DOUBLE WHAT CONGRESS WAS TOLD "When will you show leadership and stand up to your fellow Democrats who won’t fund the troop, who play partisan politics while you don’t give us the money? You want to stand up here and talk about the troops?" Hegseth said. "You won’t show any political courage to actually fund our department because you have Trump derangement syndrome and you won’t commit to anything meaningful. So, I put this on you, senator." As a part of his criticisms, Hegseth said he believes the hesitance Democrats have shown to the U.S. armed forces has stretched from before Trump’s time in office. "I mean the Biden administration ignored hypersonics," Hegseth said, referring to missiles with the capability to travel faster than sound — a breakthrough China achieved in 2019. "They just decided to pretend like that technology didn’t exist and we shouldn’t invest in it. There are things — I don’t know what Lloyd Austin did for four years. I really don’t. The amount of neglect, the amount of stale thinking and bureaucracy; it was staggering when we took over," Hegseth said, referring to the Defense Secretary under President Joe Biden. TRUMP SAYS IRAN DEAL ‘LARGELY NEGOTIATED’ AS 84-DAY WAR NEARS POSSIBLE END The confrontation at the hearings comes as lawmakers weigh the Department of War's spending needs for 2027. The administration has requested a record-breaking $1.5 trillion budget , a sizable increase over the roughly $900 billion Congress allocated for 2026.
