title: Vicious Vicki talks TNA Knockouts TV Championship tournament, why the promotion is where she wants to be
content: Vicious Vicki has been a rising talent on the women’s wrestling scene, performing for Awesome Championship Wrestling (ACW) among other places over the last year. While Vicki has been in the ACW women’s title picture, she recently was put into the tournament to crown the first ever Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) Knockouts TV champion. TNA introduced the belt at Slammiversary and she was one of the independent talents who were selected to participate. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL She explained to Fox News Digital how she was able to get into the tournament after eventually losing to Indi Hartwell. "I had a really great, still have a really great, relationship with Tommy Dreamer and a lot of the opportunities that I had had in TNA had come from him and he made me earn them like I should have," Vicki said. "I do believe that he had some sort of part in that. But it was a road in TNA for me to, about three or four years ago, getting opportunities and just kind of taking the smaller ones, taking the smaller ones, taking the smaller ones and then this was probably my first real, like my big match where I was able to kind of showcase myself a little more, which is awesome. "No matter what happens, being able to be a part of history of TNA as an unsigned talent, … there was only two independent women's wrestlers in the entire world in that tournament mixed in with some WWE people . So that to me says a lot for me, and Gabby Forza was the other one, I feel like it says a lot that the work that we had put in over the years really paid off. So, no matter what happens, I can I can say that I was a part of TNA history and that can't be erased." While TNA has received sharp criticism from fans wanting to predict that the death of the company is coming, Vicki suggested that couldn’t be further from the truth. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM Vicki spoke to TNA’s resilience and being able to battle through the ebbs and the flows that come with any part of the pro wrestling industry. "I think people just like to point the finger at everyone but themselves in life," she told Fox News Digital. "So, I just think a lot of companies, they flounder every now and then. It just happens, where there's highs, there's lows, there's highs, there's lows. It's just how it is. It's how wrestling is. It's been like that since the beginning of time. "I think TNA will survive and they have survived much worse. So, I think right now, for me personally, that's where I want to be. Obviously, I would love to be walking down the ramp at WrestleMania, but you have to think realistically and I think that's a great spot for me. I think they are doing great things. I think TNA is the spot. I do." TNA airs "Impact" every Thursday night at 9 p.m. ET on AMC.

title: TNA star Elayna Black shares why she joined company, how she wanted to be in The Beautiful People
content: Elayna Black was one of the hottest free agents on the pro wrestling market when she departed WWE in 2025. Formerly known as Cora Jade in NXT, Black hit the independent circuit performing in places like Atomic Legacy Wrestling, Black Label Pro and Game Changer Wrestling before taking time off. Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) was an option for Black, and she was very familiar with the company’s programming. She told Fox News Digital she grew up watching TNA and became a fan of Jeff Hardy and the female faction known as The Beautiful People. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL "At the time I started watching TNA, Jeff Hardy was in the company," Black said. "So, I was a huge Jeff Hardy fan … I started watching WWE first. At first, that was the only wrestling company I knew. When you're a kid, you don't really know anything else. And then slowly I discovered TNA and you discover, oh, Jeff Hardy was in WWE, and I was young, so I didn't know. So, just discovering Jeff Hardy was crazy because I was like, I love wearing black nail polish and like I was getting into my little emo phase at the time. So, I loved Jeff Hardy. "But my all-time favorites were The Beautiful People, specifically when it was the three of them at the time. It was Angelina Love, Velvet Sky, and Madison Rayne. They were like my gods. You could not tell me anything. I was going to be The Beautiful People. I was going to be in The Beautiful People. I remember my first ever phone, like flip phone, this little pink phone when I was in like fifth grade that my parents got me, The Beautiful People's theme song was my first ever ringtone. I emailed TNA when I was like 12 years old trying to convince them to let me be the first ever youngest member of the Beautiful People. Obviously, they never responded, but here I am now. And maybe one day they can walk me to the ring or something. We'll see. But The Beautiful People, those are my girls." Black finally became a main roster talent for TNA in January. She told Fox News Digital she didn’t necessarily want to sign anywhere and was trying to do what was best for her. "I think for a while I didn't really want to sign anywhere," she said. "Obviously, I knew eventually I wanted to be somewhere just because that's what I love to do," she said. "But I think for a while, my mindset was just wanting to prove myself otherwise. And I was having fun on the indies for a little bit, but life happens, some personal things came up, and I felt like I really needed to take a break just for my mental health. I started wrestling training when I was 15. I dropped out of high school to do it. "The only time I ever had time off was with an injury. So, it's been my life forever. And growing up in wrestling is also kind of difficult. So just taking the time for the first time really and I'm 25 now, so 10 years, to just kind of sit back and reflect after losing everything that I had just worked for was probably the best thing I could have done. And taking that time, I was just kind of thinking where would be best for me." Black said she was initially hesitant to sign with TNA because of its partnership with WWE . She was just coming off a WWE run and at first thought she wanted to be able to do something on her own without WWE. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM But after recalibrating, she said she believed TNA had the best environment for her and provided an opportunity for her to thrive. "At first, I was a bit hesitant with TNA just because of the WWE partnership. And that's nothing against WWE at all. I loved my time there, but that that goes back to me saying I wanted to prove myself somewhere else and I kind of wanted to be as far away from WWE as possible at the time just to prove who I was without them because I was there for so many years or a few years before that," Black said. "At the end of the day, it seemed like TNA had the best environment. I wanted to help bring TNA to the forefront and help TNA grow. "They got this AMC deal, and I was lucky enough to be a part of the AMC debut, which was great. But I'm not the one who built that. You know, I showed up on the debut. There were so many years of hard work put into getting TNA to the AMC debut and everyone there is a hard worker and everyone there loves wrestling, and it's very creatively free, which is something I think I wanted and needed to do to be able to challenge myself. Being in WWE for a long time, they kind of have what they want, and you obviously have input as well, but TNA is very, very open to ideas and everything like that. So, when I kind of thought about all that I was like, TNA is probably the place for me, which is great. I love TNA." Black credited TNA with putting women’s wrestling at the forefront. Gone were the days of bra and panties matches or other risqué types of angles. TNA grew its Knockouts Division and helped make women’s wrestling more than just filler matches. "I love the locker room. I think TNA has a great locker room environment in the women's division. Not only that, but the women put on one hell of a performance every single time," she told Fox News Digital. "I think a lot of the times, TNA maybe doesn't get the credit that it should for kind of being ahead of the times with the women, at least in my opinion. I think TNA was doing stuff that other companies weren't doing with women for a long time in the beginning. I remember watching TNA as a kid and even noticing that I was like, I want to do what the Knockouts are doing. They get to do way cooler stuff and everything like that. "So, I think a lot of times maybe TNA doesn't get the credit for kind of putting the Knockouts on the forefront very early on and trying to show what they can do. So, that's something I've always wanted to be a part of. It's something I always noticed just even as a kid, that TNA puts a lot of trust and faith in the women, which is very great and something you don't always see. I think TNA is a great place and some place every women's wrestler should want to be because they truly believe in the women and I think the women are incredible, and we're all pushing each other to be better." Black is now a contender for the TNA Knockouts World Championship. She’s one of the mainstays on "Impact" every Thursday night on AMC.

title: OpenAI says AI models acted on their own in ‘unprecedented' hack of another company
content: ChatGPT maker OpenAI said Tuesday that its artificial intelligence system hacked into another AI company on its own in what the company called an “unprecedented cyber incident.” “We had a significant security incident during evaluation of our models,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a statement posted on social media. AI startup Hugging Face said last week that it had detected an intrusion into its data processing systems that it suspected was caused by an AI agent autonomously acting on its own. “We suspected last week’s cyberattack might have come from a frontier lab, given the sophistication of the agent,” Hugging Face co-founder and CEO Clément Delangue said in a statement. “Turns out it did!” The disclosure comes amid heightened concerns about the cybersecurity capabilities of powerful models that led President Donald Trump in June to sign an executive order creating a framework for the federal government to vet the national security risks of the most advanced AI systems for up to a month before their public release. “AI is accelerating the discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities,” OpenAI said in its statement Tuesday. “The primary lesson from this incident is that model security and safety must keep pace with rapidly advancing capabilities.” Delangue said he spent the past 24 hours working with OpenAI, “and we strongly believe there was no malicious intent on their part. It’s quite mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously!” Delangue added that it “might be the first incident of its kind.” OpenAI said the intrusion was caused by a combination of its AI models, including its newly released GPT‑5.6 Sol and an “even more capable” model that is still being tested internally. OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face servers. It went to “extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal” and “found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation,” the company said.

title: Abolishing the Senate Might Be the DSA’s Best Idea
content: The Republican Party and its allied media organs have been blasting out messaging highlighting the radical views of the Democratic Socialists of America, whose views conservatives wish to associate with the Democratic Party. The particular extreme DSA stance they have chosen to highlight over the past week is the abolition of the U.S. Senate. The right-wing media is aflame with headlines such as “DSA Co-Chairman Defends Plan to Abolish Senate: ‘We Don’t Think That’s Extreme’” and “‘It’s Not Extreme’: Guess What the DSA Wants to Abolish Now.” (Answer: the Senate.) The odd thing about this choice is that, although the DSA’s platform is indeed chock-full of maniacal proposals, on this particular idea, the maniacs have a point. The Senate is a vestigial deformity upon the Constitution whose elimination, unlikely though it might be, would rank among the great democratic advances in American history. The Senate’s many admirers, chief among them senators themselves, tend to defend it as the product of ingenious design. Ben Sasse, a former Republican senator from Nebraska, offered up a typical tribute in a Wall Street Journal column on Sunday. He wrote, “The upper house is built for the long view, with six-year terms that encourage a deliberative trustee model of representation. Senators owe their states both judgment and conscience.” The truth is that James Madison and his allies did not want to create a Senate that represented states rather than people. The Constitution’s architects, despite notoriously excluding many Americans from the political community, wished those who were granted the right of self-determination to be able to do so on an equal basis. As Alexander Hamilton wrote in “Federalist No. 22,” “Every idea of proportion and every rule of fair representation conspire to condemn a principle, which gives to Rhode Island an equal weight in the scale of power with Massachusetts, or Connecticut, or New York.” The idea that people who lived in small states should enjoy more power than people who lived in large states offended Madison and Hamilton’s sense of justice. [ James Kirchick: The DSA is a parasite ] However, those Founders lived in the real world, and in that world, they had to cut deals with less-remembered Founders such as Gunning Bedford Jr. of Delaware, who threatened to walk away from the newly founded republic unless the citizens of small states were granted disproportionate rights. Madison and Hamilton recognized they had no choice but to submit. This deal is known to history as the Great Compromise. It was great not because it was perfect, but because it was politically necessary. As Madison explained, “A government founded on principles more consonant to the wishes of the larger States, is not likely to be obtained from the smaller States. The only option, then, for the former, lies between the proposed government and a government still more objectionable. Under this alternative, the advice of prudence must be to embrace the lesser evil.” This is an elegant way of saying: It stinks, but what are you gonna do? Merely because the Founders had to cut a deal to achieve an imperfect outcome does not bind the citizenry to abide by it for eternity. Other compromises the Founders made—such as protecting slavery—have long since fallen by the wayside. But the Senate, rather than viewed by posterity as the necessary evil that Madison recognized it to be, has been sacralized. In some ways, the Senate has evolved in a more democratic direction. Prior to the passage of the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913, senators were appointed by state legislatures, in many cases with the help of hefty bribes, rather than elected. In other ways, however, the body has grown even more undemocratic. When the Constitution was ratified, the most populous state had fewer than 13 times as many residents as the least populous state. Today, that ratio has ballooned to nearly 67 to 1. This malapportionment occurred only in part because of the natural growth of mega-states such as California, Texas, and New York. It was also the product of deliberate manipulation. In the late 19th century, Republicans, seeking to maintain their electoral advantage in the chamber, admitted a series of states that would not have met the customary qualifications for statehood. Most comically, they split the lightly settled Dakota territory into two states, giving them an extra pair of senators. [ Eric W. Orts: The path to give California 12 senators, and Vermont just one ] The upper chamber’s undemocratic character has been warped further by the filibuster. The Constitution specified only limited uses (such as approving treaties and proposing constitutional amendments) for a supermajority, but it has evolved into a routine requirement for legislation. In theory, a Senate bloc representing less than 11 percent of the public could prevent the passage of a law. This imbalance has been made all the more noxious by yet another distortion. Small states (many of them located in the sparsely populated Great Plains and Mountain West) tend to be rural and overwhelmingly white, which means that the Senate systematically under-weights racial minorities, who tend to live in states with the lowest per-capita voting clout. One 2025 paper calculated that, compared with a legislative body that represents all racial groups equally, in the U.S. Senate, white people functionally enjoy 1.14 votes per person while Black people have 0.84 votes, Asian Americans 0.75, and Latinos 0.67. This form of affirmative action for white people draws little notice but has an important effect. Studies have found that the Senate has a persistent tilt in favor of Republican candidates and conservative-policy outcomes . The tilt may be worse than it appears, given that Republicans have often squandered their structural advantage by nominating extreme candidates who have lost winnable races. The DSA’s platform sets out an ambition to reduce the Senate to a symbolic institution like the House of Lords, which once exerted counter-majoritarian influence over the United Kingdom but now simply affirms policies enacted by the democratically elected Parliament. That is obviously an ambitious goal with no prospect of fulfillment anytime soon. Even the more modest goal of admitting Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico as states, which would reduce but not eliminate the Senate’s conservative tilt, is probably not in reach for the next Democratic majority. But advocating for morally just, utopian policies is the sort of thing that democratic socialists ought to be doing. Republicans want to scare voters into thinking that if Democrats win the midterm elections, the United States will be on the road to a future in which the Senate is no more—or is, at best, an impotent debate club for elderly statesmen. If only!

title: New report uncovers education groups' DEI push to shape how artificial intelligence is used in classrooms
content: FIRST ON FOX : The nation's top teacher unions and education groups are allegedly embedding diversity, equity and inclusion principles into AI guidance for classrooms as schools increasingly adopt the technology, according to a sweeping report. The report by Defending Education , an education watchdog, examines AI guidance, model policies and training materials from the National Education Association (NEA), American Federation of Teachers (AFT) and other education groups, arguing they promote AI policies in the classroom centered on "equity" and "algorithmic bias." "Teachers unions and associations like the NEA and AFT at this point are nothing more than left-wing political operations funneling millions of dollars into promoting divisive DEI and gender ideologies in classrooms," Defending Education investigative reporter Casey Ryan told Fox News Digital. Ryan said the education groups are seeking "to use AI as their next frontier to reach school children in an effort to promote their worldview onto America's next generation," adding that they want to shape AI before it becomes widely used in classrooms. FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS "We cannot allow that to happen," he said. "It is imperative that concerned parents and families speak up now to ensure that the integration of AI into our schools benefits all students, rather than serve as another tool to enforce a problematic agenda." According to the report, "algorithmic bias" is the belief that AI reflects the views of its creators, often "White or Asian men," prompting education groups to promote "equity" in AI used in classrooms to "ensure that students receive politicized answers and receive a politicized education." "The integration of AI into education is not a matter of if but when," the report said. Researchers found the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), which represents more than 1.8 million members, launched the National Academy for AI Instruction , a $23 million initiative with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic that the report said is designed to establish AI "guardrails" for educators. AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’ "These are three of the largest corporations building AI that are used on a global scale and are the AI programs already used by many school districts," the report said. According to the report, a 2025 AFT resolution warned that AI "has the potential to help personalize instruction, reduce administrative burden and make learning more engaging, but without proper guardrails it can perpetuate bias, invade privacy, and undermine educational equity, job security and the professional judgment of educators." "This program is imbued with the idea from AFT’s resolution that ‘bias’ and ‘equity’ are issues within AI in schools," the report said. Researchers examined the NEA's AI in Education Hub , which the union says is "grounded in equity, ethics, and educator voice," along with a model policy requiring AI vendors to meet standards for "transparency, equity, and ethical decision-making" and undergo audits for "algorithmic bias." STUDY FINDS MORE AI PRAISE FOR BLACK STUDENTS, SOFTER TREATMENT OF FEMALES The report highlights the California Teachers Association’s (CTA) role in developing state AI guidance for K-12 schools that recommends educators "approach AI with an equity lens" while addressing concerns about "equity, bias, and access," and describes AI education as a way to address " systemic bias ." The report also cites articles published by the American Association of School Administrators discussing AI's ties to "White males" and the "New Jim Code." The National Association of Elementary School Principals (NAESP) published an article encouraging schools to ask AI vendors how they address "algorithmic biases," while the National Association of Secondary School Principals (NASSP) said AI tools should "advance and do not undermine equity," according to the report. "The goal of these organizations is to embed DEI into AI tools to ensure that students receive politicized answers and receive a politicized education in the nation’s classrooms," the report said. Fox News Digital reached out to the AFT, NEA, CTA, AASA, NAESP and NASSP for comment.

title: New FDA moves are boosting American jobs and protecting our medicine supply
content: For decades, U.S. policymakers have highlighted the vulnerabilities of relying on foreign supply chains for essential medicines. Yet over 70% of the primary manufacturing facilities for prescriptions filled in the United States remain outside our borders. Over time, a suffocating web of state and federal regulations meant that companies investing millions or billions to build facilities in the U.S. would see those investments sit idle for up to 14 months waiting for standard post-construction reviews. This paralysis has driven supply chains further overseas, hurting the Americans who rely on life-saving cures and treatments. When critical supply chains are anchored half a world away, American patients are left exposed to dangerous shortages and American workers are stripped of high-paying employment opportunities. President Donald Trump prioritized solving this problem by signing Executive Order 14293 , "Regulatory Relief to Promote Domestic Production of Critical Medicines," directing the FDA to cut red tape, incentivize domestic manufacturing and secure medicines for American patients. The FDA took that directive urgently. Moving into mid-July, we are aggressively executing on multiple fronts to spark a domestic manufacturing renaissance – removing regulatory roadblocks and creating an environment where American production can outcompete the rest of the world. TRUMP’S DRUG PRICE WAR WITH EUROPE AIMS TO MAKE THINGS CHEAPER FOR AMERICANS To rev up our domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing base from the ground up, the FDA recently launched the PreCheck Pilot Program. Designed to clear the hurdles that stall new manufacturing facility builds in the U.S., this program is already unleashing a historic wave of domestic job creation, proving we can secure our health while building a powerhouse economy. The program operates in two distinct phases. In the early Facility Readiness Phase, manufacturers receive technical and regulatory feedback before operations begin, preventing costly compliance mistakes. Next, the Application Submission Phase features enhanced FDA engagement to quickly resolve manufacturing questions, expedite the review of facility information and fast-track inspections. By identifying potential issues early, the PreCheck program reduces delays, improves regulatory predictability and accelerates the availability of U.S.-manufactured medicines. This ensures next-generation medical breakthroughs are researched, developed and manufactured right here at home by leveraging our greatest resource – the extraordinary talent, grit and might of the American workforce. Following our selection of the program's first seven corporate participants – including Eli Lilly, Regeneron, Amneal, Cellares, Fujifilm Biotechnologies, Kriya Therapeutics and Kyowa Kirin – the FDA is actively working alongside these innovators as they break ground and scale operations this summer. These companies are building state-of-the-art facilities to manufacture everything from innovative cell and gene therapies to everyday IV bags. Crucially, these first seven participants alone will anchor thousands of long-term, high-wage careers for American scientists, engineers, technicians and operators, while instantly fueling thousands of jobs across the heartland. These are the kinds of stable, family-sustaining careers that anchor communities for generations, helping revitalize local economies and ensuring our brightest minds and hardest workers can build prosperous careers right in their home neighborhoods. TRUMP EXPANDS TRUMPRX PRESCRIPTION DRUG DISCOUNT PROGRAM TO MORE THAN 800 MEDICATIONS In addition to this pilot, the FDA is moving forward with newly released draft regulations to streamline pathways for distributed manufacturing and provide greater transparency regarding foreign medicine suppliers. We are also reimagining the incentives within our control. While the FDA is required to prioritize applications based on urgent public health needs, we are now also prioritizing applications for older, generic medicines that utilize domestic supply chains. These lower-cost medicines make up roughly 90% of all prescriptions written in the U.S., yet they are the very drugs most frequently manufactured overseas. Moving production back home means bringing thousands more stable manufacturing jobs to American factories. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION When a parent goes to the pharmacy for a child’s antibiotic or a patient fights cancer, they should not have to worry about whether a factory closure overseas will cut off their lifeline. Onshoring pharmaceuticals will require a synchronized effort across HHS, private industry and state and local communities, and it is integral to the health, national security and economic prosperity of the American people. Securing our factories is only one piece of the puzzle; we must also secure the science that feeds them. Under the leadership of President Donald Trump and Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Department of Health and Human Services recently launched "Operation TrialBlazer," a historic initiative designed to bring clinical trials back to American soil by modernizing drug development and slashing regulatory burdens. Making the United States the most attractive place to conduct clinical research ensures that laboratory discoveries translate directly into high-tech production jobs on American soil. Through the PreCheck program, aggressive regulatory reform and domestic prioritization, the FDA is acting as a collaborative catalyst for domestic growth. We are protecting patients, fueling a high-tech economic renaissance and restoring American independence by putting American workers first.

title: Michelin-star chef reveals what's replacing hospital food Americans love to hate
content: "Hospital food" has long been synonymous with packaged, ultraprocessed meals — despite the fact that hospitals are meant to promote healing. In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian shared his initiative to improve what is served in U.S. hospitals, following the concept that " food is medicine ." For the last three years, Zakarian said he’s been working on changing hospital food — most notably at Tampa General, which is a $4 billion nonprofit, 1,000-bed public hospital. RFK HAILS FIRST US HOSPITAL TO PROMISE HEALTHIER MEALS: 'WE HAVE A TEMPLATE' On Thursday, July 16, Tampa General Hospital CEO John Couris signed the "Make Hospital Food Healthier" pledge during a news conference attended by Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins and Zakarian. The pledge commits the hospital to serving more nutritious, minimally processed meals to patients, building on Zakarian's menu overhaul. "We’ve changed the entire menu," the celebrity chef told Fox News Digital. "We've taken all seed oils out, sugar, maltodextrin. Anything bad in a box is gone. Anything good is brought in." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "We're serving mac and cheese. We're serving hanger steak and fries. We're serving chicken with couscous. We do all our protein shakes. No protein shakes in the box anymore. We do fruit shakes, smoothies, fresh sorbet," the chef listed. "So, you're eating like your grandmother's cooking for you." CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz has also supported Zakarian in this mission, telling Fox News Digital that the chef has "revolutionized our thinking" around hospital food. "How do we get the hospitals to do what [Zakarian] has been doing the frontier work on, get them to actually embrace food as part of the healing process ?" he questioned. "Because most patients, and most doctors, know that the food in the hospital is not going to make you better." Oz noted that while hospital food may provide some nutrients, it is generally not seen as contributing meaningfully to patients' recovery. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The biggest challenge to getting better food into hospital systems has been cost, Zakarian pointed out. While "everything is fractionalized," what’s left over after paying for supplies is put toward food, which generally "ain’t much," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "It's, like, $3.50 a person per plate, which is an extraordinarily small amount," the chef said. "You go to McDonald's, and you spend 12 bucks for a happy meal, and we give you $3.50 in a hospital. So that's an unhappy meal as far as I'm concerned." Instead of charging hospitals for each plate served, Zakarian's approach relies on a flat annual fee, saving money through a smaller, higher-quality menu . "Yummy food, not just food to fill people up," he said. " Nutritious food , bioavailable food, food that's satiating." "I'm cooking like I would cook in a restaurant. I'm cooking like my mother cooked for me. There's no difference." The chef continued, "When you're lying in bed in a hospital gown, you feel alone, you feel exposed, you feel sick … When you have a fresh protein shake or a fresh healthy smoothie, or you can order steak frites ... that [makes] your day." Freelance writer Teresa Mull contributed to this report.

title: When New York City comes second: The problem with an Israel-first mayor
content: For a man elected to run New York City , Zohran Mamdani spends a remarkable amount of time thinking about Israel. Before he has solved the city’s affordability crisis, before New Yorkers feel safer on the subway, before families see cleaner streets, better schools or a government that simply works, the socialist Mamdani has chosen to make the Jewish state and its leader a defining obsession — Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu . He has publicly declared that he would seek to have Israel’s prime minister arrested if Netanyahu came to New York . Whether or not such a thing could ever happen is beside the point. A New York City mayor has no meaningful role in international criminal law or American foreign policy. Yet this became one of Mamdani’s earliest and most high-profile priorities, and now he admits he doesn't have the legal authority to do so . MAMDANI SAYS NYC IS EXPLORING WHETHER IT CAN ARREST NETANYAHU IF ISRAELI LEADER VISITS FOR UN GENERAL ASSEMBLY Think about that. The mayor of America’s largest city looked across the ocean before looking across his own boroughs. That tells you something. It tells you where his passion lives. It tells you what keeps him up at night, and it tells you that, for all the campaign rhetoric about housing, transit and working families, Israel occupies an extraordinary place in his political imagination. So, I’m calling him the first MIGA mayor: Make Israel Great Again. The pattern did not begin there. Among the earliest actions of his new administration was revoking New York City’s adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism. Supporters argued that the definition could chill legitimate criticism of Israel. Critics saw something very different: a city stepping away from one of the world’s most widely used tools for recognizing modern antisemitism at a time when antisemitic incidents continue to rise. That decision sent a message. Whether intended or not, many Jewish New Yorkers heard it loud and clear. The administration also rolled back an executive order adopted under Mayor Eric Adams that had sought to prevent city agencies from discriminating against Israel, Israeli citizens and Israel-linked businesses through municipal contracting or procurement. Again, supporters defended the change. Again, many Jewish New Yorkers saw a familiar pattern. One decision can be explained away. Two decisions become a trend. Three decisions become an agenda. Then came reports that the administration’s international affairs office had planned a meeting with Iran ’s ambassador to the United Nations before the proposal was abandoned. Mamdani later said he had not approved the meeting and called it a mistake. Perhaps. But the contrast was impossible to ignore. THE US-ISRAEL STRATEGIC ALLIANCE – PARTNERSHIP, NOT CHARITY An administration willing to explore dialogue with representatives of the Iranian regime while publicly entertaining the arrest of the elected leader of Israel naturally raises questions about its priorities. None of this exists in isolation. Mamdani proudly identifies with a political movement in which hostility toward Israel has become increasingly central. For years, we have watched the same progression. Occupy Wall Street, campus BDS campaigns, academic boycotts, the Democratic Socialists of America , the "Squad." Every movement arrives promising economic justice. Every movement eventually seems to discover that Israel has somehow become one of its defining moral causes. No country receives comparable scrutiny. No democracy is held to quite the same standard. No conflict consumes so much attention. I know these worlds well. While I now live in Florida, I grew up in Brooklyn Democratic politics, where endorsements mattered, relationships mattered and neighborhood concerns came first. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Later, my professional life became devoted to fighting antisemitism and introducing Americans to the Israel that headlines rarely capture: its innovation, diversity, culture, resilience and humanity. For decades those two worlds barely intersected. Then New York elected Zohran Mamdani. Now they have collided. Many people were stunned to hear that Jewish voters helped elect him. The reality is more nuanced. Available exit polling suggests that most Jewish voters supported Andrew Cuomo , not Mamdani. Yet a meaningful minority, particularly younger and more progressive Jews, backed him. Every voter has his or her reasons. Some cared almost exclusively about affordability, some believed municipal politics and Middle East politics should remain separate, and some assumed campaign rhetoric would give way to pragmatic governing. The first months of this administration suggest otherwise. Israel is not an occasional topic for this mayor. It is a recurring theme. And that matters because New York is home to the largest Jewish community outside Israel . For millions of New Yorkers, Israel is not an abstract foreign policy debate. It is family. It is faith. It is history. It is identity. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER When elected officials repeatedly single out the world’s only Jewish state for exceptional condemnation, many Jews do not experience that as ordinary political disagreement. It’s antisemitism. They experience it as part of a climate that has made Jewish schools hire more security, synagogues install more barriers and Jewish students wonder whether expressing a connection to Israel will make them targets. New Yorkers elected a mayor to obsess over New York, over crime, over housing, over sanitation, over schools. Over whether a family can afford to stay in the city. Instead, they have a mayor who appears to reserve his greatest passion for litigating the legitimacy of a country nearly six thousand miles away. Every mayor leaves a signature. Some build parks, some reduce crime and some transform neighborhoods. Zohran Mamdani is writing a different legacy. He is becoming the mayor who cannot stop talking about Israel while New Yorkers wait for him to focus on New York. The Big Apple deserves a mayor whose first priority is the people who elected him. Instead, it has one who seems determined to fight battles far beyond the five boroughs.

title: Growing trend of hating men backfires as anti-marriage culture leaves single women losing out
content: A growing anti-marriage movement is being fueled by viral TikTok trends and high-profile celebrities painting men as the enemy, but according to a new column, women may ultimately be the ones losing out. In a USA Today op-ed, columnist Ingrid Jacques warned of a rising wave of "heteropessimism," defining it as women’s growing feelings of disappointment and antagonism toward relationships with men. She argued that viral trends like "divorce glow-ups" and anti-male literature have actively widened the divide between the sexes. "Studies show that married women are not only happier but also live longer and earn more than their single counterparts," Jacques wrote on Tuesday. RELATIONSHIP EXPERT CHALLENGES ONE OF AMERICA'S BIGGEST ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT DIVORCE She explained that the media modern women consume is increasingly hostile toward traditional relationships, pointing to bestselling books like "Yesteryear," which centers on a "tradwife" influencer. In that novel, Jacques notes, men are reduced to lazy or toxic tropes: "Either a man is an idiotic man-baby who lacks ambition and a brain, or he's a quintessential patriarch who pals around with other sexist pigs in the manosphere. Husbands are at one point referred to as ‘freaks.’" On Amazon, the book’s description includes , "A gripping, electrifying novel that is as darkly funny as it is frightening, ‘Yesteryear’ is a gimlet-eyed look at tradition, fame, faith, and the grand performance of womanhood." TRANS ACTOR ELLIOT PAGE ARGUES 'HEALTHY MASCULINITY' IS REJECTING EXPECTATION TO 'SHUT DOWN' The trend coincides with falling U.S. marriage and birth rates. Official U.S. Census Bureau data from December shows that just 47% of American households in 2025 were married couples, down from nearly 66% 50 years ago. Of those married households, only 37% included their own children under age 18, compared to 54% in 1975. Jacques linked the shift directly to liberal ideology, noting that left-leaning Americans choose to opt out of traditional family lifestyles "far more often than conservatives." "Wherever you look these days, women who ‘free’ themselves from the chains of marriage are being celebrated," Jacques wrote. She highlighted cultural figures who publicly champion singlehood or life after divorce, including "Eat, Pray, Love" author Elizabeth Gilbert and model Emily Ratajkowski. In April, comedian Leslie Jones criticized marriage, saying that most people she knew who got married are now divorced and arguing that "marriage is legalized slavery ." VIRAL NIKKI GLASER CLIP PROMPTS DISCUSSION OVER WHETHER MONOGAMY IS DEAD A 2024 American Family Survey found that 37% of conservative women and 28% of moderate women, between the ages of 18 and 40, reported being "completely satisfied" with their lives. However, liberal women of the same age reported only 12% feeling the same way. The sentiment has also taken over social media through trends like the TikTok "divorce glow up," where women post before-and-after photos celebrating their split. Jacques noted that in these videos, the women "typically look happier and more radiant in the ‘after’ photo." Citing Louise Perry, author of "The Case Against the Sexual Revolution," Jacques argued that young women are being alienated after getting " burned by hookup culture " and lacking real friendships with the opposite sex. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Jacques argued that, like Perry, returning to marriage, not abandoning men altogether, is the remedy for the cultural divide. "That won’t be true for everyone, of course," Jacques concluded. "But men and women need to find a way back to each other. Discounting marriage won’t get them there."

title: Trump attends dignified transfer as 4 U.S. troops killed in Iran war return home
content: President Donald Trump on Wednesday honored the lives of four U.S. service members who were killed in the Middle East and returned to their families at an air force base in Delaware. The president saluted as four transfer cases were escorted off an airplane during the dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base. The ritual is one of the most somber duties of a commander-in-chief. It was the third Trump has attended since he launched the war in Iran in February. Trump was scheduled to meet privately with the grieving families. Speaking to reporters on his way to Dover, Trump called the ritual “one of the hardest things to do as a president.” His message to the families, he said, was, “We love you. We love your child.” “There’s no games, there’s no nothing — that’s their child,” Trump said. “And all you can do is throw out your heart.” Trump was accompanied by administration officials including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Also present were Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. During the ritual, transfer cases draped with the American flag and holding the remains of the fallen soldiers are carried from the military aircraft that transported them to awaiting vehicles to take them to the mortuary facility at the base. There, the service members are prepared for their final resting place. Fallen troops came from Hawaii, Texas, New York and North Carolina Two U.S. Army soldiers killed in Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan were returned during the dignified transfer. The remains of a third service member who is believed to be the soldier missing after the Jordan attacks was also returned, as well as the remains of a soldier killed in Iraq during a detonation of an Iranian drone. The soldiers killed in Jordan were identified by the Defense Department as Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii; and Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas . The soldier who disappeared after the Jordan attacks is Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of Ozone Park, New York, the Defense Department said. The soldier killed in Iraq was identified as Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, who lived in Spring Lake, North Carolina. The White House said Feehan’s family would be joining on Air Force One later on Wednesday as Trump travels to Georgia for an event promoting his administration’s investment accounts for children. Trump previously said the soldiers died while protecting America and other nations from Iran. “We feel very badly, but you know, those great people, those great patriots were out there fighting so that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. He added that the U.S. was striking Iran “in honor” of the fallen troops. Trump vows to retaliate for each U.S. death The U.S. has launched multiple retaliatory strikes against Iran as an interim agreement to end the war falls apart. Trump on Monday said that every time Iran kills an American soldier, “they will pay for that killing many times over!” Since the war began on Feb. 28, 18 U.S. service members have been killed. Trump on Tuesday said that while almost all the incoming fire in Jordan was stopped, some made it through. “They did slip something through in Jordan,” he said. “If we had other operators, you know, it would have not happened, unfortunately.” He went on: “We’ve stopped almost everything, but when you let other people do your job with the United States — we let other people do the job — and sometimes it doesn’t work out so well.” Trump did not elaborate on his comments, and it was not immediately clear who he was saying was responsible for protecting U.S. forces in Jordan. Trump attended two previous dignified transfers since the outset of the war, most recently in March. Soldier had planned to marry fiance and attend law school Feehan, a first lieutenant who was killed Saturday, will be posthumously promoted to the rank of captain and awarded the Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge. He was assigned out of Fort Bragg, North Carolina, to the 32nd Army Air and Missile Defense Command. Feehan’s family said in a statement that their hearts were shattered by his loss. They remembered Feehan, who went by “Tivo,” as someone who “packed in more living” in his 25 years than most do in a lifetime. “He chased adventure relentlessly,” the statement said. “He believed deeply in the power of military service, especially what it builds in a person: discipline, leadership, character.” He planned to marry his fiance and attend law school after his deployment. The family said they’re starting a scholarship in his name. Gonzales, who was killed Friday, was a private with the 10th Army Air and Missile Defense Command in Ansbach, Germany. She graduated last year from Hebron High School in Carrollton, near Dallas, school officials said. Rampersad, a sergeant who was believed to have been killed in Friday’s attacks, was assigned to the 57th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade, 10th Army Air and Missile Defense Command in Ansbach, Germany. Swinton, a sergeant who was killed Sunday, will receive a Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge, and will be promoted to staff sergeant. He enlisted in the Army in 2017 and was assigned to the 55th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 108th Air Defense Artillery Brigade, out of Fort Bragg, North Carolina. ___ Binkley reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Michael Catalini contributed from Morrisville, Pennsylvania.

title: DAVID MARCUS: In booming Detroit, voters skeptical of socialism snake oil
content: It is rare to find a bartender who knows how to make a good Vuex Carre, but Emily, at Le Supreme Brasserie, knocked it out of the park. She grew up in the suburbs, but loves living her 20s downtown, and the revitalization of the Motor City she enjoys may be a problem for far-left senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. A bit later, on Sunday night, I met Nick, 29, who grew up in Detroit and now works in advertising in Chicago . He marvels at the changes he has seen in his hometown. "It’s so different now, a bunch of these places didn’t even exist a few years ago," he said. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN I heard it over and over again, and I could see it, as well. Along Washington and Woodward, the shops were buzzing, and even the heavy smoke from Canada couldn’t keep people from strolling the thoroughfares and valleys in the grand, sturdy Midwestern brick castle of downtown. Not far away, earlier in the day, I had met Sean, who was walking his attractive dog and who moved to Detroit in 2019 from Philly. He lives in one of the fancier downtown buildings and loves his adopted hometown, and the lifestyle in the city. "It’s easy going," he told me. "There is a lot to do. It’s great." SWING-STATE POLL SPELLS TROUBLE FOR FAR LEFT AS SCHUMER-BACKED CANDIDATE DOMINATES WITH CRITICAL VOTING BLOCS Sean is a committed Democrat who hates President Donald Trump. "All that matters is that we elect a Democrat," he said. "R or D, that’s all it comes down to, which is a shame, but it's how things are." For Sean, the top priority in the Aug. 4 Democratic Senate primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens is electability. That is not great news for El-Sayed, who has been pushing back against the idea that he is too radical to get elected in purple Michigan. DAVID MARCUS: SOCIALISM AND EL-SAYED RUN INTO HARSH REALITY IN BLUE-COLLAR MICHIGAN He has reason to be concerned, as I learned from James, a retired plumber in his 60s, who is Black and has been involved in civil rights movements. "This just doesn’t feel like that movement I’ve been a part of, it feels different," James told me. "It feels foreign to me." And he wasn’t alone, as it turns out. The day before, I had met Kelly, an American woman of Iranian descent who warned that today’s far-left candidates like El-Sayed "are just like in Iran." She said Muslim immigrants in nearby Dearborn, are not assimilating. "When Joe [Biden] opened that border, they were planted there," she said. Taken together, these recent encounters, from some very different people around Detroit, painted a picture that seems to be increasingly favoring Stevens, which is presumably why Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez did a three-stop tour for El-Sayed. On Monday, El-Sayid got another boost of sorts as Sen. Elizabeth Warren endorsed him, although frankly, that is about as surprising as Tony the Tiger endorsing Frosted Flakes. What is missing for El-Sayed – and all of his socialist out-of-town pals – in this city that is booming in comparison to many others in America, is any real, pressing need for socialism. Unlike New York City, where the rent is always "too damn high," in Detroit, affordability is not proving to be the same magical incantation that it was for Gotham Mayor Zohran Mamdani . Many Democratic voters I talked to wanted a steadier hand on the system, and they want to beat Trump and the GOP. But they don’t want to blow up the system which has been thriving in many ways. There may be one more trump card to be played in this tight race in the form of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer , who has thus far declined to endorse either El-Sayed or Stevens. As confusing as it may be to Republicans around the country, Whitmer is very popular among Michigan Democrats, in part because of Detroit’s revitalization under her watch. The stakes of this race for the national Democratic Party could not be higher. It is a true and fair test of whether the far-left wing of the party, led by college-educated Whites and immigrants, can replace the old party of Jefferson and Jackson led by the working class and native minorities. Another thing that stood out in Motown was that, aside from the Bernie rally itself, not one voter I talked to brought up Israel . One way or the other, this matters because, while El-Sayed’s constant negative focus on Israel may put him on the right side of the issue with most Democrats, these days, it's not a driving issue. Waiting in the background for the dust to settle is Republican Mike Rogers, who is set to take on the Democratic winner. From his point of his chances. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DAVID MARCUS

title: Dem Katie Porter makes surprising announcement about political future
content: Former Rep. Katie Porter , D-Calif., appears to be retiring from politics, telling the Sacramento Bee that it's unlikely she runs for office again after a series of failed bids for national positions. Porter, fresh off a fifth-place finish in the California governor's race, told the Bee "I am closing the door on being a candidate," in a Friday interview with the outlet. "I cannot foresee that path back," she added. Porter , who left her Congressional seat to run for the Senate seat vacated by the late Dianne Feinstein in 2023, also lost that race, garnering over 1 million votes, but still falling short of the top two candidates, Steve Garvey and eventual winner Sen. Adam Schiff . KATIE PORTER’S ATTEMPT TO BRUSH OFF VIRAL OUTBURST BACKFIRES AS CRITICS TORCH ‘WORST POLITICAL AD’ Both campaigns for the high-profile national offices were marred by personal scandals and public backlash to reports of Porter's private behavior. In 2023, while running for Senate, Porter responded to claims that she abused members of her staff, including during one alleged incident in which she chastised a staffer for catching COVID-19. The texts between Porter and her staff member showed Porter saying "you gave me COVID" and that Porter's "children have nobody to care for them." Porter denied firing the staffer for the incident and said, "I regret if this employee feels disgruntled." KATIE PORTER SAYS SHE REGRETS VIRAL OUTBURSTS AT REPORTER, STAFFER Allegations of toxic behavior were renewed when a leaked video revealed Porter screaming and cursing at another staffer during her gubernatorial campaign in 2025. "GET OUT OF MY F---ING SHOT" Porter screamed in the now-viral clip. Porter has also come under fire for the bizarre way she abruptly ended a video interview with a local reporter. The mounting scandals appeared to affect her electability. Finishing a respectable third behind Garvey and Schiff in the 2024 non-partisan "jungle primary" for the state's Senate seat, Porter garnered 1.27 million votes from Californians, good for 17.2% of the electorate, according to California's secretary of state. But in 2025, Porter finished fifth, receiving only 403,908 votes, representing only 4.4% of the electorate, according to the California secretary of state's certified election results. She told the Sacramento Bee she would be focusing on making social media posts about books going forward. Fox News Digital contacted Porter for comment.

title: Robot bird swims underwater then flies away
content: Watching a diving bird vanish beneath the water can feel almost unreal. One moment it cruises through the sky. Seconds later, it swims after prey before returning to the air. Around 100 bird species can move between those two environments. Engineers have found that natural ability incredibly difficult to recreate at a small scale. Now, researchers at MIT and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne, known as EPFL, have built a robotic bird that can complete the entire journey. The 8.8-ounce robot flies, plunges into water and swims below the surface. Then it launches back into the air using the same set of flapping wings. NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL According to the research team, it marks the first bird-scale robot to complete that full cycle through flapping motion alone. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will walk you step by step through simple ways to filter spam, clean up your inbox and recognize the messages that could put your personal information at risk. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our spam-stopping checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com . Most amphibious robots use separate systems for air and water. This mechanical bird takes a simpler approach. The robot relies on flapping wings instead of propellers. It also completes its water launch without legs or a complicated wing-folding mechanism. That design presents a major engineering problem. Water is about 800 times denser than air, so wings face far greater resistance once they enter the water. To handle that dramatic change, the robot adjusts its flapping speed. Its flexible wings also change shape as the surrounding pressure increases. In the air, the robot can flap its wings up to 11 times per second. Underwater, its flapping rate ranges from 0.1 to 6 times per second. Meanwhile, water pressure can bend the wings by as much as 90%. That flexibility shortens the effective sweep of each stroke and reduces the load on the motor. The same wings become more effective for flight once the robot reaches the air. Researchers also made the machine neutrally buoyant. As a result, it neither rises nor sinks on its own while underwater. That balance helps conserve battery power because the robot spends less energy fighting buoyancy. The hardest part begins when the robot tries to leave the water. It completes the transition in under one second using about eight to 10 wingbeats. However, the maneuver requires a careful combination of wing flexibility, tail placement and launch angle. Researchers found that moderately flexible wings worked best. A rigid wing struggles to adapt underwater, while excessive flexibility reduces the force needed for takeoff. The tail also needs to remain short and close to the body. Otherwise, it can drag through the water and pull the robot back down. An exit angle near 70 degrees produced the strongest results. A flatter approach creates too much tail drag. A nearly vertical launch can make the robot tip backward into the water. ZELENSKYY ANNOUNCES 'THE FUTURE IS HERE' AFTER WAR'S FIRST ALL-ROBOT CAPTURE The machine also gives scientists a new way to study real diving birds. Tracking the movement of a live bird beneath the surface can be difficult. With a robot, researchers can adjust one feature and measure how that change affects performance. For example, many diving birds reduce their wingspan while swimming. Researchers have often connected that behavior with lower energy use. The robot's results suggest that shorter underwater strokes may instead help birds increase speed. The team also compared the machine's propulsion efficiency with that of real birds. Both fell within a Strouhal number range of 0.2 to 0.4, which researchers associate with efficient movement. However, body size can change the launch strategy. Heavier diving birds may use their legs to help push away from the water, while this lightweight robot relies entirely on its wings. The robot's most efficient travel mode depends on the distance ahead. According to the team's data, flying uses less energy once a journey extends beyond roughly 51 feet. For shorter trips, staying underwater may make more sense. Water creates heavy resistance, so swimming becomes increasingly costly over longer distances. A future robot could use that difference to plan its route. It might swim toward a nearby target, surface and then fly to a more distant location. The prototype costs around $300 in materials and uses parts that researchers can source commercially. The team also released open CAD files for the project. That could allow universities and other builders with access to a 3D printer to reproduce the design. Eventually, the robotic bird could help scientists monitor waterways and coastal environments. Researchers imagine launching it from shore or a boat. It could fly toward an area of interest, dive to collect a sample and then return with the data. Potential missions could include taking measurements near an iceberg or observing marine wildlife from a safer distance. Flapping wings may also offer practical advantages in those environments. They avoid exposed high-speed propeller blades and could produce less noise around animals. Underwater, flexible wings may tolerate contact with debris better than rigid propellers. INSIDE CHINA’S AI ‘WOLF PACK’ DRONES BUILT WITH TAIWAN CONFLICT IN MIND The current prototype still relies on human control during key parts of its journey. Researchers manually launched the robot during several tests. Timers or basic triggers also activated parts of its diving and swimming behavior. Autonomous navigation represents the next major step. The robot would need to recognize its surroundings and control each transition without human assistance. Salt water creates another hurdle. Testing has focused on fresh water, so future versions will need stronger protection against corrosion. Longer range and improved endurance would also make the robot more useful outside controlled experiments. You probably will not see robotic birds patrolling your local beach anytime soon. Still, this project shows how future drones could reach places that traditional flying machines struggle to explore. A single robot could gather information above the water before taking measurements below the surface. That flexibility could reduce the need for separate aircraft and underwater vehicles. The low material cost also matters. Smaller research teams could experiment with the design without investing in an expensive custom platform. As navigation and battery performance improve, machines like this could make environmental monitoring more accessible. What stands out here is how much work the researchers get from one flexible set of wings. The robot changes its flapping speed, while the wings naturally bend to handle the resistance underwater. The launch back into the air makes this more than another bird-inspired drone. Pulling off that transition requires the right wing stiffness and a carefully controlled exit angle. The prototype still needs autonomous controls and better protection for saltwater. Even so, its $300 material cost and open design could give other researchers an affordable foundation to build on. Would robotic birds collecting environmental data make you feel hopeful about conservation, or uneasy about machines blending into natural habitats? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. title: Saquon Barkley tackling streaming maze as NFL keeps growing worldwide: 'I'm all about eyes'
content: Saquon Barkley knows that he is "quote unquote, one of the faces" of the National Football League. It is not an easy title to hold, but being a No. 2 overall pick turned 2,000-yard rusher, Offensive Player of the Year and Super Bowl winner will do that to you. Barkley's very first game as a Philadelphia Eagle was played in Brazil, and this year, the team will travel to London in Week 5 to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars. But as the NFL continues to grow its audience and lap the field, Barkley is "all about eyes." CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM "It’s so important that we are traveling across the country to play the game. The more eyes you can get on it, the better it’s going to be," Barkley told Fox News Digital in a recent interview. "The more people are going to want to grow up and play football, want to be involved. It’s really kind of crazy that football is probably the biggest sport, and we really haven’t even scratched the surface yet, to be completely honest. There’s so many more territories that we just take over, and I think the NFL is doing a really good job of that. "I’m a fan of getting as many eyeballs as we can in the game, help growing the game. Anytime I can get an opportunity to play in front of someone that’s never got to watch the game, I want to try to make it memorable and have an impact on them… So right now, I’m all about eyes, eyes, eyes on the game, and let’s grow this game as big as we can, and let’s have an impact on as many people as we can." That's why Barkley has joined forces with DIRECTV ahead of his ninth NFL season. As part of the campaign, Barkley recorded a spot that turned his iconic hurdle into a humorous metaphor for the obstacles football fans now jump through just to find a game. It shows why Barkley wants diehard fans to keep watching games, dare we say, the old-fashioned way. GEORGIA RUNNING BACK SUFFERS 'SERIOUS INJURIES' FROM ATV 'ACCIDENT,' COACH KIRBY SMART SAYS "It’s going to be crazy in 10 to 15 years, the way you’re going to be able to watch football games," Barkley said of today's streaming-service takeover. "It’s kind of like what I grew up on, and now to be able to have the opportunity to work with them, and to be able to not only bring it in the NFL level, but also in the collegiate level where the game continues to grow and how much eyes are continuing to get on this football game, I think it’s the only way. I think it’s the right way to do it, and for me to be able to have the opportunity to work with DIRECTV, someone I’ve been a fan of for a very long time and be able to shoot a spot with them, it was awesome." Barkley has accomplished just about everything a football player could dream of. He can retire right now and continue the golf grind (he claims Philly's top five courses trump New Jersey's top five, although Barkley and this writer obliged that Pine Valley is a Philadelphia course). But as to why he's still grinding, his answer is simple. "I love it," he said. "It’s something I’m very passionate about. My son SJ, he’s already passionate about football. I was around the same age, two or three, where I said this is something that I want to do, and I’m living my dream. I’m living the dream that I always wanted to live. So, I’m having fun with it, and as long as God keeps me healthy, and they keep giving me contracts and opportunities, as long as they want to keep me in this league, I’ll try to play as long as I can.... "Whether it’s a year, whether it’s five years, there’s going to be a time where I’m like, 'Damn, I wish I could go back into that locker room and just spend one more day with the boys, spend one more day in that weight room, spend one more day running out that tunnel.' It’s going to be a mess. So, I try to enjoy it right now." Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X , and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter .

title: Experts finally solve mystery of teenage Revolutionary War soldier 246 years after his death
content: The remains of a teenage Revolutionary War soldier have finally been identified — over 246 years after he was buried in an unmarked grave. The discovery, which researchers believe is the first identification of a Revolutionary War soldier using DNA and forensic genetic genealogy, was announced in June. Researchers at FHD Forensics used advanced DNA analysis and forensic genetic genealogy to identify the remains as Private John Pumphrey, a teenager who died at the Battle of Camden in South Carolina. MYSTERIOUS 18TH-CENTURY WARSHIP UNEARTHED AT GROUND ZERO SITE GETS NEW HOME The Battle of Camden was one of the Continental Army's worst defeats during the Revolutionary War, and hundreds of American soldiers died during the engagement. Officials believe Pumphrey enlisted in 1777, when he was between 13 and 15 years old — meaning he was between 16 and 18 years of age when he died on Aug. 16, 1780. Pumphrey's remains were uncovered at the battlefield site in 2022 during a University of South Carolina excavation. In a June news release from FHD Forensics, officials said a tiny piece of the soldier's skull was used to extract DNA, allowing researchers to uncover his identity before he was reburied with military honors in 2024. REVOLUTIONARY WAR ARTIFACTS UNEARTHED AT SITE OF INFAMOUS COLONIAL AMERICAN HEIST: 'VERY SURPRISED' "He would have been one of the youngest members of George Washington's revered 'Old Line,'" the release said. It was not "highly unusual" for young boys to enlist in the Continental Army, though it was rare, said Allison Peacock, president of FHD Forensics. Peacock told Fox News Digital that it was a "pretty regular occurrence for young boys to volunteer." She added, "They were supposed to be at a certain age, but that rule was [broken] all the time, from what we understand." HIDDEN REVOLUTIONARY WAR BAKE HOUSE IS UNCOVERED AFTER SPENDING CENTURIES UNDERGROUND Researchers were initially surprised, she said, because they knew from anthropological analysis that the soldier was very young — but they struggled to understand why someone like him had enlisted. "When we started seeing the families he was related to, they were all prominent Anne Arundel County, Maryland, founding families — the gentry class," she said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The Pumphreys were very prominent in lumber, building and land ownership, so none of our historians or the people we were working with thought it made sense for a boy that young to come from one of those families." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER After uncovering details about the turmoil surrounding his father's estate following his parents' deaths and learning that his family lived much closer to Baltimore than they had realized, they said his decision to enlist in Baltimore made much more sense. "Knowing those little details to put the story together changed everything," Peacock said. "When you see the proximity to Baltimore and you see what was going on in his family and his military record, you get a picture of what led this boy to go enlist in Baltimore." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Peacock said she is confident the remaining unidentified Camden soldiers can also be identified using the same techniques, provided the team can secure funding. "It is our understanding that it is the first time it's ever happened," she said. "We're already rewriting the story of the battle," added Peacock. "We're learning things that historians had no way of knowing until we got into the DNA."

title: ‘Hero' mom dies after using last strength to save 4-year-old son from Florida river
content: A Florida "hero" mom died after using all her strength to keep her 4-year-old son above water when he fell into the St. Johns River, allowing rescuers to pull the boy to safety, authorities and her family said. Nicole Grayson, 43, jumped into the river after her young son fell into the water at Ed Stone Park, west of DeLand, around 4 p.m. Saturday, according to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office. Investigators said the child had been playing with an unidentified object near a wooden fence along the river’s edge when he dropped it over the barrier. The boy fell into the river while attempting to retrieve it. OFF-DUTY ICE OFFICER RELIES ON 'SIXTH SENSE' TO SAVE DROWNING CHILD BEFORE DELIVERING MESSAGE TO CRITICS Grayson immediately went in after him. "My guess is he was trying to get it. He slipped in the water, deep, he slipped away in the water," Grayson’s oldest son, Dafino Devega, told FOX 35. "And then my mom, I guess she panicked, and she went in the water and tried to save him." CROCODILE ATTACK HORROR UNFOLDS AS COUPLE TRIES TO SAVE VICTIM: ‘WE FELT SO HELPLESS’ As Grayson struggled to keep her son above the surface, a witness at the park flagged down a passing boater, who threw two life preservers toward the mother and child, the sheriff’s office said. Grayson eventually became submerged while continuing to hold her son above the water. A frantic 911 caller told dispatchers that rescuers had managed to reach the child but were still struggling to recover his mother. FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT "Hey 911, can you come to Ed Stone Park?" the caller said in audio obtained by FOX 35. "We have a mother that’s drowned, and we got the baby, but we can’t get the mama." SEND US A TIP The boater maneuvered close enough to pull the 4-year-old aboard. The boy was unharmed, according to authorities. Witness Jon Reaka said Grayson appeared to expend all her energy ensuring her son survived. "She spent all her energy trying to get her kid up over the edge," Reaka told FOX 35. Reaka jumped over a railing and onto the boat, where he helped pull Grayson from the river. She was unresponsive when she was brought aboard. GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS "I jumped over the rail, jumped onto the boat and pulled the lady up onto the boat and, you know, we started CPR — I started CPR and mouth-to-mouth immediately," Reaka said. Emergency medical personnel took over lifesaving measures after arriving at the park. Grayson was rushed to a hospital, where efforts to revive her continued for several hours. She died in the intensive care unit around 10 p.m. Saturday, the sheriff’s office said. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE "I tried everything I could do to save her," Reaka told FOX 35. "You know, I feel horrible. I mean, it’s so sad what happened." Grayson was a mother of six whose final act reflected the fiercely protective way she had lived, her family said. "That’s the type of mom that she was; she was a hero," Devega said. "My mom, she was a strong woman," he added. "She would do anything to keep her kids safe." CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS FOLLOW US ON X Volusia County Sheriff Mike Chitwood praised the witnesses and the boater who rushed to help Grayson and her son. "Sheriff Chitwood and the entire Volusia Sheriff's Office send sincere thanks all who jumped in to help with the rescue, and deepest condolences to Ms. Grayson's family and friends for their loss of a mother who gave her life to save her son," the department said in a statement. GOT A TIP? Chitwood said Grayson would be remembered as a hero, "not just because of her final heroic act, but because she was a mom who would do anything for her kids."
