content: Republican outrage went into overdrive after New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced that the state had mistakenly registered 6,600 noncitizen voters , prompting calls for an immediate end to automatic voter registration through the New Jersey Motor Vehicle System (MVC). Sherrill announced on Tuesday that a "serious software error in New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle System led to the registration of roughly 6,600 people who indicated that they were not U.S. citizens between June 2023 and June 2024, almost three years prior to my taking office." Sherrill said preliminary analysis indicates that 400 individuals voted due to the error. Republican state Sen. Declan O'Scanlon told Fox News Digital that New Jersey Republicans have been raising concerns about the MVC registration system for years and "each time we were reassured that this ‘could never happen.’" "It happened, and it’s worse than anyone expected," he said. DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED In light of the error, O’Scanlon called for a pause on all voter registrations through the MVC until a thorough investigation is completed for every registration processed through the system. He emphasized that beyond any software glitch, when state Democrats "made it law for noncitizens to obtain driver’s licenses, Republicans warned that this very problem could occur." "If we know that more than 6,000 noncitizens were improperly registered to vote over two years, why on earth would we stop the investigation there? This system has been in place for years. We should be reviewing every registration processed through the MVC over the last decade," he told Fox News Digital. "Until that thorough investigation is complete, the MVC should suspend all voter registrations." In a Tuesday news conference, Sherrill emphasized that the mistake did not occur while she was in office. She criticized her predecessor, former Democratic Gov. Phil Murphy , the MVC and the state’s software contractor, IDEMIA, for their alleged role in the scandal. "It's unacceptable that the vendor released software with such a glaring error. It's unacceptable that the MVC took a year to get this issue fixed, and it's unacceptable that no one in the previous administration brought this to light," said Sherrill. IDEMIA, however, released a statement pushing back on Sherrill’s assertion that its software is to blame. The company said that its role is to "transmit information through the motor vehicle system" and that the New Jersey Department of State’s Division of Elections "is ultimately responsible for verifying eligibility to vote." This comes as President Donald Trump and Republicans push for passage of the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act, which proponents say would crack down on noncitizen voting. NEW JERSEY DEM GOV'S BLAME GAME BACKFIRES AFTER TECH COMPANY PINS NONCITIZEN VOTER REGISTRATION ON STATE Vice President JD Vance called on New Jersey senators to vote in favor of the SAVE America Act, writing in a tongue-in-cheek post on X, "If only there was a way to stop this type of ‘software error’ that allowed non-citizens to vote in our elections." "I hope Senators @CoryBooker and @SenatorAndyKim will join us in voting to pass the SAVE America Act to ensure that only eligible American voters can participate in New Jersey elections, and all elections across the United States," wrote Vance. New Jersey’s junior U.S. Sen. Andy Kim, however, said during an interview with MSNBC that "this is something that needs fixing, but it’s not this widespread systemic problem that Trump has been using and weaponizing to try to push forward a very extreme agenda," according to Breitbart . Kim said that "this is unacceptable and this needs to be fixed immediately and needs people need to be held accountable , " but added, "We also need to make sure that we’re looking at the problems in the right size, that this is not akin to what Donald Trump was talking about." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Ally Triolo, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, reacted by telling Fox News Digital that "Democrats’ refusal to acknowledge that the thousands of noncitizens found on New Jersey’s voter rolls represent exactly the kind of election integrity failure President Trump highlighted last week proves one thing: their hatred of the President matters more than doing what is right for voters and securing American elections once and for all." Back in the state capitol in Trenton, New Jersey Assembly Republican Leader John DiMaio called for both a halt to automatic MVC registrations and a "top-to-bottom" audit of the state’s voter rolls. He believes the problem "is much more pervasive than 6,600 noncitizen voters." "New Jersey Republicans have been sounding the alarm for years that the automatic voter registration process at the MVC was highly problematic," said DiMaio. "Until citizens are 100% assured that not one illegal resident will be mistakenly or intentionally registered to vote, the automatic process should be immediately halted." He also called on Sherrill to "put politics aside for once and focus on election integrity" by cooperating with the federal government to "get all the non-citizens off the rolls." CNN'S JAKE TAPPER HITS DEMS FOR REJECTING ILLEGAL VOTING CONCERNS AMID NEW JERSEY VOTER ROLL CONTROVERSY In the state senate, Minority Leader Anthony Bucco told Fox News Digital that many of the issues stem from "the fact that New Jersey has been allowing undocumented immigrants to obtain a driver’s license since 2020." "Over six years ago, Trenton Democrats chose to allow undocumented immigrants to obtain driver's licenses despite our opposition, and they placed voter registration in the hands of the MVC—an agency with a long history of administrative failures," he explained. New Jersey Sen. Kristin Corrado, who serves as ranking member of the state Judiciary Committee, said that before the scandal broke out, she had sent six letters to the Murphy administration warning of voter registration issues. "Democrats wrote this law, Democrats implemented this process, and Democrats failed to fix the obvious problems that followed," she said. "Now we are learning that a catastrophic government failure allowed thousands of non-citizens to be registered to vote, and suddenly everyone is acting surprised." Republican Assemblyman Greg McGuckin likened the 400 illegal votes to "negating the votes of U.S. citizens." "The problem is much larger than Democrats are willing to admit," he said. Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill, Kim, Booker, New Jersey Senate President Nicholas Scutari and General Assembly Speaker Craig Coughlin for comment.

title: Inside NYC's 'perfect scam': Luxury cars, dusty shelves and the EBT secret behind the counter
content: Stocked with food that expired years ago and lined with dusty shelves, some New York City bodegas and delis have allegedly been operating as fronts for organized Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) card-skimming schemes, using hidden devices to steal information and ultimately taxpayer-funded benefits, according to an expert who is sounding the alarm. Criminals attach hidden skimming devices to checkout payment terminals to capture EBT card data while using pinhole cameras or keypad overlays to record customers' PINs, according to the FBI. The stolen information is then used to create counterfeit cards and drain Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, costing consumers and financial institutions more than $1 billion each year. "A large percentage of these convenience stores are actually EBT ATMs," Haywood Talcove, CEO of LexisNexis Risk Solutions Government, told Fox News Digital "Their sole purpose is to traffic cards, not sell food." Speaking after joining the Secret Service on a recent fraud operation in New York City, Talcove continued: "I saw firsthand a can of tuna that expired three years ago. I saw firsthand pancake syrup that was two years expired, sardines that were expired. What struck me is the industry that is built around trafficking these EBT cards, taking away money from individuals and their families that actually need it." SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS According to the Secret Service , the agency's New York Field Office conducted a three-day operation across Brooklyn, the Bronx and Queens in June that uncovered 35 illegal skimming devices and prevented an estimated $36.5 million in fraud, marking its fourth anti-skimming operation in New York City this year. Eligible households receive monthly SNAP benefits on an EBT card, which works like a debit card and is used to buy eligible food at authorized retailers, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Talcove said he saw multiple stores on the same block with shelves stocked with expired food, which led him to believe some were operating primarily to facilitate EBT fraud rather than as legitimate grocery sales. During the operation, the Secret Service uncovered skimming devices on checkout payment terminals that can capture EBT card data that criminals can encode onto counterfeit cards for unauthorized purchases or withdrawals. "The logical question you ask yourself is, 'How can there be enough economic activity to sustain stores that are all selling the same thing and they're very small?'" he said. Talcove said "that's not why they're there," adding the condition of many stores led him to believe some businesses were operating primarily to facilitate EBT fraud rather than as legitimate grocery stores. "They're there to not provide nutrition because across the street is a wonderful supermarket with fresh food and fresh fish and produce and shelves that aren't dusty that don't sell food that's expired," he said. Although the fraud may appear to be carried out by only a small group, Talcove said it runs much deeper than that. "You start looking at these groups and you very quickly realize they're criminal and they're organized ," he said. FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS' Michael Peck, assistant special agent in charge of the U.S. Secret Service's Criminal Investigative Division, told The City Reporter in June that criminals have packed as much as $1.2 million in stolen cash into dishwashers before shipping it overseas, and that the runners installing skimming devices earn about $150. The City Reporter, citing the Secret Service, also reported that many of the organized crime groups behind the EBT skimming schemes originate in Eastern Europe and are "living large off the scam, renting $10,000-a-month apartments and Lamborghinis." However, Talcove said the fraud extends beyond bodegas and delis, arguing many other retailers fit "into this category." He also said the SNAP program does not require itemized purchase records, making suspicious transactions harder to detect. "I've got firsthand insights into one that was pretending to be a store, but it was actually a laundromat," he said. "I'm looking at one right now on the West Coast that is pretending to be a store that is actually a strip club accepting EBT." Talcove called the fraud the "perfect scam," citing weak identity verification, outdated card technology , and limited purchase records. "Number one, you're not going to get caught, number two, the government never runs out of money, and number three, the SNAP program has fundamental flaws in its administration," he said. But Talcove said the "real victim here" is the families on SNAP who don't receive the food they need, something he said he witnessed firsthand in New York City. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, more than 250,000 retailers nationwide are authorized to accept SNAP benefits. "The problem there is they have families," he said. "They have children that are hungry and the money that was intended to go to the child is being diverted to something that it was never intended to do." Emphasizing the impact, Talcove said hard-earned taxpayer dollars are being lost while criminals take advantage of those "who show up every day, that try to do the right thing." ALLEGED FEEDING OUR FUTURE FRAUD RINGLEADER TRANSFERRED FROM SOMALIA TO FACE US CHARGES "They're transnational in nature," he said. "They are taking advantage of our empathy because they understand that you're not gonna stop somebody from getting an EBT or SNAP benefit, because who would want to take food away from the hungry?" Talcove proposed "a concerted effort" to remove suspicious stores from the SNAP program, upgrading EBT cards to chip technology , strengthening identity verification, and monitoring large purchases to detect potential fraud. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a New York City Department of Social Services spokesperson said EBT skimming is a "nationwide crisis," saying the city has been working closely with state officials and law enforcement to help "vulnerable" New Yorkers who may be impacted. Just this month, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced the state will begin replacing current EBT cards with more secure, chip-enabled cards in early 2027 to help stop fraud. Following five years of investigations, Talcove praised the Secret Service but argued arrests alone won't solve the problem. "It is just so part of the ecosystem now," he said. Talcove said "once you see it, you can't unsee" the "unconscionable" fraud where businesses disguise themselves as normal stores while operating as something else entirely. "How is it that a laundromat is pretending to be a place where you can buy food?" he said.

title: Pat McAfee forced to address ESPN layoffs on air during awkward segment, but the answer is simple
content: Things look a little different at ESPN today. Haven't you heard? The World Wide Leader laid off dozens of employees this week, including Ryan Clark , Cam Newton, Tom Pelissero and Karl Ravech. Others were let go as well, but those are some of the big names circulating the internet as of today. This isn't the first round of layoffs at ESPN — or for any company. Frankly, this is at least the third or fourth round of layoffs at ESPN since I started working at OutKick four years ago. It's become a yearly story at this point. EXCLUSIVE: ESPN TO PART WAYS WITH CAM NEWTON AS PART OF TALENT LAYOFFS THAT ALSO INCLUDED RYAN CLARK Anyway, something else that's become a yearly topic is why ESPN is letting folks go, with several people placing the blame on Pat McAfee. That's right. Pat McAfee! He earns roughly $30 million a year, and is reportedly in negotiations with ESPN to double that moving forward. Obviously, those numbers are going to raise some eyebrows when these layoffs happen. NFL Hall of Famer JJ Watt joined the "progrum" on Tuesday, and ... didn't shy away from the elephant in the room: "Slow, slow news day over there on the ESPN airwaves, huh?" Watt said to begin the interview. "I mean, besides the fact that you’re getting $100 million… Did they keep anybody? Or is everybody fired to pay you? I’m trying to figure that out." Goodness gracious. Just a vicious way to start an interview. Brutal stuff. Look, it was obviously in jest, and McAfee responded by laughing it off. He's not stupid. He's not immune to the narrative on social media right now. "We do not appreciate that," he said. "That is the narrative, and I’m certainly taking it on the shins. The boys and I are very proud of the work that we have done. Thanks." Here's the bottom line: ESPN views Pat McAfee as an asset. The network has put him everywhere since the two partnered up a few years back. He's on College GameDay . He's on the sidelines for the biggest college football games, sometimes even getting his own simulcast feed. His show is on the main channel every day. He travels to big sporting events outside of football for his show. Just last week, he was at the Home Run Derby, which was notable given it was the first year it wasn't on ESPN in decades. It's clear that ESPN believes in McAfee and wants to continue to invest in him. It's probably not a bad investment to make given he's arguably the biggest all-around sports personality in the media. He's also self-made. ESPN did not create Pat McAfee. ESPN invested in McAfee — and his team — years ago. Since he joined College GameDay in 2022, ratings have gone up. It's not all because of McAfee, of course, but that's not a coincidence. "The first time we licensed the show through ESPN, one of these happened, we got blamed," McAfee said later in the interview. "This time, we’re getting blamed as well. Which I guess I can understand, but I mean, there’s billions and billions of dollars in these companies, and hard decisions have to get made. "And we don’t like any of them, and we hope we’re an asset to the company going forward." And that's what McAfee is to ESPN — an asset. A big one. He's proven that, time and time again, since joining the network. Think about all the big interviews you see out of the World Wide Leader right now ... where do they come from? The Pat McAfee show. Not First Take. Not NFL Live. Not SportsCenter. McAfee's radio show. Think of all the viral moments we see every Saturday during the fall. Where do they come from? McAfee's kicking segment during College GameDay. Or McAfee's outlandish intro during the opening scene. Like it or hate it — and I know plenty of folks hate it — it's clearly working. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS Pat McAfee didn't cost Ryan Clark his job . Ryan Clark lost his job because he brought nothing to the table for ESPN, beyond an occasional headache because he said something stupid. ESPN chose to cut ties with a liability, and put more money into an asset. That's not a new or novel concept. It's how businesses have been run for years.

title: DOJ gives New Jersey 5 days to hand over voter data after noncitizen registration scandal
content: Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon doubled down on the DOJ's demand for New Jersey's voter registration data Wednesday after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill's public revelation that around 6,600 noncitizens were added to the rolls through the motor-voter process. Dhillon’s letter to Sherrill came as a slew of lawmakers called for audits and bipartisan cooperation to address the findings, while the Justice Department noted it remains in litigation against Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell seeking New Jersey’s electronic voter database . "Ensuring that U.S. citizens' votes are not illegally diluted by noncitizens' votes is of paramount importance," Dhillon wrote. "We therefore write to formally request additional information to assess New Jersey's compliance with various federal statutes, as provided in our July 7, 2026, letter to the Lieutenant Governor. As we stated in that letter, we stand ready to help New Jersey election officials comply with the Help America Vote Act of 2002 and the National Voter Registration Act of 1993, as outlined in our memorandum titled, Federal Law Requirements for State and Local Election Officials." DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED Dhillon noted that about 400 of the roughly 6,600 noncitizens New Jersey said were mistakenly registered to vote and cast ballots. She gave Sherrill five days to provide the names, personal information, registration dates and precincts of the 6,600, as well as the methods and times by which the 400 who voted cast their ballots, while treating the letter as a legal preservation-of-records request typical in litigation. With the DOJ already engaged in litigation against Caldwell and the state, Dhillon said she would notify the judge in that case of the new development as the department continues to seek statewide voter registration lists from states including New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania. NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION When reached for comment, the DOJ provided a separate letter Deputy Attorney General Jesus Osete sent to Caldwell and New Jersey Division of Elections Director Donna Barber on Wednesday, again requesting electronic voter registration data. Osete said the DOJ has grounding to "ascertain New Jersey's compliance with the list maintenance requirements" of the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 and the Help America Vote Act of 2002. He added that the New Jersey Division of Elections must also verify that no additional noncitizens are registered on the state's voter rolls. The letter was filed as an exhibit in the Justice Department's ongoing lawsuit against New Jersey seeking access to the state's electronic voter registration database . Meanwhile, the French technology contractor that works with the State Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) said late Wednesday that responsibility lies not with the MVC but with the Department of State, led by Caldwell, and the Division of Elections. Sherrill spokesman Sean Higgins slammed the DOJ in comments to Fox News Digital on Thursday, saying the Trump administration has a "long history of weaponizing" the agency for political purposes and of attempting to "overturn election results." "Governor Sherrill has been clear that she will use all the legal tools available to her to protect New Jerseyans' personal information," Higgins said, pointing again to Sherrill's public remarks Wednesday and noting the governor's "disgust" at the vendor and former Gov. Philip Murphy's administration. IDEMIA said in a statement it has worked with the MVC for four decades to process eligible individuals seeking to register to vote when conducting drivers licensing business. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "IDEMIA’s role is to transmit information through the motor vehicle system. The voter registration information is transmitted to the New Jersey Department of State, Division of Elections, which is ultimately responsible for verifying eligibility to vote," said the company — whose American base is in Reston, Virginia. "Information submitted by IDEMIA must still be validated and adjudicated by the Division of Elections." Meanwhile, the top Republican on the state's Judiciary Committee said she has tried multiple times to press the issue of voter-roll integrity with Democrats — who control all branches of government — since 2019. "I have been warning... New Jersey needed stronger safeguards to protect the integrity of our elections," state Sen. Kristin Corrado, R-Totowa, said. "I sent six separate letters raising concerns and calling for action and introduced legislation that would have provided a commonsense safeguard by preventing the MVC from prompting non-citizens to register to vote but my warnings were repeatedly ignored by the Democrats," she said in a statement that included some of the letters sent to the Murphy administration. "Now we are learning that a catastrophic government failure allowed thousands of non-citizens to be registered to vote, and suddenly everyone is acting surprised," she said. The DOJ appeared to signal that the New Jersey case strengthens the Trump administration's push for stronger election integrity measures nationwide as multiple states continue to resist requests for information sharing.

title: The Top Gun: Maverick Theory of Pete Hegseth
content: When audiences first met Pete “Maverick” Mitchell in 1986’s Top Gun , he was a lieutenant at the Navy’s elite school for fighter pilots. The movie doesn’t give his age, but that would probably have put Maverick, as he teamed up with his buddy Goose in the skies over California and the glistening volleyball pits by the sea, in his mid-to-late 20s. When Top Gun: Maverick was released, 36 years later, Mav was still flying. With his aviators and winsome smile, he looked great for a man in his 60s. But Maverick was still only a captain. Captain is a senior Navy rank, equivalent to full-bird colonel in the Army, but Maverick’s contemporary Iceman, in contrast, had progressed to four-star admiral and the head of Pacific Fleet, one of the Navy’s biggest jobs. Most important, Maverick is more stuck in his captain’s mentality than he should be for his age and experience. Maverick’s dogged, iconoclastic love of flying, career consequences be damned, is a theme throughout the movie. “You can’t get a promotion, you won’t retire,” an exasperated admiral, played by Ed Harris, says after reading through Maverick’s file, “and despite your best efforts, you refuse to die.” Top Gun: Maverick is a solid action flick. You could spend a lot of time on the military forums of Reddit, though, reading about why its premise and plot are ridiculous. Beyond the details of military life, consider Maverick’s love interest, played by Jennifer Connelly. She is a dive-bar owner and single mom who somehow has a fancy sailboat and a vintage Porsche that a browse online tells me is worth $200,000. But one aspect of the film has proved implausibly accurate. Maverick is a seasoned military man who resolutely refuses to grow up. He remains stuck in the same rank he has occupied for years, attached to the same mentality, concerns, and priorities. Although three decades have passed, he hasn’t progressed, instead spending his time on rebellious flying, seaside sports, and drinking in dive bars. His is an arrested development. The most unrealistic aspect of this portrayal is that, in 2026, that profile would make Mav not a superannuated flight instructor, but secretary of defense. At 46 years old, Pete Hegseth is considerably younger than Maverick. Yet since he became Pentagon chief 18 months ago, I’ve repeatedly heard from military officials that Hegseth appears frozen in the mindset of a person in a much more junior station than he now occupies. Hegseth joined the Army National Guard after college. Had he starred in a National Guard equivalent of Top Gun , we might have met him when he led a platoon in Iraq in 2005 or trained local forces in Afghanistan in 2011. We know from his book that he was preoccupied with battlefield-level concerns: no letup in pounding the enemy, no second-guessing frontline troops and their actions, no concessions to nitpicky “jagoffs,” his derisive term for military lawyers. By 2021, he had reached the rank of major in the Guard. But he resigned in anger after being sidelined from the protection of Joe Biden’s presidential inauguration because of an internal complaint that one of his tattoos might be a sign of white nationalism (a claim he denies). By then he had detoured into the media, becoming a Fox News host. Four years later, he got his own sequel, as President Trump’s unlikely pick for secretary of defense. [ From the July 2026 issue: Being Black in Pete Hegseth’s military ] But since taking the Pentagon’s top job, in January 2025, Hegseth has acted more like a company commander than a member of the Cabinet. He has shown an intense, animating interest in matters that typically would preoccupy a junior officer rather than the civilian head of the world’s most powerful military, someone who leads almost 3 million personnel in a world replete with danger. When Hegseth summoned hundreds of generals and admirals to the Pentagon last fall, for example, he chided them for being fat and sloppy. He has also shown an unusual focus on physical fitness. His workouts, jaw-clenching pull-ups and all, regularly appear on social media. (Sorry, sir, but the 64-year-old Cruise has you there.) If he detests anything more than fat generals, it’s facial hair—no more “beardos,” he has said. And last week, he released a video announcing that the military would start testing the testosterone levels of troops older than 30 to help achieve a “High-T Department of War.” You can debate the merits of those policies, but the United States is currently engaged in a war with Iran, staring down the prospect of a much larger conflict with China over Taiwan, and facing a revolution in warfare technology. (Hegseth also is overseeing attempts to reform the Pentagon acquisition process and to adopt AI.) One former Army officer told me Hegseth reminded him of what he and buddies were like as senior lieutenants or captains. “He’s not so junior that everything is still new and exciting,” the officer told me. “He’s been around long enough to see some warts—generals gaining weight, too many waivers for beards—but not long enough to have any perspective.” When I asked the Pentagon about this and other observations, the spokesperson Joel Valdez, in a statement, called them “unjust partisan critiques.” He added: “Meanwhile, the rest of real America applauds the generational changes and disruption to the status quo that Secretary Hegseth has achieved at the Department of War,” Hegseth’s preferred name for the Defense Department. The plot of Top Gun: Maverick is built around Maverick’s appointment as the leader of a high-risk mission against an unnamed enemy country that bears an uncanny resemblance to Iran. Maverick and his fellow pilots must fly deep into enemy territory to blow up an underground uranium-enrichment site that is protected by surface-to-air missiles and advanced enemy aircraft. (Another head-scratcher for the Reddit crowd is why, in the movie, the Navy forgoes its own fifth-generation fighter, the F-35, and dispatches Mav and his team in older F/A-18 Super Hornets.) The Hollywood sequence shows off spectacular air maneuvers. But the premise has distinct echoes in the Trump administration’s own war with Iran. Last June, the U.S. and Israel, to use Trump’s word, “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear-enrichment program by air, in what no doubt would also have made for exciting viewing. But Hollywood is not real life, and air strikes alone seldom secure strategic objectives. The U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. The Pentagon’s campaign of air strikes on Iranian targets, which is expanding again after weeks of a shaky cease-fire, has not put an end to Iran’s nuclear stockpiles or know-how, and has probably hardened its leaders’ resolve to attain a bomb. Neither has it stopped Iran from striking Gulf neighbors, recently killing two U.S. service members in Jordan . Rather, the war has given Iran a new confidence that it can withstand a U.S. assault and assert control over the Strait of Hormuz. From the start of the war, Hegseth has been a strong proponent of unshackled force against Iran in ways that sounded as if he were speaking from down in the ranks and thought he was unlikely to be overheard. (His braggadocio included a vow to give adversaries no quarter, in defiance of the Uniform Code of Military Justice.) But unlike Maverick, who makes a triumphant return to his carrier in a stolen Iranian F-14, Hegseth doesn’t look headed for a Hollywood ending. [ Read: The Pete Hegseth exception ] That brings us to flyovers. Like Maverick, whose penchant for buzzing control towers at top speed has made him the bane of Navy brass since Ronald Reagan was president, Hegseth often sees military rules less as ironclad laws than as guidelines to be broken because breaking them is cool. Hegseth gained prominence on Fox by advocating for reprieves for troops charged with war crimes, a stance that forged his bond with Trump. Since taking office, he has shown a habitual disregard for rules, in both their purpose and their application. (After The Atlantic embarrassingly revealed that he had shared classified information on the commercial messaging app Signal , Hegseth argued the information was unclassified because he had, without taking any action, deemed it so.) And, like Maverick, Hegseth disdains rules against showy flyovers. Last week, an F/A-18 Super Hornet from the Blue Angels, the Navy’s flight-demonstration team, zoomed dangerously low along the Florida coast, stirring up sand and umbrellas, startling some beachgoers—and, it must be said, delighting many others. The Blue Angels launched a probe into the incident. The unit’s commander, Captain Adam Bryan , suggested on social media that the low altitude of the flyover was unintentional and said the squadron was undertaking a “heavy review” to ensure future safety. But all that didn’t sit right with Hegseth. The next morning, he posted sarcastically on social media that “the flyovers will continue until morale improves.” Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, whom Hegseth installed after firing Cao’s predecessor, then weighed in with a Hollywood scriptwriter’s cheesy panache to say the incident debrief was complete. “No reprimands. No firings. No problem,” he wrote above a video of the jet screaming along the beach. “That’s the sound of Freedom!” One former Navy officer familiar with the Blue Angels told me the flyby was “clearly out of the parameters” of what the unit would normally perform; typically pilots maintain a standoff distance and altitude from spectators to ensure the crowd remains safe. This is, after all, a demonstration unit whose whole purpose is to wow the public and showcase what military pilots can do. Several officials I talked with brought up a 1994 incident in which an Air Force pilot with a record of safety violations stalled and crashed his B-52 during an air-show rehearsal, killing all on board. In 2002, an air-show calamity in Ukraine killed 77 spectators. What if the Blue Angel Super Hornet had hit the beach? The fact that it didn’t shouldn’t negate a thorough inquiry. “The Navy’s instincts were 100 percent right,” the former officer said of the Navy review. It was the second time this month that Hegseth intervened in a flyover, boasting he would “fix” the suspension of National Guard helicopter pilots who flew very low over Myrtle Beach. “Carry on, Patriots,” Hegseth wrote . And in March, he publicly overruled the Army’s suspension of Apache pilots who flew by the house of the MAGA-friendly musician Kid Rock. Hegseth even made a show of taking Kid Rock on an Apache flight afterward . The military system is premised on rule-following, hierarchy, and discipline; it’s how you get troops to do the onerous and sometimes dangerous things they’re asked to do in service of their country. Hegseth has already challenged that premise in ways both meaningful and petty, by circumventing the normal promotion process to push out officers far below him or to stall their advancements, and by firing senior officers set for even higher rank. His showy action on the flyovers undermines that culture, too. Guy Snodgrass, a former pilot and Top Gun instructor who served in the Pentagon during Trump’s first term, told me that Hegseth likes to talk about good order and discipline. “But a central part of that is letting the chain of command work,” he said. “If you cut their legs out from underneath them and send a message that anything goes, you risk losing a central element of military professionalism.” Many of the troops who will heed Hegseth’s signals are young, less than 20 years old, with the prospect of a long military career ahead of them. They may not have the training or worldliness of more experienced Blue Angels pilots. What message does Hegseth’s intervention send them? The former Army officer told me the danger is that commanders will begin looking the other way when violations occur. “That is the beginning of the end,” he said. “That’s when discipline begins to crumble.” At the end of Top Gun: Maverick , Maverick flies off into the sunset with his gal in an antique P-51. He just led a legendary mission, so maybe Navy leaders would get over his chronic insubordination and give him a worthy new job. But I’m guessing the Navy doesn’t promote him, either. Mav may be an icon of the air, but they know he’s not good for the force.

title: A Novel About the Benefits—And Costs—Of Being a Rebel
content: At the beginning of the 21st century, one book mapped, with uncanny accuracy, where American literature was headed. A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius , by an upstart writer named Dave Eggers, was powered by a voice that was at once self-deprecating and self-aggrandizing. It was ostensibly a memoir of the period when Eggers raised his little brother, Toph, after their parents’ deaths, but its characters consistently break the fourth wall, and the book frequently doubles back to explain and contradict itself. Although the work was a critical favorite and a Pulitzer finalist, Eggers’s ironic tone struck some readers as overly precious—few books have inspired such devotion and exasperation in equal measure. Most prescient, Eggers eagerly highlighted the invented and imprecise elements of his story, foreshadowing a culture (literary and otherwise) in which the boundary between reality and fiction would grow ever more porous. Back then, Eggers’s persona was as visible—and as polarizing—as his writing . The same year that Genius was published, 2000, he responded to an interview request from The Harvard Advocate with an email rant. The student who’d reached out asked him about “selling out”; he objected, strenuously, to that framing. Success, he wrote, doesn’t make an artist inauthentic; it simply makes more things possible. Embittered critics who sneer at how a creative person makes money won’t be remembered, he argued; all that matters is the work. Three years later, the publishing company he ran put out a magazine, The Believer , that disavowed snark in its book reviews. And for a while, he managed to balance a devil-may-care imaginative attitude with commercial success, rejecting both the cynicism of the critical elite and the compromises of corporate publishing. In 2004, The New York Times described Eggers “as the magnetic center of a literary counterestablishment” and noted that his recent book of short stories had been released “with a characteristic disdain for the rituals of the publishing industry: no reviewers’ galleys, no back-cover blurbs, no publicity.” The first page of his novel You Shall Know Our Velocity was printed directly on the front cover—launching the story before a reader could open it—and was initially sold only through independent bookstores and his own publishing outfit, McSweeney’s. When Eggers rereleased it a year later, he’d added an entirely new middle section that altered the shape and meaning of the book. But 11 novels, three works of nonfiction, and a number of screenplays and children’s books later, Eggers isn’t the counterestablishment; he’s just the establishment. His work has won him more accolades—and, perhaps more notable, it’s grown more conventional. Books such as A Hologram for the King , published in 2012, and The Circle , from 2013 , settled into familiar forms, despite their urgent subjects (America’s reputation abroad, predatory social media), and critics admired their conscience more than their invention. His youthful audacity survived mainly in packaging and sales: He issued a special edition of one book bound in fur, for example, and refused to sell the hardcover edition of another novel through Amazon. And by this point, the cultural tide had also turned against his earnestness. In 2013, Gawker made that Harvard Advocate interview its prime example of “smarm”—a pose of unearned, largely hypocritical positivity even worse than the “snark” it sought to oppose. Tom Scocca, the writer of the Gawker article, declared that Eggers was “full of shit.” [ Read: “The Comebacker,” a short story by Dave Eggers ] Yet Eggers really had built something new. Another magazine venture of his, a literary journal called Timothy McSweeney’s Quarterly Concern , began by publishing only work that had been rejected by other publications. He’d also started other ambitious endeavors, including the national education nonprofit 826 National and a college-scholarship program for first-generation attendees. Eggers may no longer be an upstart, but in the 2020s, he maintains this parallel track of making art and opportunities—he is creating the conditions in which others might flourish. These complex relationships—between art and institutions, between artistic integrity and worldly achievement—animate Eggers’s latest novel, Contrapposto . The book primarily follows two characters, Robert “Cricket” Dibb and Olympia Argyros, from childhood to old age. When the pair meet as children, Cricket is a budding visual artist who spends his days drawing and dreaming; Olympia seeks to cultivate Cricket’s talents while harboring art-world ambitions of her own. Over the course of their lives, they fall into each other’s arms and then separate again and again. Cricket’s heart is always pointed firmly toward Olympia’s, while her attention moves restlessly from him to a succession of other boyfriends and artists. As they grow older, Cricket and Olympia come to embody what I think of as the two sides of Eggers’s career: Cricket continues to pursue his own idiosyncratic creative calling, and Olympia becomes fluent in the art world’s systems of prestige. By naming his novel Contrapposto (an Italian word that describes a human figure putting most of their weight on one foot, like Michelangelo’s David ), Eggers seems to be revisiting The Harvard Advocate ’s question: What “foot” should artists lean on—artistic purity or market viability? Olympia sees in Cricket a spark of startling originality that deserves wider recognition, if only he would seek it. She encourages him to imagine art as a public practice, shaped by the programs and relationships that sustain it. But Cricket resists this vision, preferring a more solitary idea of artistic devotion, and the story’s sympathies lean in his direction. This uneven pose gives Contrapposto its richest subject but also exposes its defining weakness. Eggers, whose early work was celebrated for formal daring, has written a surprisingly traditional tale about the conflict between passion and the organizations that help give it shape—a book that stages rebellion while rarely risking much rebellion of its own. Cricket first encounters Olympia when he is 10 and far from home, during a long bike ride soon after his grandfather’s death. Olympia is spending time with another boy, but once she recognizes Cricket from school, she recruits him to vandalize a local playground with risqué puns. Cricket takes pride in his graffiti, his first commission; it gives him “a blossoming sense of fulfillment and purpose.” Sometime later, Cricket is at an art lesson, and Olympia happens to be taking a piano lesson in the same house. They walk home together, Cricket carrying his latest painting, and the girl persuades him to enter an art contest. Cricket and Olympia’s relationship follows this pattern for much of the book—she disappears for a time, then appears unexpectedly. She’s full of energy, sophisticated references, and plans for both of them. She expresses and even demonstrates her affection for Cricket, but she never dedicates herself fully to him. There is always someone else—sometimes a would-be rock star with whom she’s infatuated, sometimes a painter or sculptor she has taken up as a cause. Whether Olympia is falling in love or nurturing talent, she leaves Cricket feeling displaced. Read: The death of the artist—and the birth of the creative entrepreneur Unfortunately, Eggers’s depiction of Olympia at this stage occasionally seems trite. Sometimes she resembles a manic pixie dream girl—the sort of figure the film critic Nathan Rabin once described as existing only “to teach broodingly soulful young men to embrace life and its infinite mysteries and adventures.” Eggers seems unaware that he is reproducing this trope; rather than playing with the cliché, he appears captive to it. We never know Olympia’s thoughts or feelings, merely her words. Although this is ostensibly a book about friendship, such a relationship—at least a literary one—requires access to the interior life of both participants. Instead, we have Olympia on a pedestal, where she is never Cricket’s equal. This asymmetry does more than flatten Olympia: It imbalances the novel. Contrapposto stakes its drama on a genuine contest between two visions of the artistic life, yet it grants full humanity to only one of the contestants. And Olympia’s vision deserves more airtime, because the novel clearly understands that talent alone rarely makes an artistic life possible. As she rises in the art world, Olympia encourages Cricket to pursue the opportunities that might give his work a public audience: college, gallery shows, meetings with patrons—ways of accessing the networks through which artists are recognized and sustained. This begins in their youth, when she persuades Cricket, after a few wayward years out of high school, to enroll in college. He does so (with her, of course), and she introduces him to the art scene on campus. But life in the academy only sharpens his suspicion of it. Rather than committing to his classes, Cricket gravitates toward an iconoclastic professor who publicly denounces his colleagues for their fidelity to settled artistic norms, and Cricket abandons the education that Olympia had hoped would foster and advance his talent. He will repeat this pattern all his life: cultivating his gift in private, at a remove from the systems that might have ushered it into the world. Olympia understands what Cricket refuses to learn—that a career is built as much as it is willed, that success usually demands compromise. Hers is, admittedly, conventional wisdom that any mentor would offer. But a truth does not have to be original to deserve an advocate. Eggers made his name by deriding, and then usurping, the literary establishment, in the process defying the tired binary of pure artist versus sellout. But he has written a novel that fails to inhabit the one character who might complicate that same well-known divide. Yet Contrapposto excels as a study of the development of an artist. Eggers writes with passion and precision about each step of Cricket’s progress, from his early tentative efforts to his growing mastery. We witness as he takes his first lesson, and as he begins to find his voice. Years later, we watch as he struggles to perfect a new skill: Cricket came to know the strange tragedy of painting, for most who try to do it: that there is such joy in the brush, such abandon in filling a canvas with paint—the mind disappears; all we are is what we see; we summon orgies of color, making a tiny perfect world—only to back away from our canvas and realize it’s shit. Eggers’s commitment to showing each stage of Cricket’s growth is essential. (In a metafictional twist, we can judge that development for ourselves: The pages are illustrated with Eggers’s own drawings, presented as Cricket’s.) By depicting the frustrating, ecstatic, plodding, and astonishing process of creating art, he argues convincingly for the importance of discipline as a way of building your life. Cricket is far more interested in improvement than recognition because he believes that cultivating ability, instead of fame, yields its own considerable rewards. This is the book’s most resonant idea: that by committing to a daily practice of self-improvement, a person is, beyond their chosen practice, also becoming someone who can perceive what others cannot, who seizes moments and experiences instead of letting them pass by. [ Read: A strikingly complex portrait of a Founding Father ] Eggers seems to be both Cricket and Olympia: He wants to carve a lane for himself as a vibrant, essential artist while blazing a pathway for others who wish to do the same. And the author of A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius and You Shall Know Our Velocity might have seemed especially well suited to take on this dilemma with formal risk. Instead, Contrapposto often settles for familiar rhythms: the sensitive male artist, the elusive woman who inspires him, the old drama of purity versus compromise. Perhaps this is inevitable. Cricket is presented as the rebel, yet his rebellion is curiously backward-looking: He has little use for the contemporary or the abstract, instead drawing models and painting traditional scenes. Olympia, meanwhile, represents status and accommodation, but because the novel denies her meaningful interiority, it cannot fully imagine the seductions or burdens of her position. The result is a book that makes a case for artistic freedom while repeatedly reaching for inherited forms: in its structure, in its gendered imagination, even in the drawings it offers as proof of Cricket’s independence. The writing is quite pleasurable in parts, and the conclusion is genuinely moving. But it is not a work of staggering genius.

title: Democrats lure ‘politically homeless’ Gen Z toward socialism — a counterattack is taking shape
content: Democrats are targeting "politically homeless" young people by offering them a sense of belonging, conservative activist CJ Pearson warned, arguing that the left is aggressively steering Gen Z toward socialism and DEI. "When I look at why young people are at least flirting with socialism right now, I think it's because they're politically homeless. I think they're looking for a place where they feel heard, where they feel seen," said Pearson. Pearson’s warning comes as he launches Next250, a political action committee aimed at organizing young conservatives, registering voters in swing states and countering support for socialism and DEI among Gen Z. The PAC also plans to spend $1 million on digital ads targeting young and minority voters in Georgia. Pearson said Democrats have been more aggressive than conservatives in reaching young voters who feel politically alienated or uncertain about where they belong. SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM "The left is vigilant," he said. "Every single day, they are trying to indoctrinate America’s young people. Every single day, they’re trying to pollute their minds with untruths and just downright delusion." Pearson pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has embraced the democratic socialist label and supported government-run grocery stores, rent freezes and universal child care. The movement also gained ground when three congressional candidates endorsed by Mamdani — Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier — won their Democratic primaries. "What I am saying to my generation who are looking at folks like Mamdani as potential solutions to a problem," said Pearson. MAMDANI DOUBLES DOWN ON DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISM WHILE INSISTING WALL STREET, BUSINESS LEADERS CAN WORK WITH HIM Pearson said he sees a similar dynamic at play in the debate over diversity, equity and inclusion, arguing the policies have fostered what he called the "soft bigotry of low expectations." "The left loves to put young Black men like me in boxes. I'm a young Black man who grew up in the Deep South to a mother who chose life, who was raised by his grandparents," said Pearson. Despite what he described as the left’s assumptions about his background, Pearson said the values he learned growing up — including faith, patriotism and a strong work ethic — made conservatism a natural fit. KEY TRUMP AGENCY PUTS TOP UNIVERSITIES IN CROSSHAIRS OVER ALLEGED RACE-BASED DORM PROGRAMS Since taking office, the Trump administration has sought to roll back DEI initiatives throughout the federal government, arguing the programs promote discrimination and merit should guide hiring and admissions decisions. Pearson said he is building on his success organizing events for young conservatives to launch Next250, a political action committee aimed at countering support for socialism and DEI on college campuses. His PAC will go head-to-head with the ideology embraced by younger students by rallying conservatives in deep blue areas and swing states for voter registration. He sees partnering with fraternities and sororities as a way to build a force capable of pushing back against socialism and DEI. "We're going to take this MAGA party on the road. We're going go to swing states like Georgia, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa. And we're going to throw these events and we're going to welcome young people around to them and we are going to have voter registration. We are going get them to the polls," said Pearson. He added that the left's embrace of socialism and DEI candidates has already backfired for them. The left wants to "accuse us being a Nazi. Well, that man had a Nazi tattoo on his chest and Democrats had no problem with it," said Pearson referencing former Maine Senate nominee Graham Platner who withdrew his candidacy after a bombshell rape allegation. Pearson also plans to deploy $1 million for digital ads that target both young and minority voters in his home state of Georgia . "America has been on a generational run, a 250-year run that was marketed by innovation, opportunity, and truly the hallmark and the pillars of the American dream. But if the left gets their way, there will not be another 250 years," said Pearson.

title: After Democrats' shake-up, Collins faces toss-up against Platner replacement in must-win Senate race
content: The first Fox News Power Rankings of the 2026 midterm elections and a new poll both indicate an extremely close contest between longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Troy Jackson, the candidate set to replace ex-nominee Graham Platner as the Democratic challenger, in what's expected to be a premiere Senate battleground. The Fox News Power Rankings, which gauge the competitiveness of elections using data, reporting and analysis, ranks the showdown in Maine as a toss-up. The midterm ballot box battle is one of roughly a dozen Senate contests that will determine if the Democrats win back the chamber or if Republicans hold onto their slim majority. Meanwhile, a Pine Tree Poll conducted over the past seven days by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center indicates Jackson with a slight three-point edge over Collins among likely general election voters in Maine. WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN: CHECK OUT THE FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS ON THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, is on a glide path to replace Platner at Saturday's Maine Democratic Party nominating convention in Bangor, after winning the vast majority of the 500 voting delegates chosen this past weekend by Democrats in the state's 16 counties. And most of Jackson's top rivals for the nomination backed him after dropping out of the race on Sunday. While the delegates on Jackson's slate are not required to support him at the convention in Bangor, Maine, he is now considered all but certain to secure the nomination. A fifth-generation logger and a one-time conservative Republican who became a Democrat over two decades ago, Jackson came in third place last month in Maine's Democratic gubernatorial primary . Platner dropped out earlier this month, amid calls from top Democrats in Maine and across the country to immediately exit the race following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but stepped aside. FIVE THINGS TO KNOW ABOUT TROY JACKSON, WHO'S ABOUT TO REPLACE GRAHAM PLATNER AS THE DEMOCRATS' SENATE NOMINEE Jackson, who had campaigned alongside Platner during the primary, quickly made the case that he was the best equipped candidate to grab the mantle of the progressive and populist movement that had backed Platner. Along with Platner, Jackson had the support of progressive champion Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont as he ran for governor, and he is currently backed by Our Revolution, the group born in 2016 out of Sanders' first presidential campaign. Jackson, similar to Platner, is running on a platform aimed at working-class voters. He backs raising taxes on billionaires, the universal healthcare system known as "Medicare-for-all," abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and he opposes military aid to Israel at a time that Democrats are increasingly divided on support for America's longtime Middle East ally. Collins, as she runs for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, is facing a rough political climate for Republicans, amid GOP President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings, persistent inflation and what polls indicate is an unpopular war with Iran. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The senator, known as a moderate Republican who at times has voted against Trump, last month received bipartisan praise after reaching a milestone by casting her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote. But Democrats are taking aim at Collins over her comments that she didn't regret her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, despite his crucial vote four years later to overturn the landmark Roe v. Wade abortion ruling. And following the fatal shooting in Maine earlier this month involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, Democrats heavily criticized the Senate Appropriations Committee chair for her support for ICE funding. But Collins has a history of defeating the Democrats' efforts to oust her from the Senate. Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the then-Maine House speaker, but the senator ended up winning re-election by nearly 9 points. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the U.S. Senate . That means Democrats would need a net gain of four seats in the midterms to retake the majority, which they lost in the 2024 elections. The Senate race in Maine, along with battles for Republican-controlled Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio, are ranked as toss-ups in the Fox News Power Rankings.

title: Republicans aren’t stopping: GOP to unleash another ‘big, beautiful bill’ with a new target
content: FIRST ON FOX: The No. 2 leader in the House of Representatives has confirmed plans for a fourth "big, beautiful bill" that would tackle government waste and abuse of federal dollars. "If you're a single waitress, working three shifts at a diner, Democrats voted against you keeping your tip money … so that they can give that money to fraudsters in Minnesota who were sending it to terrorist organizations," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., told Fox News Digital, referring to Republicans' first sweeping party-line budget bill that President Donald Trump dubbed his "one big, beautiful bill." "It's insane, but that was really going on. There’s more of it. We want to root that out. So we're gonna move yet another reconciliation bill to focus on things like rooting out waste and fraud, to give that money back to taxpayers." TOP REPUBLICAN PUSHES FOR RECONCILIATION 3.0 TO ADDRESS AFFORDABILITY The budget reconciliation process allows the party in power in Congress to pass sweeping fiscal policy legislation while completely sidelining the other side — in this case, Democrats. It does so by bypassing the Senate filibuster — which needs 60 votes to overcome — allowing the upper chamber to line up with the House's own simple majority threshold. But the measures in a reconciliation bill must adhere to a strict set of rules, such as not touching Social Security and only including policies that would affect the federal budget. GOP'S $95B DEFENSE PACKAGE SURVIVES CRITICAL HURDLE AMID FISCAL HAWK REVOLT Congressional Republicans have passed two reconciliation bills so far, one focused on Trump's tax priorities and another replenishing funds for the president's immigration crackdown. The GOP is working on a third that would add some $95 billion in federal spending over the next 10 years. It includes $73 billion toward the U.S. war with Iran , $12 billion in aid for American farmers, and $10 billion for states to implement election security measures that were part of the SAVE America Act . But some House fiscal hawks are threatening to oppose the measure over its lack of spending cuts to offset those dollars. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought both pitched a fourth bill during a closed-door meeting on Tuesday morning in a bid to assuage those concerns, multiple people told Fox News Digital. Scalise's comments are the first public confirmation from a member of House GOP senior leadership that such a bill was in the works. "We want to move that as soon as we finish reconciliation 3.0. So when we were working on reconciliation 2.0, we were already starting to put together 3.0, but we waited until we passed 2.0. Then we went right to work on this latest reconciliation bill," Scalise said.

title: Dem Rep Seth Moulton says party has no immigration plan, is only ‘opposition to Trump’
content: Democratic Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., acknowledged Tuesday on MS NOW's "Money, Power, Politics" that Democrats have failed to give voters a clear immigration plan and rely too heavily on opposition to President Donald Trump, as he discussed the party's challenges in Arizona's gubernatorial primary . "We don’t have a plan for immigration . We’re not able to say what, actually, Democrats should do to fix the problem," Moulton said. "All we are is opposition to Trump." The Massachusetts congressman and U.S. Senate candidate said he had tested voters' understanding of the party's position during town halls across his state. BIDEN ADMINISTRATION FORCED A FALSE CHOICE ON AMERICANS ABOUT IMMIGRATION "I’ll ask people, ‘How many of you are opposed to Trump’s immigration enforcement?’ Every hand in the room goes up," Moulton said, adding, "Like, I’ve asked thousands of people in Massachusetts this question." The congressman also faulted Democrats for dismissing other voter concerns, including inflation, during former President Joe Biden's administration. "Under Biden, we said inflation is not really a big deal. It’s transitory. It’s going to go away," Moulton said. "The point is we have this history of kind of just like washing over problems and not addressing real concerns that voters have." DYING FORMER CONGRESSMAN BARNEY FRANK TELLS DEMOCRATS THEIR FAR-LEFT MESSAGING IS COSTING THEM VOTERS Fox News Digital reached out to the Democratic National Committee for comment but did not immediately receive a response. When host Stephanie Ruhle noted that Republicans benefited from having a defined immigration approach, Moulton contrasted Trump's enforcement agenda with his party's response. "This is criminal what Trump is doing," Moulton said. "And the fact that we don’t even have an answer to that is a real problem." HOUSE REPUBLICANS MOVE TO MAKE TRUMP'S BORDER POLICIES PERMANENT Moulton outlined his own approach, calling for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), prosecution of officials who break the law and reforms encouraging legal immigration . "So, yes, abolish ICE, prosecute these people for breaking the law, but then show how we’re going to fix the problem," he said. The congressman said the current system made the legal route unnecessarily difficult. "Right now, it’s easier for people to come across the border than to go through the bureaucratic process," Moulton said. Moulton's congressional website states that he supports comprehensive immigration reform that secures the border, curbs illegal immigration, expands legal pathways and provides a path to citizenship. In January, he backed legislation intended to allow ICE officers to be prosecuted for misconduct. Rep. Moulton is challenging Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., in the state’s Sept. 1 Democratic Senate primary. A University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll conducted June 18-23 found Markey leading Moulton 41% to 35% among likely Democratic primary voters, with 23% undecided. The poll had a 5.1-point margin of error.

title: Former Bernie Sanders official accuses senator of pushing most antisemitic candidates 'in a generation'
content: Former campaign official for Sen. Bernie Sanders , I-Vt., Joel Rubin called out the Vermont senator last week for pushing the "most categorically anti-Israel, antisemitic candidates" he's seen in recent years. "I think what Sanders and the Sanders operation have done is shove into our system the most categorically anti-Israel, antisemitic candidates that we’ve seen in a generation — if ever, certainly within the Democratic Party — and it’s by design," Rubin said in an interview with Jewish Insider . "The goal is to undermine Democratic unity and even rationality on Israel at this stage," Rubin said. SANDERS UNDER FIRE FOR PROPPING UP PLATNER AS DEMS TORCH HIS TOXIC ENDORSEMENT 'PATTERN' Rubin, who was also a State Department official under President Barack Obama , previously led Jewish outreach for Sanders' 2020 presidential campaign. However, following Sanders' past support for former Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner , who sported a tattoo resembling a Nazi "totenkopf," a skull-and-crossbones design, Rubin has since concluded that his former boss is now intentionally pushing antisemitism. Rubin went as far as to refer to Sanders as an "outright hostile actor" pushing a "hate-based narrative" surrounding Israel along with several rising Democratic politicians. "I’m extremely disappointed. I feel like it violates the goals of promoting peace in the Middle East and the two-state solution, and I believe that it exacerbates the pain and distress that the American Jewish community is experiencing right now in Israel policy," Rubin said. "I had higher hopes for a senator who is Jewish, and his team who knows very well what’s out there." FETTERMAN DEMANDS BERNIE SANDERS APOLOGIZE FOR BACKING ALLEGED 'PREDATOR' GRAHAM PLATNER IN MAINE SENATE RACE He warned that these efforts would leave Democrats vulnerable in elections against the Republican Party, particularly as support for Israel appears to be a new breaking point for progressive candidates. "I don’t know what’s going on inside that operation. There is no line. There is no bottom. There is no low," Rubin said. "And what it’s doing now is gutting American Jewish confidence in the Democratic Party, which is not a way to win elections, and it’s unethical as well, considering American Jews have been a bedrock community supporting the Democratic Party." "We need leadership, and the progressive community needs to stop scapegoating Jews for all problems in the world," he added. CLICK HERE TO FOLLOW FOX NEWS MEDIA AND CULTURE ON FACEBOOK Fox News Digital reached out to Sanders' office for comment but did not immediately hear back. Along with Platner, Sanders has campaigned for and endorsed Melat Kiros in Colorado and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan , who have both criticized Israel for committing an alleged "genocide" during its war in Gaza. Sanders was also one of several Democratic members of Congress who have supported efforts to cut $3 billion in aid to Israel .

title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Judge Boasberg whines about Trump’s power and then gets caught exceeding his own
content: Chief Judge James Boasberg is frustrated ... and he is not alone. Recently, the D.C. federal judge reportedly groused that the D.C. appellate court had ordered him to reconsider a case about whether the D.C. government engaged in biased enforcement against political graffiti. Conversely, the litigants are equally irked over what they see as Boasberg's bias after he responded by, again, dismissing their claims without a trial. For a second time, Boasberg has barred pro-life groups from access to a jury after members were arrested for writing in chalk, "Black Pre-Born Lives Matter" on a sidewalk while Black Lives Matter writings were left untouched. I wrote earlier about the emerging body of " Boasberg's Law ," cases in which the judge has increasingly shown an untethered and expansive view of his own authority. Recently, Boasberg was found to have committed an "abuse of discretion" in twice finding that the Trump administration was in contempt of court for failing to turn around deportation flights. DC APPEALS COURT ORDERS JUDGE BOASBERG TO HALT TRUMP CONTEMPT PROBE OVER DEPORTATION FLIGHTS My disagreements with Boasberg are not over the underlying issues, but rather the court's rejection of basic limits on its own authority. While chastising President Donald Trump for exceeding his authority, Boasberg has been reversed for exceeding his own. In the earlier case, Boasberg dismissed grand jury subpoenas in the probe of Fed Chair Jerome Powell . I have been critical of that probe, but Boasberg's refusal to allow the subpoenas to be executed was based on an opinion that was rife with open hostility for Trump, dubious sources and biased observations. I have similar reservations in this latest case. During the Black Lives Matter protests of 2020, streets in Washington were covered with BLM graffiti and the police watched as protesters wrote slogans and slurs on stores, streets and sidewalks. The government itself even commissioned a massive painting of the message on a street near the White House. GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS However, when the Frederick Douglass Foundation and Students for Life of America wrote their pro-life version of the slogan, they were immediately arrested and the chalk protest removed. The D.C. Circuit's reversal of Boasberg in the case was a major victory for free speech. Boasberg had applied the wrong standard to kill the case, holding that the group could not challenge the selective enforcement of the laws. In reaching that conclusion, Boasberg applied the wrong standard, imposing the heavy burden of proving that the city was engaged in "invidious enforcement." While that standard was used correctly to dismiss an equal protection claim, it is not the standard for a free speech challenge. The court did not hide its dissatisfaction with the thrust of Boasberg's opinion in dismissing the First Amendment claim : "The First Amendment prohibits government discrimination on the basis of viewpoint. 'To permit one side … to have a monopoly in expressing its views … is the antithesis of constitutional guarantees.' The protection for freedom of speech applies not only to legislation, but also to enforcement of the laws." The appellate court sent the case back to Boasberg with the opportunity to apply the correct standard and to create a substantive record before issuing a ruling on the free speech claim. Boasberg took the case and ruled again that the groups would not be allowed a trial . The new dismissal was issued despite the standard that, in seeking such a dismissal before a trial, the court must accept all material facts in favor of the nonmoving party or, in this case, the pro-life and pro-free-speech litigants. Boasberg rejected the factual claim that they were "similarly situated" to the BLM protesters. The litigants presented the results of discovery on the point, but Boasberg dismissed the claim on his own subjective view of the evidence. They have now filed again with the appellate court to appeal his order. Some of Boasberg's factual findings are baffling. For example, he maintains that the groups did not show that MPD officers "even witnessed any specific defacement during [Black Lives Matter] protests." However, the groups presented such evidence as bodycam video of officers watching as a protester spray-painted 'I can’t breathe' on the street near the White House two weeks after the arrests of the pro-life protesters. They submitted other video evidence of officers watching protesters spray-paint BLM messages outside of the Department of Justice. Moreover, they presented what they claimed was guidance from Assistant Chief of Police Jeffery Carroll, in charge of the Metropolitan Police Department's Special Operations Division, in the application of different treatment for graffiti. Carroll reportedly admitted to being "present" at BLM protests featuring "defacement" of property, public and private, and Lt. Jason Bagshaw admitted that he also saw defacement "related to" BLM protests. This does not mean that a jury would rule for these litigants, but rather that the court cannot substitute its judgment for a jury when a credible and supported claim has been made by litigants. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Boasberg declares that no such credible evidence was presented. The fact is that a reasonable jury could conclude that there was different treatment shown in the enforcement of these laws based on the content of the speech. The biased enforcement of laws to crack down on speech is a common reality in other countries where courts enable such selective enforcement. In countries such as Iran and China, no level of evidence is sufficient to overcome the bias of courts in showing a preference for one side. Judge Boasberg has had a distinguished career that is now being undone by a lack of restraint in these decisions. Again, I believe that the judge has been on solid ground in some of these conflicts, including criticizing the use of "intemperate and disrespectful" language in filings and demanding compliance with his orders. However, while Chief Judge Boasberg has described the president's claim of expansive powers as "awfully frightening," the same can be said about a judge who substitutes his own judgment for juries and disregards legal standards for disfavored groups. The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution." CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JONATHAN TURLEY

title: Jason Alexander apologizes after Courtney Stodden says 2012 comedy sketch objectified her as a minor
content: Jason Alexander is taking accountability for his past mistakes. The 66-year-old actor recently apologized to Courtney Stodden for participating in a 2012 Funny or Die sketch in which he held a cellphone up to her chest and made comments about her body when she was a minor. "Looking back at the comedy sketch in which Ms. Stodden and I participated in 2012, I completely agree that it was inappropriate and I truly regret it," he told Fox News Digital in a statement. "But more importantly, I am deeply sorry for any harm or distress it has caused Ms. Stodden. I offer her my sincerest apologies." His apology comes one day after Stodden called out Alexander on Instagram as one of the writers of the sketch, adding, "As an adult, that fact has become harder—not easier—for me to understand." GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE' In the Instagram post, she shared a photo of her and Alexander in the sketch, in which she is wearing a bikini, and the actor is rubbing a cellphone across her chest. "I was 17 years old in this photo. The older I get, the more impossible this is to understand," she wrote. "During this comedy sketch, Jason Alexander repeatedly rubbed his phone across my breasts while saying there was 'no signal' in my head but 'plenty of signal' in my chest. Later in the sketch, he joked that when I turned 18 he’d like to take me behind the couch and 'have his way' with me." She added that as a minor she "didn’t have the legal power to decide whether I wanted to participate" and that "the contracts were signed by adults." At the time, she was married to Doug Hutchison, who she tied the knot with when she was 16 and he was 51, noting the paycheck for this appearance went to him. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "I was the only child in the room. I felt so alone," she added. "Looking back now, I don’t see comedy. I see a 17-year-old girl whose body became part of an adult joke. People still say, 'You chose to be there.' Legally, I couldn’t make those decisions for myself. That’s the point." She ended the post by acknowledging that while she isn't able to change what she went through, she finds herself asking, "How did so many adults look at a minor and decide this was acceptable?" CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER "That’s exactly why I speak out today," she concluded. "Children deserve laws that protect them. They shouldn’t have to become adults before realizing the law should have protected them all along." The caption also included a call to support California Assembly Bill 1267, which aims to permanently end child marriage by setting the minimum legal age for marriage in California to 18 with no exceptions. Stodden and Hutchison got married in 2011 despite their 34-year age gap. They split up and got back together a few times before officially calling it quits in 2016, although divorce papers were not filed until March 2018, with the divorce being finalized in March 2020. She announced their divorce in an Instagram post featuring her wedding photo, calling it "an emotional day," but assured her fans "it’s for the better." "I look back at this picture and feel absolutely taken advantage of ," she wrote. "I’ve been scared to even speak up about feeling groomed or being verbally abused during the almost 10 year marriage because I was a child and he was 50 when we married but I’m a woman now and it’s time for me to put my big girl pants on and speak on this matter." She continued: "I’ve felt completely trapped, manipulated and at times abandoned by adults // growing up in such an environment — it became a lonely and dark place."
