title: Kelsey Grammer warns of chilling danger facing Americans who forget nation's founding history
content: Actor Kelsey Grammer issued a warning about the state of American education , arguing that citizens who fail to learn the nation's founding history risk being manipulated. Speaking on "Planet Tyrus" Tuesday, Grammer called for an overhaul of the nation's education system while pushing back against critics who dismiss the Founding Fathers as "old White guys in wigs." "If you don't know where you come from, you don't know who you are. If you don't know who you are, you can be controlled," Grammer warned. SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH "There's a whole bunch of things that just have got to stop with our educational system, and we got to retool it. There's no question," he said. Grammer recently starred in the film, "Young Washington," which follows the Founding Father before he became the nation's first president. Grammer also hosted the six-episode Fox Nation series "The Patriot War," narrating key points in the American Revolution ahead of the nation's 250th anniversary. The former "Frasier" and "Cheers" actor said America's past serves as a blueprint for its future — one he believes many young people are dismissing. KELSEY GRAMMER URGES AMERICANS TO LOOK TO FOUNDING FATHERS FOR GUIDANCE AS NATION FACES DEEP DIVISIONS "Yeah, I'm pretty tired of the old White guy in [a] wig thing," Grammer told Tyrus. "I mean Thomas Jefferson was 33 when he wrote what is arguably the most important political document in the history of man," he said. Grammer emphasized that the American Revolution was fought on radical ideas rather than identity and called for a stronger push to teach early American history. "It never had anything to do with the way you looked," Grammer said. "It had everything to do with the way you thought and the way you dreamed, and that's all America." WATCH THE FULL 'PLANET TYRUS' INTERVIEW ON YOUTUBE He argued the Founding Fathers did not claim America would be perfect but envisioned an evolving quest for better. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The land of the possible. Yeah, absolutely. It's always [going to] fall a little short, but that's just it. It's the world of becoming. We're becoming a more perfect union, always, rather than we just are one," Grammer said. Grammer said that most of the 56 people who signed the Declaration of Independence "ended in ruin" by sacrificing everything for the nation. He added, "Some of their children were murdered, some of their wives were raped," and said their spirit of resilience in hard times remains today. "They paid the ultimate sacrifice, the ultimate one. And they would probably do it again. And I think that sort of character is what still is in most of us. I believe in America that way," Grammer said.

title: Former NFL player gets funding from sports notables, including Roger Goodell, for AZ primary race
content: Jay Feely, who spent 14 seasons as an NFL kicker for six teams, took a big step toward becoming a United States congressman representing a district that includes parts of Phoenix and most of Scottsdale by winning an Arizona Republican primary Tuesday night. Feely defeated former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik and businessman John Trobough in a race in which he had the endorsement of President Donald Trump but was accused by his opponents of not being conservative enough. HALL OF FAMER TONY DUNGY ENDORSES MICHELE TAFOYA IN CROWDED MINNESOTA REPUBLICAN PRIMARY FOR US SENATE Feely will face the winner of a still-uncalled Democrat primary between former state Rep. Amish Shah and former broadcast journalist Marlene Galán-Woods in the general election. "Why did I decide to run for office? It is a desire to leave this country better for our children and our grandchildren," Feely told his supporters at his victory celebration. "That's it in its core. "You know, what we're doing is fighting for the future of this country. I truly believe that. When you look at the two parties, they've never been further apart ideologically. Never. And the Democrat Party has embraced Democratic socialism. "They have chosen to move further to the left. They are talking about abolishing the border. They're talking about abolishing the police department. They are talking about abolishing the Senate now. They want to get D.C. and Puerto Rico statehood. "The things that they are talking about are changing the very foundation of this country, and what has made it great for 250 years. And we're not going to let it happen." The Democrats spent approximately $7 million in their primary race, which illustrates how important they believe getting the right candidate to face off against Feely would be. Feely, making his first bid for public office at age 50, was also well funded for his primary battle and, not surprisingly, at lot of that cash came from the sports world. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell contributed $7,000, which is the legal maximum for an individual. Cardinals owner Michael Bidwill similarly gave $7,000 to lead a handful of owners joining the Feely cause. Atlanta Falcons owner Arthur Blank ($3,500), New England Patriots owner Bob Kraft ($7,000), Miami Dolphins owner Stephen Ross ($5,000) and Denver Broncos owner Rob Walton ($7,000) all contributed. Cleveland Browns owner Jimmy Haslam also donated. Former players similarly helped fund Feely's campaign. Former quarterbacks John Elway, Rich Gannon and Trent Green contributed. So did Jeff Saturday, Todd Heap, Richie Incognito, and Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS And this: Charles Barkley contributed the maximum $7,000. Feely should expect a tough campaign and close race in the coming months regardless of his opponent. District 1 was reliably red from 1953 to 2009, but massive population growth over the years and a 2022 redrawing of the district's lines turned it into a race Democrats won five times starting in 2013 and believe they can flip this year after losing in 2022. title: Sophie Cunningham sparks social media meltdown by speaking out to protect women's sports
content: WNBA star Sophie Cunningham sent shockwaves in the ongoing culture war over the WNBA and trans athletes in women's sports on Tuesday after revealing her stance on the issue to ESPN. Cunningham's recent statements sparked debate on social media after she revealed she is in support of protecting women's sports. "I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" Cunningham said. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." Many prominent figures praised Cunningham for speaking out. GOP politicians, including Ted Cruz and Eric Schmitt, even chimed in. Cunningham's statement also garnered praise from athletes and activists involved in the " save women's sports " movement including Riley Gaines, Jennifer Sey and Martina Navratilova, as well as other conservative influencers. However, Cunningham's statements also prompted some backlash from those who believe biological male trans athletes should be allowed to compete in women's sports. Some users compared Cunningham's take to that of Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve, who recently told reporters that she opposes bans on trans athletes in women's sports. Cunningham previously garnered backlash from the left in March 2022 after re-sharing a tweet from CBS Sports host Josh Pate about the controversy surrounding former Penn transgender swimmer Lia Thomas competing on the women's team. "Female collegiate athletes deserve so much better than this," Pate’s tweet said. "To my teammates, friends, family, supporters and fans, you know that I stand with all people, especially my fellow athletes. I do not judge, but support all races, religions, sexual preferences and gender equity. We all have a place in this world to compete and I hope we are able to grant everyone that opportunity fairly." she wrote. Cunningham has emerged as one of the biggest stars in the WNBA over the last year, especially among conservatives . Riley Gaines, who tied with Thomas at the 2022 NCAA women's swimming championships, told Fox News Digital on the last day of June, after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled to uphold state laws that keep biological males out of women's sports, that she hoped the ruling would be a "clarion call" for athletes like Cunningham to speak out in support of protecting women's sports. "Let this be a clarion call, not just to Simone, but to every, I think especially elite female athlete, professional female athlete, the likes of Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, Serena Williams, to link arms," Gaines said.

title: Why Are Groceries So Expensive?
content: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts questioning whether the Trump administration has any plan at all to meet the challenge of debt and deficits. Then, David is joined by Vincent Smith, director of agricultural policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute and professor emeritus of economics at Montana State University. Frum and Smith discuss the high price of groceries, Trump’s lack of a plan to address it, and whether any relief is coming to Americans. Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of Edith Hamilton’s Mythology . The following is a transcript of the episode: Vincent Smith: The story that you have heard from many Trump-administration officials—that the tariffs will lower the prices, people who import goods from other countries will pay for those goods —that is simply empirically nonsense. This is Economics 101, by the way. And I’m afraid that some of the Trump officials, if they actually believe what they’re saying, have flunked Economics 101. David Frum: Hello. Welcome to The David Frum Show . I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic . My guest this week will be Vincent Smith, a professor of economics at Montana State University. We’ll be discussing the high price of groceries and whether there is any hope that those prices will cease to rise so rapidly anytime soon. This week’s book is Edith Hamilton’s Mythology , a book selected in homage to the recent release of Christopher Nolan’s movie The Odyssey . But before either the dialogue with Vince Smith or the discussion of Edith Hamilton’s mythology, some opening thoughts building on l ast week’s discussion with Maya MacGuineas about the burden of debt and deficit created and bequeathed by the Trump administration. One of the questions you might have left over from last week’s discussion about the crushing burden of debt and the danger of the inter-interest cost to the American taxpayer is whether the Trump administration has any plan at all to meet the challenge of debt and deficit. It says it does. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent has been promoting a plan he calls “three plus three plus three.” The idea is: If the United States can somehow raise its growth level to 3 percent, if it can produce 3 million more barrels of oil per day, then by the time the Trump administration ends, the deficit will have been driven down to about 3 percent of GDP, which is a sustainable level. Right now, if you wanna have—if you wanna collect the numbers, the deficit is running at about 5.7 percent of GDP, a figure that is not considered sustainable. So that’s his promise. If you can get the growth up to 3 percent, if you can produce 3 million barrels a day more oil than the United States is now doing, then there is hope that the deficit numbers can be brought down to 3 percent of GDP, a level that is sustainable, that doesn’t continue to accelerate and get worse. In other words, the plan is to grow our way out of it. Now, more growth would be a good thing, but let’s talk about whether this plan is feasible or not. Three percent is not an impossible growth number for the United States, and when the United States came out of the pandemic under President Biden, there were quarters when the growth rate neared 3 percent annually. And it was not beyond imagination that the United States might actually achieve 3 percent annually. It hasn’t achieved that kind of figure in the second Trump administration, and the Trump administration badly wants it to. But the policies don’t line up with anything they say they wanna do. Economies grow for two reasons. They grow because they add more factors of production, typically more population or maybe more resources of some kind. Or they grow by becoming more efficient—by using the resources they have more efficiently. So one is called extensive, and the other is called intensive growth. Add more factors of production, you get more growth. Use them more efficiently, you get more intensive growth. The Trump administration’s policies crush both extensive growth and intensive growth. They have an anti-immigration policy that is making the labor force grow very, very slowly and, in fact, probably shrink in an aging population. And their protectionism means that the economy operates less efficiently. So they have fewer resources to use, and they’re using them less efficiently. That is why the growth rate has been so disappointing in the first year plus of the Trump administration. The Trump administration is gambling everything on an AI-productivity miracle. By applying the new technologies of artificial intelligence, the American economy will get so much more efficient that even though the population isn’t growing—and even though the efficiency of every other part of the economy is being damaged by Trump’s protectionism, his high tariffs—the AI miracle will add so much to growth so fast that it will overcome the slow growth in population because of the immigration crackdown and the inefficiencies of protectionism. It might, but it isn’t, and it isn’t happening soon. But there’s a little caveat that the Trump people don’t tend to notice. Which is: Supposing this AI miracle does show up and the economy suddenly becomes much more productive, one of the immediate consequences of the AI miracle will be an elimination of many, many categories of jobs. Now, that doesn’t mean that employment will vanish forever and people will never have anything to do, the way some AI doomsters predict. I don’t agree with that at all. There will always be things for people to do. But there will be a period of shock where machines do things that people used to do, and people will have to find new things to do using the powerful new machines. And in that period, employment will shrink, and there goes your extensive growth. And even if you believe, and maybe it’s true, that the AI revolution will create more intensive growth, and so although there are fewer people working, they’re generating more wealth—the other thing the Trump people keep forgetting is when the economy grows faster, that creates more demand for capital. And that means the Federal Reserve raises interest rates. And when interest rates rise, of course, the federal government, which owes so much money, pays more in debt service. So they’ve got a box that—even if you believe their own theory—can’t possibly work. Their numbers really don’t add up, as the Congressional Budget Office keeps pointing out. And keeps pointing out that the United States, even under the most optimal scenario—the best case, what the CBO calls the best realistic case—is that deficit simply doesn’t get any worse than it is now and the debt continues to grow. There’s almost no scenario where “three plus three plus three” works. Administrations often sell things, and that’s maybe not a surprise. But it is kind of alarming to realize that the administration has a plan for what it regards as one of its most important domestic problems that doesn’t make sense according to any of the experts, and that it’s hard to believe that the people pushing the plan even can really believe. And yet they keep saying it, because they keep offering some kind of promise of a better tomorrow to make up for the bad realities of today. As you make up your mind whether the present crew can be trusted with more power in government or less power in government after the 2026 elections, keep in mind: They really don’t know what they’re doing. And to the extent they do know what they’re doing, they know that it won’t work. And now my dialogue with Vince Smith. [ Music ] Frum: Vince Smith is professor emeritus of economics at Montana State University and director of agricultural policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute. He spent more than three decades on the Montana State faculty in the Department of Agricultural Economics, and including stints directing the Agricultural Marketing Policy Center and the Initiative for Regulation and Applied Economic Analysis. He’s the author or editor of nine books, including multiple volumes of Agricultural Policy in Disarray , and has published well over 100 articles making the case that the federal government’s approach to supporting farmers is expensive, poorly targeted, and resistant to reform. He’s a familiar voice in The Wall Street Journal and a helpful source to me in my articles for The Atlantic about food prices and food markets. Vince, welcome to The David Frum Show. Vincent Smith: Oh, pleasure to be here, David. Thank you for inviting me. Frum: Now, we are at a moment when food prices are high. Americans are suffering the cost. There’s understandably a lot of unease and a lot of complaint. Everyone is looking for someone to blame. The president of the United States has been calling on grocery stores to cut their prices. He wants to blame them. The new mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani, is calling for state-owned grocery stores to squeeze out price gouging and profiteering by the grocery-store industry, which he alleges is a terrible problem. Those who study agricultural economics look for broader explanations. No one has studied these markets deeper than you. Why are food prices high? Why are they rising? Who’s to blame? Smith: Well, it’s a fascinating question. So let me reframe the debate a little bit. We have the perception that food prices are high. And the question is: Are they high relative to other prices, given that we’re experiencing some inflation? Particularly, we saw very high rates of inflation in 2022 and 2021 during COVID. And correspondingly, we did have very high, by historical levels, rates of inflation in the basket of goods that we use to measure average food prices. And we saw, for food away from home in, for example, 2022, an 8 percent rise or approximately 8 percent rise in the price of a typical food basket. In-home food prices in COVID really surged even more. There was an 11 percent increase overall. Subsequently, in recent years, for example, in 2022, while food away from home has continued to increase at a little bit faster rate than the overall rate of inflation—for example, in 2024, prices for food away from home, that rate of increase was about 4 percent. Whereas for food at home in 2024, prices only went up by 1 percent or thereabouts. So if we set aside on average what prices were doing for food in ’22 and ’23, the last two, three years, food prices have increased at about the rate that they have increased historically. That is, very close to the overall rate of inflation. But I think what matters here is that food is different than some of the other commodities that we purchase, in that we go to the store every day. So if the price of coffee goes up a little bit, we notice that because we are so regularly at the grocery store. If the price of bread is 20 cents higher this week, I notice that, and I feel the pain in some important way. The other thing that makes food different and makes us more aware of what’s going on with the price of food is that it is an essential. It is something we cannot do without. So especially for lower-income consumers, when the price of food goes up and their incomes do not change—which is very typically the case, whether they’re on a fixed income or whether they’re in a moderate-income job—you have to buy bread, you have to buy protein, and so on. And so you’re aware that the share of your fixed income that goes to food is going up, especially when you’re low income. And then there are individual commodities where when the price jumps, everybody screams. And the classic example of that are eggs. And over the last four years, we’ve had two very significant periods where avian-flu disease has affected the domestic supply of eggs very significantly, and we’ve seen those prices—in 2022 for example—more than double. And fairly recently in 2025, we saw very sharp increases in the price of eggs, which almost everybody buys almost all the time. So we feel the pain. The callous economist would say, Well, food prices are really not going up that much faster than anything else. But the compassionate economist would say, It’s a pain that is felt, and it’s particularly felt by people on modest and low incomes . Frum: So the contention, if I can reduce what you just said, is that we have an inflation problem, and food prices are part of the inflation problem. But we don’t have a food-price-inflation problem separate from the general inflation problem. Smith: Fundamentally, that’s a very fair interpretation. There are fractions of a point at which food prices over the last few years have gone up a little bit faster annually [over] the overall inflation rate. Food is one of the places where every household notices when the price in dollar terms—in nominal terms, as economists say—goes up, because we just go to the grocery store a lot, as compared to, say, the home-improvement stores like Lowe’s or whatever. So we notice things more with food than with many other commodities. Frum: There is one price, one food price that has been outrunning the rest and maybe rising faster than inflation. And you and I have talked about this before, and that’s the price of beef. And beef plays— Smith: Yes. Frum: — a very special part in American diet, in American culture. I mean, eating beef is part of almost what it means to be an American. The steak, the hamburger. And the fact that beans or pork may not be rising as much is cold comfort to Americans who say, That’s why we work as hard as Americans do, harder than anybody in the world works. We work so hard in order to enjoy the American way of life, which begins with that cut of beef. And beef prices have been going quite bonkers over the past half decade. During the Biden administration, there were accusations of all kinds of collusion and price-fixing. You and I spoke about that at the time. Tell us the story of what is happening with beef prices. Smith: Well, very quickly, last year beef prices on average, beef and veal prices, rose by almost 12 percent compared to an overall inflation rate of somewhat a little bit less than 3 percent. And a food-inflation rate overall of about 3 percent, just under 3 percent. So yes, and if you look at food, beef prices on average, they’ve been going up almost twice as fast as the average rate of inflation for several years. The story here is, at least in my view, and I think the view of many economists who very carefully look at issues of market power among beef-processing plants, is that they are not the cause of the problem. The beef-processing-plant story is pretty straightforward. Yes; there are only four major processors of meat, in particular beef, in the country. And yes, that might imply they have some market power, both on the buying side and on the selling side. What that means—buying animals from feedlots and farms, and selling meat to Costco or Safeway or any other outlet. But because they are operating very large facilities, their actual average cost of producing cuts of beef from the animals is way lower than for small-scale, essentially boutique, processors. The sort of process actually that currently the Trump administration and the secretary of agriculture want to subsidize. Those are high-cost operations. They are boutique operations because they deal with specialty meats. Because processing costs for those meats are going to be high no matter where you send them, because the runs are so small in creating product for the consumer. They are, in the view of almost all economists who look carefully—these subsidies for small-scale operations are effectively a complete waste of federal dollars if the goal is to reduce the price of hamburger at your local grocery store. So if I look at the big producers, consumers—and to some extent, farmers—lose on the swings where the swings are market power. But they gain in terms of lower prices for consumers and higher prices for cattle. And one of the ironies, by the way, here is that there are some cattle-farm groups that want to blow up all the large-scale operations in the belief that then they will get a higher price for their beef, either at the feedlots or if they sell direct to processors at the processing plant. The evidence is, they’re entirely wrong. And frankly, on a bad day, I would describe the position of those producers, from an economic perspective, taking a double-barrel shotgun, pointing it at their feet, and unloading both barrels. It’s a financially really bad idea for them. And that’s not my view; that’s the view of numerous studies. Frum: But we want a villain to the story. The mayor of New York proposes grocery stores. The Biden administration proposed the beef-processing plant. The Trump administration flails around and points all kinds of fingers of blame. We want a villain here. We want an explanation. If there are no villains, what’s the explanation? Smith: Well, if you want to call it a villain, what you have to say is pretty straightforward. Ranchers have been downsizing their herd sizes over the last seven or eight years for a whole variety of reasons. One is: Growth in global demand for beef has led to an increase in beef prices. So now you have a cattle herd, and you’ve got old cows that are not as productive in providing calves that will end up very quickly, relatively quickly, going into the supply chain about 18 months after they’re born. Do you sell that older calf that is less productive in terms of generating offspring for a relatively high price of beef? Or do you keep it so that you can sustain and expand your cattle herd? Well, the price incentives for the last few years have been: Take the money now from that older cow—cull it—because that’s the optimal from your business-plan perspective way of going. So one story is that growth in global demand, which itself was pushing up beef prices, period, globally—and we operate in a global market—that’s, if you like, the villain. How dare other people in countries like China want to consume more beef, including American beef? Is that a bad thing or a good thing? A very interesting question for cattle producers in the U.S., but they’re gonna say it’s a good thing. And consumers are going to say, Oh, dear, that means we’re paying relatively more for our beef, and we’re gonna adjust our consumption patterns. Frum: Why doesn’t the growth in beef prices cause ranchers to buy more cows or raise more cows and build their herds? Why are they shrinking their herds if the demand is going up? Smith: It’s a very intriguing question. Let me just say, you add to that in 2022, 2023, severe drought in many, many of the major cattle-producing regions in the U.S., and forage prices go up. So sustaining your herd becomes very expensive as well. And that in particular has contributed to the surge in prices that we have seen over the last two years, because high feed costs led to a reduction in herd size. Because why keep a cow that’s not that productive in the first place when you don’t really have the feed for the cow and the calf available to you, except at very high prices? A reason why we’ve seen a shrinkage of the herd size has been because it’s economically profitable for ranchers to do that. They’re optimizing in terms of profit maximization and risk minimization by having reduced herd size. And the beef guys that I talked with, the beef economists that I talked with, are now wondering if we’re at a tipping point where we will begin to see some growth. But it’s not going to happen this week. It’s not going to happen before the November elections—which is of great concern to the Trump administration. It’s going to happen maybe over the next three years. And for a political process that focuses on four months from now, that’s not going to help them. So these other measures that are being put about by the secretary of agricult

title: FCC Chairman Carr says spectrum auction will make wireless faster, cheaper while raising billions for Treasury
content: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Wednesday took a major step toward setting up the United States to be the global leader in wireless innovation, which Chairman Brendan Carr believes will make wireless both faster and cheaper for consumers. The FCC voted to adopt rules to auction 160 megahertz of spectrum in the Upper C-Band by July 2027, which combines terrestrial wireless operations across the entire C-Band to create a single "super-band" spanning 440 megahertz (3.70-4.14 GHz) of prime, mid-band spectrum. While the details are technical for most Americans, Carr said he is simply fulfilling the Trump administration’s agenda. "One of the things that President Trump did right off the get-go was restore U.S. leadership in wireless. During the Biden years, we fell drastically behind other countries when it came to making spectrum available," Carr told Fox News Digital . HOW THE US MESSED UP ITS NEW 5G ROLLOUT: ‘IT WASN’T OUR FINEST HOUR’ Indeed, the U.S. fell behind countries like China during the 5G rollout during the Biden era. But Carr said the passage of Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut authorized and directed the FCC to bring more airwaves into the commercial marketplace, in order to both increase speeds and drive down prices. "When most people pick up their smartphone, they usually don't think why it works or what it takes to make it faster or better. But the FCC is now poised to do exactly that by bringing more spectrum, usually invisible airwaves that your phone actually operates on, and push more of that into the commercial market, so we get more competition, faster speeds, more downward pressure on prices," Carr said. FCC REVIEW OF SPORTS BROADCASTING RULES DRAWS THOUSANDS OF COMMENTS AMID STREAMING BACKLASH, CHAIRMAN SAYS The order adopts competitive bidding procedures, allowing wireless providers to bid on wireless licenses. "That's expected to raise many billions of dollars for the U.S. Treasury, anywhere between $30 to $60 billion or more," Carr said. "So, it's going to be a good win for consumers in that they get faster speeds and better price services," he continued. "It's also a win for the government as well, because we're raising significant revenues by doing that." Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz , R-Texas, also celebrated the move, saying it will "result in better coverage and faster speeds for consumers." FCC CHAIR HAS NO REGRETS OVER THE DRAMATIC JIMMY KIMMEL SAGA LAST YEAR The order reconfigures 160 megahertz of the Upper C-band in the contiguous United States for terrestrial wireless flexible use in 3.98–4.14 GHz, with a 20-megahertz guard band at 4.14– 4.16 GHz, according to the FCC. It also folds the Lower C-band and Upper C-band into a single 3.7 GHz Service from 3.7–4.14 GHz in the contiguous United States for terrestrial wireless flexible use and largely harmonizes the licensing, operating and technical rules across the entire band. The FCC said this promotes "a successful co-existence environment with adjacent band radio altimeters through the adoption of specific technical measures and a carefully coordinated timeline for the introduction of terrestrial wireless operations in the Upper C-band starting in December 2030 that aligns with forthcoming radio altimeter retrofit requirements to be issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)."

title: WATCH: Tlaib tells Mamdani to 'call me' for help arresting Netanyahu as Democrats remain divided
content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s abandoned pledge to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu divided House Democrats, with some backing his proposal while others said the mayor lacked the legal authority to carry it out. "Arrest him," Rep. Rashida Tlaib , D-Mich., told Fox News Digital. "He’s a war criminal." Throughout Mamdani’s campaign, he repeatedly insisted that he would order the New York Police Department (NYPD) to enforce the warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) and arrest Netanyahu for his role in the war in Gaza. MAMDANI GOES BACK ON CAMPAIGN PROMISE, SAYS NYC CAN'T ARREST NETANYAHU But Mamdani finally acknowledged his inability to do so as the city lacks the "independent legal authority" to do so. On Tuesday night, he took to social media with a video calling on the federal government to execute the warrant by the ICC to arrest Netanyahu, also stating to be "equally clear" that the prime minister is "not welcome in New York City." "I think that whether or not he has the authority about it, I don’t really have an opinion on," Rep. Summer Lee, D-Penn., said. She continued, "But I do think that Netanyahu is a war criminal." "I wish that we had a country that didn’t excuse war criminals," Lee said. Tlaib also offered Mamdani help with the arrest as she wasn’t sure if he had the authority to complete the arrest. "I don’t know if it applies to citizen’s arrest," she said. "If he needs help, tell him to call me." CNN LEGAL ANALYST CALLS OUT 'UTTERLY RIDICULOUS' CLAIM BY MAMDANI ABOUT NETANYAHU ARREST Rep. Jerry Nadler , D-N.Y., was one of the few House Democrats that Fox News Digital spoke with who immediately shut down the idea that Mamdani would be able to pursue this arrest under any avenue explored by the city, arguing it would violate a treaty with the United Nations. He said, "There's a treaty under which the U.N. is lodged in the United States. Pursuit to that treaty, any diplomat can come to the U.N. and be immune from process." The U.N. Headquarters Agreement is a 1947 treaty between the United States and the United Nations that governs the legal status of the U.N. headquarters in New York and provides protections for foreign officials attending U.N. meetings. MAMDANI SAYS NYC IS EXPLORING WHETHER IT CAN ARREST NETANYAHU IF ISRAELI LEADER VISITS FOR UN GENERAL ASSEMBLY The U.S. is not a member of the ICC, nor is it a party to the Rome Statute, which requires member countries to arrest individuals wanted under ICC warrants. Mamdani’s call on the federal government to arrest Netanyahu comes after President Donald Trump posted to Truth Social on Monday that the prime minister "will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form." Secretary of State Marco Rubio also recently threatened to "dismantle" the ICC as he claims the court’s force of international law is overreaching its powers and "threatens every aspect of our political and legal system."

title: Mamdani dodges on ‘political theater’ of empty Netanyahu arrest threat, calls for US action and NYC protests
content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani declined Wednesday to say when he learned the city had no authority to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after repeatedly campaigning on a promise to detain the Israeli leader if he came to New York. Pressed over whether the now-abandoned arrest threat amounted to "political theater," Mamdani said his administration had reviewed the applicable laws and concluded that only the federal government could execute the International Criminal Court warrant. "It’s clear that the city does not have the authority to execute this warrant," Mamdani admitted at a New York City Hall news conference Wednesday, urging the federal government to act on the ICC warrant even though the U.S. is not a member of the ICC and does not recognize the court’s jurisdiction in the U.S. or over Israel, which is also not a member. With the Trump administration already fully rejecting his call to arrest Netanyahu for being a "war criminal," Mamdani called for New Yorkers to take to protest "if anyone feels a level of frustration or opposition." MAMDANI GOES BACK ON CAMPAIGN PROMISE, SAYS NYC CAN'T ARREST NETANYAHU "I believe that this is an arrest warrant that should be executed, and also that I would follow the laws that we had, and I would be respectful of those laws," he added. "And that is why I asked my administration to review of all applicable laws. And I believe, however, in that same finding, that the United States government does have the ability to both joining the International Criminal Court and executing that work, and that is something that I want to see happen." Short of that, Mamdani suggested that people protest when the Israeli leader visits for the United Nations General Assembly, potentially in September. "This is a city where, if anyone feels a level of frustration or opposition, protest is something that we will always respect," Mamdani told reporters. "I leave it to New Yorkers themselves to make that decision." The mayor was repeatedly asked why he did not resolve the legal question before taking office, given that experts had challenged the legality of his arrest pledge during the campaign. HAMAS, HEZBOLLAH FLAGS FLY AT ANTI-ISRAEL PROTEST MINUTES AFTER MAMDANI CONDEMNS TERROR PLOT AGAINST JEWS Mamdani would not provide a date for when his administration informed him that the city lacked the power to carry out the ICC warrant. "That’s a review that I asked them to do," he said. "They made it clear that this is not possible through applicable law." Mamdani said Palestinian New Yorkers disappointed that he cannot fulfill his arrest promise had reason to be frustrated, declaring that Netanyahu would no longer be welcomed by City Hall. "I understand it because we are talking about someone who has been charged with crimes against humanity , someone who has visited the city on many an occasion and who has been welcomed by previous mayors," Mamdani said. "I want to make it very clear that that welcome ends with me," he continued. "I will not be welcoming Benjamin Netanyahu or any other war criminals when they come to this city." NYC REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER SLAMS MAMDANI ANTISEMITISM OFFICE AS A ‘BLACK HOLE’ LACKING PUBLIC-FACING RESOURCES Mamdani also faced questions over criticism that his focus on Netanyahu created a one-sided account of the Israel-Hamas war . Asked directly whether he considered Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack to be genocide , Mamdani did not use that term. "I consider Oct. 7 to be a horrific war crime," he said. "I’ve considered it to be something that should be deeply opposed with every single fiber of our being." Mamdani said his approach was rooted in what he called the "universality of humanity," arguing that officials should not "pick and choose which crimes against humanity we oppose." The mayor also said he would support honoring ICC warrants against Hamas leaders as well as Netanyahu. "My interest in executing that warrant is not specific to Benjamin Netanyahu, but to anyone who they put a warrant towards for war crimes and crimes against humanity," Mamdani said. He accused Netanyahu of having "orchestrated this genocide" in Gaza and described the Israeli prime minister as a "war criminal." Israel has repeatedly rejected genocide allegations and condemned the ICC case as illegitimate. Mamdani said he remained committed to protecting Jewish New Yorkers, including those who disagree with his position. "My responsibility to them is to ensure that they are cherished, they are celebrated and they are safe in their city," he said, "and that never are they made to feel as if their opinions on any one issue is the precondition for that safety."

title: Nolan Wells independent autopsy doesn't point to foul play, former medical examiner says
content: Attorney Ben Crump revealed that the results of an independent autopsy into Nolan Wells' death are "inconclusive" as a former medical examiner said the findings aren't consistent with a "cover up" or any wrongdoing. Crump announced the independent autopsy's results on Wednesday at the NAACP National Convention in Chicago, stating that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head. He said Dr. Roger Mitchell , who performed the autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion "pending further investigation." The official autopsy hasn't yet been completed. "Why is this dark red here in the back of his head?" Crump said. "This pathologist cannot rule out if any intervening non-accidental factors contributed to or caused the death of Nolan Wells." When asked by Fox News Digital about the case, forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden said the head injury doesn't point to foul play. "So that could be from bumping into something in the water. There's a lot of debris in the water, for example. It depends how deep it is, but it's describing a really superficial impact that could have happened before death or after death," Baden said. SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "What he's describing is a minor injury that could be... totally innocent," Baden said. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Baden said Mitchell was "reaching for straws" in the independent autopsy report, adding that the findings are consistent with accounts from local law enforcement that his death was accidental and no foul play was involved. GOT A TIP? Wells, 18, initially disappeared July 4 after he went with friends on a boat trip to Horn Island, which is a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Officials and search crews searched for two days before a National Park Service ranger located his body on July 6 while on the island's northwestern tip. Officials haven't released a cause of death as officials continue to investigate .

title: 10-foot great white shark spotted swimming dangerously close to young people
content: A 10-foot great white shark was spotted swimming alarmingly close to a group of young swimmers along the Southern California coastline — with the children appearing completely unaware of the predator nearby. The encounter was captured on drone video by Carlos Gauna, a wildlife photographer known as the "Malibu Artist," who said it was one of the few times he felt genuinely uneasy while observing sharks. "I don't often get nervous, but this was one of those rare instances where I did," Gauna wrote on Instagram. "The young swimmers had no idea." SHARK SIGHTINGS TRIGGER BEACH ALARM AFTER SWIMMER IS BITTEN DURING SUMMER SPIKE The shark had a large boat propeller strike wound across its back and dorsal fin, Gauna said — which he believes may have affected its behavior. "My observations showed the shark to be rather active," he wrote, adding that he watched it breach twice in one day. "Because of the injury, I don't know if it's searching for easier prey or if it's more alert," Gauna also wrote. "Either way, this shark does approach humans at a higher frequency. At least by my observations." The wild video sparked hundreds of comments — with many viewers saying they would immediately leave the water if they noticed a drone hovering overhead. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "If I'm swimming and see a drone over me, I'm out of there," one user commented. Others said the footage showed that great white sharks often investigate people without attacking. "It just proves they aren't interested in us," one viewer wrote. "It went to see what the splashing was and turned away. It still had my heart racing, though." Several commenters also suggested that beachgoers should be alerted when sharks are spotted nearby, with some proposing warning lights or audible signals to help swimmers safely exit the water. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Fox News Digital previously reported that shark experts have urged beachgoers to stay alert this summer as sightings increased along several U.S. coastlines. Marine biologist Mike Heithaus of Florida International University told Fox News Digital that shark bites remain unusual, even during the busy summer beach season. "People should always be aware of local conditions and listen to lifeguards , but shark bites are very rare," he emphasized. He recommended that people avoid murky water, that they stay away from areas where large schools of fish are visible and that they avoid places where other people are actively fishing.

title: Florida coach brings laughs, no filter and Lane Kiffin comparison rebuttal to first SEC media days
content: TAMPA, FL- While Lane Kiffin was contemplating his move to LSU from Ole Miss , Jon Sumrall was making a different decision on his coaching future beyond Tulane. Sure, while they both were deciding whether to take a different job, the circumstances surrounding the moves were not on the same wavelength in terms of coaching in the SEC. The conversation surrounding the coaching carousel will be discussed for decades, most likely being taught in business ethics classes on college campuses in the future. Greg Sankey addresses SEC breakaway talk as Michigan tries to steal spotlight with AD Warde Manuel decision For Kiffin, he had to decide on whether taking the LSU job was worthy enough for him not coaching Ole Miss through the college football playoff. As for Jon Sumrall, he was making a decision on which opportunity in the SEC would be the better fit. Was it going to be Auburn, or Florida? Obviously, we know how that part turned out, with Sumrall now entering his first season as the Gators' head coach . Taking to the podium on Wednesday morning in Tampa, the conversation about whether both Kiffin and Summrall were dealing with the same type of dilemma was spurned by a question about his decision to leave Tulane. While Kiffin and Sumrall have discussed the situation numerous times since last December, there was one part of the process that the two coaches did not agree on. They were not the same situations, at all. "I'd say no two decisions are alike, right," Sumrall noted. "Lane and I are friends, and talked several times during the process in October and November about what it was looking like about how things were going to unfold. "Lane said 'you and I are going through the same thing' and I'm like, 'No Lane, we're not. If you leave, you're leaving an SEC school to go to an SEC school'. I was leaving Tulane . But, it was challenging to do it, but I wouldn’t have done it any other way. I wanted to make sure I left Tulane the right way. If any university told me I couldn't coach in the playoff game I don't think I would've taken the job just because I couldn't leave the team I had coached all year." No, he's not wrong, though I'm sure Kiffin will have a rebuttal on Thursday when he takes the podium as the LSU head coach . If the incident that transpired during the Florida head coach's news conference had taken place during a team meeting, the reporter whose phone started playing an interesting choice of music would have been kicked out of the room in Gainesville. Luckily, this hilarious moment took place during the third day of SEC news conferences, far away from the meeting rooms just up the road from Florida's campus. Kentucky football coach channels Curt Cignetti, delivers SEC Media Days quote everyone will remember While speaking on his decision to leave Tulane, it just so happened that a reporter was away from his computer, and could not make it in time during Sumrall's press conference to turn it off. This led to a funny exchange with the Gators head coach, while he was also poking fun at Lane Kiffin. "You would be kicked out of our team meeting, I swear," Sumrall said to the room. "Like you're lucky I'm not going throw this podium right now. That drives me crazy. I would say who is that, but I'm not going to embarrass anybody." There might not be a more authentic coach in the SEC, besides Pete Golding, then Jon Sumrall, as both of them make their conference debuts this season. Also, if you thought either coach was going to get through a press conference without cussing at least once, you most certainly lost that bet on Wednesday in Tampa. Georgia coach sounds off: If Congress won't act, SEC should just break away from NCAA and govern themselves While speaking about Golding, the Gators head coach had nothing but praise for the Ole Miss ball coach, while also making light of Tulane being destroyed by the Rebels twice last season with two-different head coaches. "Pete is going to be himself. He's not going to change," Sumrall mentioned about Pete Golding. "I have an appreciation for that. You have to be authentic. I think he's going to do a phenomenal job. Really do. Happy for his opportunity there. "Watching him, those teams to me...you know, we played them the first time at Tulane and they beat the sh*t out of us. We played them the second time, different head coach, still beat the sh*t out of us." I for one welcome the coaches who don't put a filter on their words. Give me an authentic coach, no matter the situation, and I'll show you a guy that will at least become a popular leader among fans. title: Iran War Day 145: Trump: U.S to Bomb Bridges and Power Plants if Iran’s Hormuz Attacks Continue
content: President Donald Trump on Wednesday again threatened to bomb Iran’s civilian infrastructure after the 11th consecutive night of American strikes on the Islamic Republic. In a Truth Social post Wednesday morning, Trump wrote that “any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz,” the U.S. “will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT.” CENTCOM claimed Tuesday night that its latest round of strikes targeted “Iranian military operations centers, maritime capabilities, aircraft hangars, drone storage facilities, and military logistics infrastructure.” Iran fired ballistic missiles and drones at Jordan , Bahrain , and Kuwait . Iranian media reported that U.S. strikes hit parts of Iran’s electricity grid and water supply facilities. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported that “strikes on power plants and transmission substations along the coast have knocked out cooling systems” and that residents of Khuzestan Province describe “rolling blackouts.” Iran’s central military headquarters warned Tuesday that any U.S. attack on the country’s nuclear facilities would be considered an expansion of the war across the region and would be met with a “powerful” response. The statement came after Trump’s threat to bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain “very heavily.” Shipping tracking data from Kpler shows that there were only nine verified transits of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, and 13 verified crossings on Monday. Verified transits through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also dropped Tuesday to 29 total, down 34 percent from the previous day. Yemen’s Houthis have declared a “maritime embargo” against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. Axios reported Wednesday, citing a White House official and an Israeli source, that the U.S. and Israel are discussing a potential Oval Office meeting between Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu next week. It would be Netanyahu’s seventh visit since Trump returned to office, which Axios notes is “more than any other world leader.” In a Wednesday press gaggle at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland before flying to Delaware’s Dover Air Force Base to attend the dignified transfer of fallen American soldiers, Trump downplayed opposition to the war reflected in most opinion polls . “Americans aren’t against the war,” he said.“Americans love to fight. All real Americans love the sting and clash of battle. They just don’t want high gas prices!” The price of oil continued to rise, with Brent Crude above $95 per barrel on Wednesday morning. Gas prices remained elevated, with AAA reporting the national average price of regular gas at $4.06. The post Iran War Day 145: Trump: U.S to Bomb Bridges and Power Plants if Iran’s Hormuz Attacks Continue appeared first on The American Conservative .

title: "No one cares": The DSA primary challenge House Democrats are happy to ignore
content: Don't expect a lot of public lamentations from House Democrats next month if Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.) loses to his Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-backed primary opponent. Why it matters: That would be a drastic deviation from r ecent DSA primary wins , which set off alarm bells among the Democratic establishment. In the telling of both progressive and moderate House Democrats, Thanedar's anomalous political profile and the makeup of his district will make it difficult to extrapolate from the results of his race. "It's somewhat of a unique circumstance," Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), a top ally of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios. Another House Democrat, granted anonymity to offer a blunter assessment of how members are viewing the race, told Axios: "No one cares." State of play: Thanedar will face off with state Rep. Donavan McKinney in an Aug. 4 primary that has been the toughest of his career. Thanedar is without the main advantage that helped him win his predominantly Black, Detroit-based seat in the last two cycles: A divided Democratic primary field of Black opponents. Progressives are also putting their backs into unseating Thanedar this cycle, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), DSA, Indivisible, the Working Families Party and Justice Democrats all endorsing McKinney. Thanedar, a wealthy businessman who largely self-funds his campaigns, is backed by AIPAC, House Democratic leadership and both the Congressional Progressive Caucus and center-left New Democrat Coalition. Between the lines: Unlike in New York , Colorado and elsewhere , House Democrats aren't looking at this race as a watershed fight between the DSA and Democratic establishment with national implications. "You're talking about Detroit," said Meeks, noting that the city "has a large African American population" but no Black members of Congress. Another senior House Democrat offered a similar assessment, telling Axios: "This [race] has so many nuances because of the cultural issues in Detroit ... I don't think it's indicative of anything larger." That's an assessment both ideological wings of the caucus also agree on: Said a senior Congressional Progressive Caucus member: "I really think it's about a very strong Black candidate representing a Black district and votes the current congressman's constituents are upset with." A top New Democrats member told Axios: "Of course DSA is going to claim victory — that has nothing to do with that district." What we're hearing: Thanedar's oddball political persona and r ogue efforts to impeach President Trump have made him something of an outcast figure in the caucus. "I don't think anybody would miss him at all," said a fifth House Democrat who spoke to Axios on the condition of anonymity. A sixth lawmaker fumed that Thanedar "f***ing screwed us" by defying pleas from both leadership and rank-and-file members not to pursue impeachment, with several others saying he is not a "team player." While Thanedar has forged some relationships, colleagues largely characterized him as reserved, isolated and eccentric. When asked about him, multiple House Democrats replied facetiously: "Who?" The other side: Thanedar told Axios he has "not put a huge emphasis" on endorsements from colleagues and "only recently approached members" but is "proud of the endorsements I have." He pointed to endorsements from more than a dozen colleagues including Jeffries and several other members of Democratic leadership, adding that "more members are expected to endorse us soon." The Detroit congressman also said he "did not run for Congress to be popular on the Hill," telling Axios his "main focus has been, and will continue to be with constituents in my district." "Any of my colleagues are more than welcome to walk around my district with me and see firsthand the love my constituents have for me, and the love I have for them," he added. Between the lines: Jeffries and his deputies endorsing Thanedar this week was in keeping with a leadership policy of supporting incumbents in all but the most extraordinary cases. A second senior House Democrat, asked about the endorsement, told Axios that leadership will generally stick by any member as long as they are "doing what they need to be doing and keeping their nose clean." The same principle applies to endorsements from ideological caucuses: "We support our incumbents," the top New Dems member told Axios. The bottom line: "No one is staying up at night worrying about him," said the first House Democrat who spoke to Axios anonymously.

title: Charlie Woods' shot at the U.S. Junior Amateur ruined by clueless golf fan's phone: 'Really, dude?'
content: At least he didn't confiscate the phone like Rory. Charlie Woods, the son of Tiger Woods, attempted to win the 2026 U.S. Junior Amateur ended on Wednesday during a 14-for-2 playoff at Saucon Valley Country Club. But a camera click on a fan's phone threw off Woods' concentration, causing him to chunk a shot out of the thick rough. According to Golf Channel , the incident took place on the first hole of the playoff which was to determine the final two match-play participants. "Really, dude?" Charlie, 17, responded after hitting his third shot on the Par 5 from the deep stuff. JORDAN SPIETH SAYS GAMBLING IS FUELING ROWDY GOLF CROWDS AND WANTS THE SPORT TO ADDRESS IT SOON Charlie was left with a 35-foot chip for birdie, but he finished with a bogey and his dream of winning the Junior Amateur was over after carding a +5 over two days. If there's good news from this situation, it's that the Charlie Woods' detractors didn't get another f-bomb to use against him like they got on Tuesday when Tiger took a page out of his playbook by dropping a massive f-bomb on the par-3 11th hole. "Oh, f–k you," Charlie responded to his tee shot. It's unclear what the problem was with the shot. He made par on the hole. SERGIO GARCIA DESTROYS HIS DRIVER IN FRUSTRATION AT THE MASTERS, RECEIVES CODE OF CONDUCT WARNING As for the phone going off, the golf community seems to be split on how this played out. "Golfers are so lame. Guys can hit 95mph cut fast balls with 50,000 people screaming. A little noise doesn't impact your ability to swing a stupid golf club at a ball that isn't moving," one Twitter analyst observed. There seems to be a deep belief that Tiger needs to drill Charlie on how to battle through such nonsense. "Tiger's Dad would have berated Tiger if he let a camera click affect him...He used to do everything possible to piss Tiger off during a round to get him to focus," another fan noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS It's not like Tiger hasn't tried to rattle his son for moments like he faced Wednesday. Remember, Earl Woods famously used to throw golf balls and coins at his son to throw off his concentration. Charlie has faced similar warfare. TIGER WOODS BREAKS MONTHS-LONG SILENCE WITH PATRIOTIC MEMORIAL DAY MESSAGE, SALUTE TO LATE FATHER However, after the way this Junior Amateur ended, Tiger needs to start snapping his iPhone camera in his son's backswing. It's back to the drawing board for the Woods' family.

title: Wisconsin woman's honeymoon ruined by diarrhea after she came down with Cyclosporiasis
content: We all have stuff that comes up in our lives that we file away in a keep-to-ourselves section of our brain. Having a horrible case of diarrhea that ruins your honeymoon isn't one of them. That's a story you not only tell everyone, it's one that you run out and make sure the news is aware of. Otherwise, you're faking it through answering the question "how was your honeymoon?" Nobody wants to put themselves in that situation. The moment you let it slip to one person that you had diarrhea so bad you ended up in the hospital, everyone is going to want to know about it. STOMACH BUGS SURGING AS DOCTORS SAY CERTAIN TRAVEL ESSENTIALS COULD SAVE YOUR TRIP Getting the news involved makes that far less awkward of a situation. Now, instead of your friends and family being the only ones who know that your marriage got off to a crappy start, the whole world can learn about it. It's some personal housekeeping mixed with a public service announcement. Newlywed Gretchen Pleuss is the hero most of us aren't brave enough to be. She caught Cyclosporiasis during her honeymoon at Yellowstone National Park and a couple of days into the camping trip was glued to the toilet with a bad case of the runs. "It was just like incessant diarrhea. It was watery and constant," she told 12 WISN . "I felt fine until we got out here, and a couple days into camping here, I started having symptoms." CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW Pleuss' symptoms included stomach pain that got so bad it landed her in the hospital. That's where doctors confirmed that she had the Cyclospora parasite. She wasn't about to let the incessant diarrhea keep her from trying to enjoy her honeymoon. Sure, it was ruined by constant trips to the bathroom and a visit to the hospital, but the couple was staying positive. "It's still our honeymoon, so we're making the best of it," Pleuss said. "Our vows said in sickness and in health, so we're just getting an early start on that." They're also getting an early start on having some stories to tell. For as long as they're married, they'll always remember their diarrhea-filled honeymoon, a marital test right out of the gate.

title: Memphis pizza shop says business is booming after refusing service to National Guard troops
content: A Memphis pizza restaurant that drew national attention after refusing to serve National Guard members says business is booming instead of busting, with supporters flocking to the restaurant in what some have dubbed a "buy-cott" after conservative activists called for a boycott. Miles Tamboli, owner of Tamboli's Pasta & Pizza, said he refused to serve the Guardsmen on July 11 because he opposes the federally led Memphis Safe Task Force, arguing the use of National Guard troops in local law enforcement has made the city less safe rather than more secure. The company faced severe backlash online after refusing service to four uniformed members of the Memphis Safe Task Force. Tamboli told Fox News Digital July 15, "I stand behind that decision completely." The Guardian reported Tuesday that the response locally has been supportive. MEMPHIS PIZZA JOINT SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER OWNER REFUSES TO SERVE NATIONAL GUARD TROOPS "The Italian 'junt' (in Memphis parlance) opened with a full house and had a line waiting by 5.30pm," The Guardian reported. "Waitstaff said the shop was never that crowded that early; extra crew was brought in to help. Business is up ‘a great amount,’ Tamboli said. The packed house on Friday was evidence." One customer, Sarah Jones, said, "While I do not blame the National Guard for being in Memphis since it was not their choice, I stand by businesses refusing service as a form of resistance and protest." Another customer, Carol Bigam, a retired FedEx worker, said, "If you have a business — a small family-owned business — that says, ‘You know what, I’m sorry, I can’t serve you, I just don’t believe you should be here,’ it really should be OK. Is he not allowed free speech? He was very professional about it. Give me a break, man." ICE RESUMES NATIONWIDE TRAFFIC STOPS UNDER NEW POLICY REQUIRING BODY CAMERAS Tamboli told Fox News Digital July 15 that he opposes the Memphis Safe Task Force, a federally led initiative established in September 2025 by President Donald Trump to stop violent crime in the city. The task force combines local police with agents from various federal agencies, the Tennessee National Guard and state troopers to enforce public safety laws. "What the Task Force has actually done is make this city harder to live in," Tamboli said. "Its own records show that the overwhelming majority of its arrests began with routine traffic stops, not violent crime. Families in this city are now afraid to drive to work, afraid to take their kids to school, afraid to be seen. Our own schools reported that fear drove children to stop showing up to class. "And this month, a 20-year-old Memphian named Tyrin Johnson was shot and killed by National Guard troops during a foot chase, with no body camera footage and no answers for his family," he continued. "None of that makes us safer. It makes us less safe, and it does the most damage to the people who were already struggling." BAKERY OWNER WHO WENT VIRAL WITH RESPONSE TO CRITICAL INFLUENCER SPEAKS OUT ON WHY SHE DEFENDED HER BUSINESS In a statement to Fox News Digital , Tamboli said, "Business the week after roughly doubled our normal volume. It was the busiest stretch we've had in this building, with a line out front before we opened most nights. I hear the real question in yours, whether this is a blip, and it isn't. The support hasn't slowed down, I expect it to last, and I'm running my business like the lasting increase it is. The records exist, and I stand behind every word of this, and I'm not going to turn my private sales reports into a public document." He said he does not believe conservative customers have stopped coming to his restaurant. "I see every message, every email and every phone call that reaches this place, and I have not heard from a single regular customer telling me they won't be back," Tamboli said. "Not one. I don't track anyone's politics and my register doesn't record it, and I serve every guest who walks through my door the way I always have. The one exception is the uniformed deployment, and that was the entire point. "Here is what I'd rather you spend your ink on. Four people are dead at the hands of this task force since it came to Memphis, in a city where violent crime had already fallen to a 25-year low before they arrived. One of them, Tyrin Johnson, was 20 years old. Another, Jonah Neal, was in the middle of a mental health crisis when a federal agent killed him, and I'd bet most of your readers have never heard his name. "If a president sent soldiers and federal agents into your town, and four of your neighbors ended up dead, you would not be asking a pizza owner about his Friday sales," Tamboli continued. "You would be asking why it happened, and you would be furious and you would be right to be. That is the outrage this deserves, and it is missing only because it is happening here and not somewhere the country is used to watching. "A small business owner using his First Amendment right to run his place by his own conscience is about as American as it gets," he added. "The people trying to punish that speech, the ones review-bombing me and the ones cheering the government on, are the ones who walked away from the Constitution they claim to love. You do not get to wave the flag and boo free speech in the same breath."

title: IndyCar teams come to terms on the series' first-ever charter sale, which shakes up the grid for 2027
content: The NTT IndyCar grid is going to look a little different in 2027 with news that the first sale of an IndyCar charter has been completed, and it will bring a new team to the grid. Albeit one that fans are very familiar with. On Wednesday, it was announced that Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing had agreed to sell one of its three charters to Drewy & Reinbold Racing, with the transaction subject to IndyCar approval. TRUMP TOUTS INDYCAR DRIVERS' 'SPECIAL' ABILITY AT FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX SHOWCASE, SEEMINGLY ENDING HOT DEBATE It's the first sale since the charter system was introduced in 2024, and it will see RLL dropping from a three-car operation down to a two-car operation, and DRR rejoining the egrid full-time with a single car. Dreyer & Reinbold last competed in IndyCar full-time back in 2012 and has become a regular fixture in the Indianapolis 500. They had two cars in this year's field, which were driven by Conor Daly and Jack Harvey. This news comes just weeks after the death of DRR founder and owner Dennis Reinbold on June 13. TRUMP TOUTS INDYCAR DRIVERS' 'SPECIAL' ABILITY AT FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX SHOWCASE, SEEMINGLY ENDING HOT DEBATE "I want to thank Bobby Rahal, Mike Lanigan, David Letterman and Jay Frye for the way they approached this from our very first conversation," DRR CEO Derek Reinbold said in a statement. "They treated this as a partnership between two organizations that want to see each other succeed, and this announcement today reflects that. The teams did not name any drivers or which of RLL's three cars' charters will head to DRR. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE RLL currently fields the No. 15 Honda driven by Graham Rahal, the No. 35 Honda driven by Louis Foster, and the No. 47 driven by rookie Mick Schumacher. According to FOX Sports' Bob Pockrass, both Rahal and Foster are under contract for next season, while Schumacher is not. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS That has led to speculation that Schumacher is the odd man out. He is, however, coming off a season-best finish at Nashville . After the race, he told Pockrass that he feels there's a high chance he will be on the grid in 2027. We'll see how it shakes out, because this has already been one of the crazier IndyCar silly seasons in recent memory, with even the likes of Christian Lundgaard — who has two wins on the year and his fifth in the standings — hunting for a new ride for 2027.

title: Phillies star JT Realmuto makes inexplicable base-running blunder to end the game, leaves manager dumbfounded
content: Every once in a while, a big leaguer looks like a little leaguer on the diamond. Unfortunately for the Philadelphia Phillies , star catcher J.T. Realmuto’s Little League-esque blunder ended the game. In the bottom of the ninth inning of the Phillies’ 2-1 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers on Tuesday at Citizens Bank Park, the Phillies had runners on second and third with one out. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM Justin Crawford, who pinch-ran for Alec Bohm, was on third base, while Realmuto was on second base. Right fielder Brandon Marsh was up against closer Tanner Scott. Marsh hit a weak ground ball to third base, and Crawford started to go home but stopped after a few steps. Interim Phillies manager Don Mattingly said postgame the contact play was on, which means Crawford was supposed to run home no matter what. However, Crawford said the contact play was on unless the ball was hit to third base. So Crawford, now caught between third base and home plate, got in a rundown. Realmuto ran to third base but inexplicably turned around to go back to second base when he saw Crawford run back to third base. ANGELS THIRD BASEMAN BRINGS BASKETBALL ONTO THE DIAMOND, TURNS SLICK DOUBLE PLAY WITH UNCONVENTIONAL MOVE Mookie Betts tagged Crawford out and then whirled and fired to second baseman Tommy Edman to nab Realmuto going back to second, completing a chaotic 5-2-6-4 double play to end the game. Phillies announcer John Kruk was in disbelief after seeing Realmuto run back toward second base. "Oh no, JT! Oh no," Kruk said. Realmuto said postgame it was a bad baserunning play. "Just a bad baserunning play, really," Realmuto told reporters postgame. "We were going on seeing it through there, and once (Crawford) gets in the rundown and I'm on third base, there’s no reason for me to go back to second. Just a lack of judgment. You can't make two outs on that play. I’ve just got to stay in scoring position." ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! "Just a lapse in judgment. I thought Crawford could get out of the rundown for some reason. The chances of that are so small, you just can't take that chance there of making two outs on one play." Realmuto said he should have played it through in his head before it happened and been more proactive in his preparation. Mattingly said he wasn’t sure what his star catcher was thinking. "I don’t know what JT was thinking there, honestly, because he got to third," Mattingly told reporters postgame. "With contact on," Mattingly said, "just hoping (Crawford) stays in (the rundown) long enough to get Marsh to second, and you end up in the same spot." "I’m not quite sure what he’s thinking. I don’t know if he thought that (Crawford) was going to get back or they were going to let him get back. It’s something we’ll talk about." SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS The baserunning blunder comes in the midst of a down season for Realmuto. The three-time All-Star catcher is hitting just .215 with seven home runs, which well below his career batting average of .268. The Phillies (56-46) will look to bounce back from the tough loss and take the third game of the three-game set against the Dodgers (64-38) on Wednesday at 6:40 p.m. ET. title: Mamdani sets internet ablaze with video explaining cave on plan to arrest Netanyahu: 'What a joke'
content: New York City socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani was widely mocked by conservatives on social media Tuesday after announcing that one of his campaign platforms, arresting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, isn’t a tool he has at his disposal. In a video post on X that was viewed over 36 million times, Mamdani called Netanyahu a "war criminal" while conceding that New York City could not enforce the International Criminal Court's warrant for the Israeli leader’s arrest on its own despite the mayor saying he had looked at exploring avenues to do so. Mamdani has often said on the campaign trail and as mayor that he wanted to arrest Netanyahu over what the mayor calls a "genocide" in Gaza. While Mamdani’s post was well received by many on the political left, conservatives on social media quickly mocked the mayor over the situation while taking issue with his determination to enforce the ICC warrant, which the United States government does not recognize. MAMDANI’S ‘DERANGED’ ISRAEL TAKE RESURFACES AS HE TARGETS NETANYAHU "Trying to find where Mamdani called for the arrest of the Hamas terrorists who plotted the October 7th attacks," Arkansas Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders posted on X . "Disgusting and Disgraceful." "This may be the most horrific package of lies against the State of Israel ever promoted by a government official," former U.S. Ambassador to Israel David M. Friedman posted on X . "Even Hamas does not lie to this extent! It is despicable and entirely unbecoming a mayor of New York City. To those who voted for this Jew-hater, shame on you." "Zohran Mamdani calling Benjamin Netanyahu a war criminal is utterly ridiculous," Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., posted on X . "The same crowd that rushes to condemn Israel never has much to say about the terrorists who started the war, massacred civilians, raped women, kidnapped children, and still hide behind their own people. Mamdani wants the headline that comes from attacking Netanyahu, not the consistency that comes with confronting Hamas." MAMDANI CALLS OUT DEMOCRATIC PARTY AS 'WELL-PAID CONSULTANTS AND BIG MONEY INTERESTS' "The mayor of New York is just straight up promoting antisemitic blood libel courtesy of Hamas propaganda from an official government social media account tonight," New York City Republican Councilwoman Vickie Paladino posted on X. "As I was saying… he doesn’t have the authority," US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz posted on X . "More political theater." "I had a dead homeless body in front of my apartment, but the mayor’s focused on playing Model UN," Sam Raus, David Boaz Resident Writing Fellow at Young Voices, posted on X . "What a joke." "Zohran Mamdani admitted tonight that he has zero legal right to arrest Netanyahu," political commentator Eyal Yakoby posted on X. "Like everything that he does, it was all just an act for clicks on social media." Although Mamdani acknowledged he could not arrest Netanyahu as mayor, he called on the federal government to execute an International Criminal Court's arrest warrant if the Israeli leader visits New York . "I want to be equally clear: Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large," he said. In a press conference on Wednesday, Mamdani answered more questions about his position and said, "my interest in executing that warrant is not specific to Benjamin Netanyahu, but to anyone who they put a warrant towards for war crimes and crimes against humanity." Mamdani was asked at one point what he would say to those who are disappointed that Netanyahu can't be arrested by authorities in New York City. "I'm simply saying that this is a city where, if anyone feels a level of frustration or opposition, protest is something that we will always respect," Mamdani said. "I leave it to New Yorkers themselves to make that decision and when it comes to Palestinian New Yorkers who are disappointed, I understand it because we are talking about someone who has been charged with crimes against humanity, someone who has visited this city on many an occasion and who has be welcomed by previous mayor and I want to make it very clear that that welcome ends with me." Mamdani continued. "I will not be welcoming Benjamin Netanyahu or any other war criminals when they come to this city, and I do believe that our federal government should join the International Criminal Court and ensure that there is accountability when it comes to crimes against humanity." Fox News Digital’s Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report .
